2005.description: Abdullah bin Moawiyah bin Abdullah bin Ja'afar bin Abi Talib raised his claim to Caliphate on the basis of his relationship to house of Ali. (He (Ibn Moawiyah) was a great grandson of Ja'afar (brother of Ali the fourth Pious Caliph)). He commenced his revolt at Kufah at the close of 127 AH, but was immediately defeated and ejected eastwards. He occupied Jibal, Isfahan, Ray, Hamadan and Darabgerd. Anonymous coins like this one were issued briefly at mints within this region. (Upon his defeat by Umayyad forces he was revealed to be a homosexual by some of his commanders taken captive and propagation of this fact rapidly diminished his support.) By early 129 AH he had lost his bid for caliphate and was on the run, being closely pursued by Ummayads. He was ultimately taken prisoner by governor of Herat, where he had gone to seek refuge and which was then under control of Abu Muslim Khurasani's partisans (Leader of another group of Shi'ite rebels in Khurasan and other eastern provinces). Upon his claim to legitimacy for Caliphate the governor of Shi'ite rebels at Herat strongly objected to his patronymic "Ibn Moawiyah". He was executed at Herat in 129 AH by orders of Abu Muslim Khurasani.
2005.keywords: Abdullah bin Moawiyah - Alawid rebel 127-129 AH

Published by kind permission of the auctioning company DR. BUSSO PEUS NACHF.
Auction #378-379 (28-30 April 2004)

1414. ARGHUN 683-690 H./1284-1291 AD. Gold dinar 688? H., Hamadhan. Four lines of Uighur inscription above sun bird and mint name in Arabic, the Ilkhan's name to the right downwards. Rev. Creed, mint and date around. Probably unpublished. 3.70 g. Extremely rare GOLD Very fine. 
 This is the first time that a pictorial coin type of the Ilkhans is found in gold. It may be assumed that dies for the silver coinage were used for this issue in Hamadan which was unusual in the 13th century but common after Ghazan Mahmud's reforms at the end of the century. Of the final digit of the date only the letter mim is visible. As the sunbird type was introduced only in 687 H. there can be no doubt about the correct reconstruction to thaman / eight.

5024.description: The Umayyad Caliphate was the first Islamic dynasty and remained in power until the rise of the Abbasids in AH 132/749 AD. Most Umayyad coins are anonymous and are assigned to reign by date. This coin is one of the most interesting dirhams from the Umayyad era that I have handled. It is a contemporary imitation of an Umayyad dirham from the Maghreb region of North Africa. The coin is 26 mm in size, and the pattern from which the imitation was copied is from the reign of Caliph al-Walid I (AH 86-96/705-715 AD). It has the mint name Wasit, the most common Umayyad mint located in present-day Iraq, and is dated AH 93. The coin grades a nice VF. The genuine type is Album 128, although the imitation has no Album number. The style of the coin is very neat, but it does not look like the calligraphic style of Wasit. The attribution as a contemporary North African imitation came from Steve Album.

5027.description: The Samanids began as governors under the Abbasids and later rose to be a major independent dynasty ruling from their capital at Bukhara in present-day Uzbekistan in the 9th-11th Centuries. This is an attractive and interesting gold Dinar, 23.5 mm in size and weighing 4.15 grams, from the reign of Nasr II bin Ahmad (AH 301-331/ 914-943 AD). It was struck at Nishapur ( in present-day northeastern Iran), and it is dated AH 331, the last year of Nasr’s reign. This example is especially interesting because it has the initials of the die engraver at 1:00 on the obverse margin. I have been unable to read the name, The Samanid empire was on the Silk Road, a major trade route between east and west, and Samanid coins were major trade coins along this route. Hoards of Samanid dinars and dirhams have been found as far away as Scandinavia. This coin grades a nice XF, above average for coins of this dynasty and reign, with a slightly clipped flan that does not affect any of the legends. Album 1449.

Dābūyid Ispahbads of Tabaristan. Kayān(?). Æ Pashiz (17mm, 3.55 g, 11h). Dated PYE 108 (AH 142 / AD 759). Crowned Sasanian-style bust right; “xvarrah” in Pahlavi behind, the name(?) “Kayān”(?) in Pahlavi before; open circle border / Fire altar; “108” in Pahlavi to left, “Tabaristān” in Pahlavi to right; circle border. Ex Morton & Eden LTD: Auk 54, lot 71.
REVOLUTIONARY PERIOD, UNCERTAIN KHARIJITE ISSUER 
Dirham, 'Tanbarak' 133h 
OBVERSE: In outer margin, divided by four annulets: 
la - hukm - illa - lillah 
WEIGHT: 2.57g 
REFERENCES: Klat 198; Wurtzel 29 (mint-name read as Tanbuk), Album 207.2. 
CONDITION: Mount removed and also pierced, otherwise good fine and very rare 

NOTE: Both the correct reading and the location of this enigmatic mint remain uncertain. Two previous suggestions, Bayburd and 'Tanbuk', can now be discounted. Bayburd, a city in Turkey to the north-east of Erzincan, was apparently under Byzantine control when this coin was struck, while the penultimate letter of the mint-name is clearly 'r' or 'z' rather than 'u', which disposes of the mythical 'Tanbuk'. 'Tanbarak', the version adopted here, is not directly attested but does fit the Kufic version of the mint-name. Apparently there were several fortresses in Iran called 'Tabarak' and it has been suggested that 'Tanbarak' may somehow be related to this name. 
(The coin was uploaded 2012-04-01)

7947.description:
Published by kind permission of the auctioning company DR. BUSSO PEUS NACHF.
Auction #380-381 (3-5 November 2004)

1138. ANTI-BUYID REBELLION? Fractionl dinar 410 H., Sîrâf. Lillah / lâ ilâha illâ allâh continued with a 180° turning: allâh / muhammad rasûl, mint/date-formula in marginal legend. Rv. Lillâh / muhammad / rasûl / allâh / 'alî walî allâh, margin Qur. 9:33. Unpublished? 0.68 g.GOLD Extremely rare
 The historical background of this coin remains obscure. No specific information about the history of Sîrâf in 410 H. Seems available. The lack of a Buyid name is sufficient evidence for the asumption that the town was not under Buyid control, when the coin was struck. In 409 H. The Buyid Sultân ad-dawla had dismissed his vizier of the Banû Fasânjus family, a native of Sîrâf. But is is not evident that this could have provoked an uprising. The reference to 'Ali point to a Shiite group that acknowledged neither the 'Abbasid nor the Fatimid caliphate. A similar attitude can be found on contemporary anonymous coins of the 'Alids of Hawsam in Gilan.The coin type with the counterstanding parts of the creed can be found in the Fatimid coinage at a slightly later date (Halab dirhams about 440 H.). If the Fatimids borrowed it from this Sîrâf issue then this could hint to some kind of relation.The small size and the light weight may result from a festal use for scattering (nithâr), but the tiny silver coin of Sultan ad-dawla from Sâbûr (Treadwell p. 33 SbND) may also indicate the existence of monetary experiments at this period in Fârs that are insufficiently understood.
estimation: 1000,-- EUR

7948.description:
Published by kind permission of the auctioning company DR. BUSSO PEUS NACHF.
Auction #380-381 (3-5 November 2004)

1079. Dirham 328 H., Hajar, with the name of the heir Abû l-Fadl. Lâ ilâha illâ /llâh wahdah /lâ sharîka lah / abû l-fadl ibn / amîr al-mu'minîn, inner marginal legend mint/date formula, outer marginal legend Qur. IX 33. Rev. In circle lillâh / muhammad / rasûl /allâh / ar-râdî billâh . marginal legend Qur. XXX ¾ Unpublished. 3.52 g. Unique and important Very fine
 This dirham looks like an ordinary 'Abbasid coin but the mint system once organized and centralized by al-Mu'tadid conceals the fragmented state of the caliphate under ar-Râdî. Only the establishment of new mints indicates occasionally historical changes. In this case the mint of Hajar in Eastern Arabia was one of the centres of the Qamatids, an Ismâ'îlî group who at this stage were one party involved in the civil war raging between a number of warlords like Bajkam, general of the Turkish guards, Ibn Râ'iq and the Barîdîs. The Beduin Qarmatids under the leadership of Abû Tâhir Sulaymân al-Hajarî were religiously regarded as sectarians by the 'Abbasid. As Isma'ilis they had a natural proximity to the Fatimid rivals of the 'Abbasids. But their own point of view is explained by this coin as reconcilable with Orthodox Islam. The Qarâmita were ruled by a committee, the Sâdat ar-ru'asâ, which remained anonymous on most of the coins struck under their rule. The military leadership was subordinate to the Sâda. Therefore it is not surprising to find no reference to the actual rulers of Hajar on this coin.Abû Tâhir Sulaymân had followed this brother already in 301 H. In 311 H. His troops sacked al-Basra, the following year al-Kufa. A strong attack on Iraq in 315 H. Lead to the permanent acquisition of the stronghold of ar-Rahba in the Jazîra. Their most famous raid followed in 317 H., when the Hajar. A following intervention of the Fatimid caliph al-Mahdî to restore the sanctuary seems to have lead to an alienation of the Qarmatids from their fellow Ismâ'îîis, although they did in fact return the stone and much of the booty. The caliphate of ar-Râdî and an embassy of his to Abû Tâhir in 322 lead to a treaty which confirmed he possessions of the Qarmatids. In 325 H. Abû Tâhir had come to al-Kûfa but retreated to his home. Apparently it was on the basis of this treaty that the present coin was struck..The style of die cutting leaves little doubt that the dies were in fact produced at the central die cutting workshop, probably in Baghdad. The name Hajar is found spelled with either form of ha as initial letter in contemporary sources. Ibn al-Athîr, Beirut ed., vol. 8 p. 334 even gives examples of both versions on the same page.
estimation: 6000,-- EUR

7949.description:

7950.description:
994. UMAYYADS. 'ABD AL-MALIK IBN MARWÂN 65-86 H./685-705 AD. Dirham 78 H., Jayy. Still unpublished outside auction catalogues (Peus Nachf. Auctions 369; lot 1469 and 378; lot 1215, the latter identical with this coin). 2.80 g. Second known specimen and of highest importance Corroded marginal area with chips, otherwise extremely fine
 The question why the successful post reform dirham type was designed in the East and not in Damascus lead to an interesting controversy in the Islamic Coins Group. This resulted in some clarifications of the role of al-Hajjâj, who had to carry out the Iranian part of the reform. Furthermore it may be of importance that al-Hajjâj's right hand in Jibâl, Qabîsa ibn Abân, had already taken part in experimenting with the coinagein the mints under his control, primarily Jayy, in the immediately preceding years. He was probably still in office at the end of 78 H. And may have been faster than his superior, which would explain why no post reform dirham of 78 H. Could be found so far.

7955.description:
988. ANONYMOUS SYRIAN COINAGE UNDER 'ABD AL-MALIK. Drachm 72 H., Dimashq. Arabic muhammad / rasûl allâh downwards to the right of Sasanian type bust, the conventional Pahlavi benediction formula khurra afzut behind the bust, in second marginal quadrant bismillâh. Rev. Conventional Sasanian type with fire altar and attendants and in Arabic to right dimashq, to left date thantayn wa sab'in, three circles around and crescents with stars to the four sides and an extra outer circle around. 3.80 g. Of the highest rarity an historical importance. 
The evolution of drachm types in Damascus in 72 H. can be outlined fairly well. This variety must have been the initial attempt to introduce a silver coinage in thenewly established (?) Damascus mint and thus marks the start of 'Abd al-Malik's monetary reforms. The type with the prophet's name in front of the Sasanian bust was soon given up in favour of the type with the Pahlavi name Khusro and the same short religious inscriptions in the margin (SICA 278). As a thir stage th extra reverse circle was given up and the unchanged religious legend was arranged around the lower half of the obv. margin (M.S. Jazzar, An Arab-Sassanian Dirham of Dimashq year 72, as-Sikka 2.3). This leads to th extended religious legend struck both in 72 and 73 H. (see next coin). There may have been religious reservations against a close association of the Sasanian bust with the prophet's name. An interesting parallel was published recently by A. Shams Eshragh (ONS Newsletter 178 Winter 2004 p. 45): a drachm struck in Garm Kirman 70 H. with a Pahlavi version of the phrase muhammad rasûl allâh in front of the bust on an otherwise anonymous type, perhaps attributible to Mus'ab ibn az-Zubayr and certainly to a non-Umayyad authority. That coin gives another hint to the dependance of 'Abd al-Malik's reform ideas on previous developments in the Zubayrid coinage, to which the socalled Foroughi drachm is another testimony as an epigraphic Pahlavi precurser to the post reform dirhams. 
Very fine

7956.description:
989. ANONYMOUS SYRIAN COINAGE UNDER 'ABD AL-MALIK. Drachm 73 H., Dimashq. As above but with the name of the Sasanian shahânshâh Khusro in Pahlavi to the right of the bust, in the marginal quadrants Arabic clockwise bismi llah - lâ ilâha illâ llâh wa - hdah muhammad ra - sûl allâh, Rev. Conventional Sasanian fire altar type with mint and date in Arabic, to the left dimashq, to right thalath wa sab'in, to both sides of the upper crescent in the margin a dot. Gaube 15; Shams Eshrag 137 identical with SICA 1 279 Var. 3.69 g. Of great rarity and considerable historical importance.
 A good example of the modified type of early drachm coinage from Damascus with the disassociation of the religious inscriptions from the image. This image could be taken as the mark of garantee for a long established denomination and therefore it was only logical to include again the name of Khusro II, whose silver coins had been accepted in every day use in the Muslim community from the days of the prophet. This coin type and the name was obviously not understood as propagating the rule and the religion of a pre-Islamic power. At the same time the inclusion of the name could help to conceal the slightly reduced standard of the new coins, which has been commented on in auction 378 no. 1203 also with reference to the present coin.

1015. HISHAM 105-125 H./724-743 AD. Dirham 107 H., Marw, probably imitative. Unpublished. 2.59 g. Probably unique Centers weak, otherwise very fine
 The date of this dirham does not fit well into the general development of mint distribution policies of the period. The style is irregular with a few minor mistakes (in rev. Margin the letter lam in rasûl is missing and the phrase ends with half a word al-mushr...) and the weight is clearly too low. According to the weight it might belong to the group of North African imitations that was produced at the end of the Umayyad period, using various Eastern mint names and early dates (cf. Klat 167 and 677). The reverse reproduces the early variety with the third line commencing wa lam yûlad, which has not been found so far on North African imitations. So the origin remains mysterious, although there can be no doubt as to the early medieval date of the coin.
 
estimation: 1000,-- EUR

8084.description:
Ex Morton & Eden LTD: Auk 54, lot 27.
ARAB-ARMENIAN, MUHAMMAD B. MARWAN 
Drachm, 'ŠY' ('Shiraz', but possibly struck in Harran), circa 75-78h 
OBVERSE: Bust of Khusraw II to right with name hwsrwy in Pahlawi before, Arabic Muhammad in margin. Roman letter T replaces star in crescent at 6 o'clock. 
REVERSE: Fire-altar with attendants; blundered date-legend to left, mint-letter š to right. Uncertain letters or symbols replace stars to either side of flames. Roman letter M replaces star in crescent at 3 o'clock. 
WEIGHT: 3.20g 
REFERENCE: cf SCC 17 (same obverse die) 
CONDITION: About extremely fine 

NOTE: This and #8108 are clearly linked to the group of drachms struck in Armenia or Azerbaijan during the 70s Hijri, but they are remarkable for the Roman or Greek letters which replace stars in crescents on one or both sides. It is difficult to tell whether the letter on the reverse of the second piece is 'M' or capital Greek S, but by analogy with the letter 'T' on the obverse which has the crescent placed above the letter, 'M' is perhaps more likely. 
Further research is needed before the meaning and significance of these letters can be fully assessed but some preliminary observations can be made. Firstly, replacing stars in this way seems to be unparalleled not only among Arab-Armenian coins but in the wider series of Arab-Sasanian drachms. Secondly, these letters are the only symbols on these coins which are not in the Pahlawi or Arabic scripts. Thirdly, Armenia was one of very few places in the Islamic world where the Greek or Roman alphabets would have been in common use, unlike the former Sasanian lands where the Persian language and Pahlawi script had dominated before the coming of Islam. This all suggests that the use of these letters was a local and possibly short-lived phenomenon reflecting circumstances peculiar to the region. It is difficult to see that they could have had a religious significance, and if they refer to an individual it is unlikely to have been anyone with a Muslim name, although a moneyer or die-engraver at this early period might well not have been a Muslim. Alternatively they might be part of a system for labelling and controlling the dies themselves. In either case, these letters give evidence that Arabic was not yet fully established as an administrative language in the region and that Greek-speaking workmen or officials were still involved with minting in Armenia at the time. 
(The coin was uploaded 2012-03-31)

Small donative silver coins were periodically struck from the time of al-Mutawakkil (AH232-247) until al-Muttaqi (AH329-333), with some later issues of the Buwayhids and Saffarids. The fractional issues normally bear very short marginal text, or as is the case on this piece, no marginal legends at all. Almost all were struck without mint and date. Most are found either worn, holed or ex-mount.

9768.description:
Ex Stephen Album Auction 12: 57

ARAB-BYZANTINE: 'Abd al-Malik, 685-705, AE fals (3.08g), Sinjar, A-3530var, uncertain mint reading, could be blundered form of Qinnasrin, pleasing Very Fine. 

This extremely rare type is likely from the previously unpublished mint of Sinjar in Syria, for the following reasons:
1. The town of Sinjar lay along the medieval highway from Halab (Aleppo) to Homs, close to the border between the Jund of Qinnasrin (Aleppo, Halab in Arabic) and the Jund of Homs (Hims). The star to the right of the circle-on-steps is standard only at the mint of Hims but is found occasionally on fulus of Halab, in the Jund of Qinnasrin.
2. The scholar Rene Dussaud reported in 1927 that there is archeological evidence that Sinjar was an active town in the early Islamic period.
3. This specimen was found at Sinjar.
4. Extremely rare, only 3 specimens confirmed to exist, this lot specimen, one the Ashmolean Museum (SICA-1:686), and a piece of poorer quality in a private collection in England. The consignor believes that a 4th specimen may exist, also found at or near Sinjar.
(The coin was uploaded 2011-12-29.)

Ex The New York Sale XXVIII: lot 1214
Estimate: 600 USD
ISLAMIC. Abbasid Pretender , Anonymous, al-‘Abbas b. al-Ma’mun(?). Dirham, without mint name, 22x(2?)h. AR 4.30 g. Rev. field: al-‘adl-lillah. Very rare. unrecorded in major references.
(The coin was uploaded 2011-11-26.)

What is interesting about this remarkable coin is that it is a donative coin, as shown by the absence of a mint name and by its weight, which is that of a mithqal, not a dirham. It must be assigned to 221-23--if the first letter of the numeral seems to be an alif, it would be 221 or 222.

So, although it is anonymous, it was probably minted on the direct order of al-`Abbas. Presumably none of his sub-governors would have the authority to do such a thing.
One correction: the word above the reverse is al-`adl, not adil. The meaning of top and bottom is "justice belongs to God."
This is the same coin as ICA 17, 313.

14191.description:
ARAB-BYZANTINE. Imitating Heraclius. Circa 685-710 AD. AV Solidus (4.36 gm). North African mint. NON EST dS NIS IPSE SOL C ET NON ABEH, crowned facing busts, as of Heraclius and his son Heraclius Constantine / dEd NCIPIA SOAC...NOANC:SC, transformed cross (globe) on steps. Apparently unpublished as a full solidus with the globe cross, but cf. Walker, Arab-Byzantine, pg. 55, HSA.1 for legends on a similar solidus, and pg. 55, 144 for the type as a semissis. Near EF, possibly the only known example. (See color enlargement on plate 19.) ($10,000) 
Ex Dreesmann Collection, Part I (Spink, 13 April 2000), lot 1846; purchased from J. Schulman, 14 November 1967. 
 
The Arab-Byzantine coinage of Syria-Palestine and North Africa illuminate a true watershed in world history, when the classical, Christianized western society was supplanted by a completely novel culture, that of the Muslim Arabs. For all its importance, the coinage is still notable for the glaring gaps in our knowledge. Most notably, our understanding of the chronology is still subject to great debate. For the gold dinars struck at Damascus we have a firm date for the start of the standing Caliph type, the earleist dated AH 74 (693/4 AD). For North Africa we have a bronze fals with transformed cross on steps, similar to the above solidus, dated AH 80 (699/700 AD). Many scholars have assumed the undated gold types to be near contemporaries to the dated issues, i.e. circa 700 AD. However, the earliest reference to an Arab gold coinage is related to events of 688 AD, when Justinian II and 'Abd al-Malik signed a truce agreement, ceding territory to the Arabs upon a weekly payment of 1000 solidi, one horse and one slave. Theophanes the Confessor asserts that a few years later Justinian objected to al-Malik's new coinage, and his supposed response was the introduction of the Christ portrait solidus. This would suggest that Islamic style gold coinage was introduced before 692 AD. However, scholars have asserted that Theophanes' account is an anachronism, actually refering to the introduction of orthodox Islamic dinars at the end of the 7th century AD. The debate revolves around when the Arabs would have developed the required infrastructure and economy to support a distinctive gold coinage. At a very early period they had the services of officials trained in Byzantine administration (hence the Islamic kalima translated into Latin), and by the 670's had established an empire stretching from North Africa to India. By the beginning of the reign of Justinian II all the elements would have been in place to support a new gold currency. All that is needed is a secure date derived from archaeological discoveries.

16179.description:
Ex Morton & Eden, Auction of 25 May 2005, Lot 577:
Abbasid, al-Radi, dinar, al-Kur 325h, obv., with ornate lam-alifs and fleuron in lower field, rev., with highly ornamental rendering of Muhammad, with fleuron on ha, three links of cable pattern between second mim and dal, the top of which is also ornamented, 3.40g, of crude style but evenly struck, about very fine and of the highest rarity, apparently unrecorded as an Abbasid mint E2500-3000 With the exception of this specimen, the mint-name of al-Kur is known only from a unique Umayyad dirham dated 88h (Klat 536) Klat (p. 17) lists three possible locations for it: '1. A river in Fars. 2. A river which separates Irminiya from Arran. 3. A district to the east of Al-Mawsil.' This piece not only confirms the reading of the mint-name but also sheds further light on the possible location of the mint. On both this specimen and the Umayyad coin, the calligraphy points to a mint in the North (the Umayyad dirham in particular has a very distinctive form of Kufic associated with the North and West). The date of the dirham also supports this view, as it was struck at a time when minting of silver was confined to Damascus, Wasit and a few short-lived mints in the Caucasus. On balance, it seems more likely that the mint-name refers to the northern river Kur rather than the district near al-Mawsil, while a location in the southern Iranian province of Fars can surely be ruled out. The river Kur formed the northern boundary of the province of Arran. Al-Kur was presumably an Arabic form of the earlier Greek name Cyrus, just as the Araxes to the south became Arabicized as al-Ras. From its source in the mountains west of Tiflis in Georgia, the Kur flowed past Tiflis, Shamkur, Barda`a and Barzanj into the Caspian Sea. Le Strange notes that the fish caught in the river were salted and exported; these salt fish were called Sarmahi. It is not uncommon for mediaeval Islamic mints to take the name of a province or geographical feature rather than to indicate the town where the coins themselves were struck. In this case it is not possible to identify the mint-town with certainty, although some tentative suggestions can be made. The town was, presumably, located on or near the river itself. This excludes a number of places including Baylakan, the chief town of Arran after the decline of Barda`a, which was nearer to the Aras than the Kur. Of the major settlements on or near the river, Tiflis and Barda`a can probably be eliminated, since they appear in their own right as mint-names for both the Umayyad and Abbasid period. Two other locations are more likely. One is Shamkur, which retains the kur element of the river's name, and which lay on the main road from Barda`a to Tiflis. This town was apparently known as al-Mutawakkiliya following its rebuilding by the caliph al-Mutawakkil in 240h (Le Strange, p. 179), but this name may have fallen into disuse by the time this coin was struck. Another is the town of Barzanj, a significant commercial centre sited at a crossing of the river on the road leading east from Barda`a. If this was the location of the mint, the name al-Kur might have been used to avoid confusion with the similarly-spelled town of Barzand, situated roughly one hundred miles to the south in the district of Mukan.

Christianity made early inroads into Persia, the Caucasus, and central Asia. The kingdoms of Armenia and Georgia converted in the 4th century, and both Christians and Jews were generally welcome in the lands controlled by the Persians. Groups engaged in trade travelled along the Silk Road as far as China and set up their own communities along the way. It can be assumed that this fascinating small copper coin was struck by an isolated eastern Christian bishopric in the aftermath of the Sasanian collapse in the face of Arab invaders. An important document of early Christian history.

ARAB-BYZANTINE. Tiberias (?) mint. Circa 680-690 AD. Æ Fals (18mm, 2.88 gm, 6h). Byzantine style standing emperor, holding long cross and globus cruciger; bird on standard to left / Large M; monogram above, ANO XTII flanking, « -/DAM below. Walker 7; SICA 560. EF, glossy green patina. Rare in this state of preservation. 
This type is traditionally attributed to Damascus based on the exergual legend. However the obverse motif of the bird perched on a T-shaped standard appears later on signed Umayyad issues of Tiberias (cf. SNAT 302). It is likely that these are issues of Tiberias copying the types of the main Umayyad mint at Damascus.

18199.description:
umm Ja`far Zubaydah bt. abú al-Fadl b. al-Mansúr, 762-831/ 145-216 AH
Ex Baldwin's Auctions Limited, Islamic Coin Auction 10, July 20, 2005: 
 ISLAMIC COINS, Gold and Silver Coinage of the World of Islam, ABBASID Zubayda, wife of al-Rashid, Dirham, Jazirat al-Raghistan 183h, rev field: amr al-sayyida / umm wali al-'ahd / abaqa allah / ghaya ('by command of the lady, mother of the heir apparent, may God preserve her, so be it!'), 2.91g. This dirham was struck by order of Zubayda bint Abi Ja'far b. al-Mansur, wife of Harun al-Rashid and mother of Muhammad al-Amin, at a palace compound probably on an island near Baghdad. It is, in all likelihood, the earliest coin struck by authority of a woman in the history of Islam. The issuance of this coin is directly connected to the matter of the caliphal succession. In 175h al-Rashid designated his second, but purely Hashimid, son Muhammad al-Amin as his heir. In the succeeding years it became clear that his eldest, but slave-born son, 'Abdallah al-Ma'mun, was better suited to rule than his younger brother. In 183h al-Rashid therefore designated al-Ma'mun as the second heir to the throne. While Zubayda had been a kindly stepmother to al-Ma'mun, her over-arching ambition was to see that al-Amin, the only heir to her body, became caliph after al-Rashid's death. One can easily imagine that this imperious and powerful lady determined to make her position unmistakably clear by issuing this coin as a sharp reminder that she was the mother of the heir. About extremely fine, unrecorded and of the highest rarity. Estimate - 5000-6000 
REMARK: Cf. ## 35 and 12380
18199.keywords: 183 h Jazírat ar-Rághistán umm Ja`far Zubaydah bt abú al-Fadl

18229.description:
ISLAMIC COINS, Gold and Silver Coinage of the World of Islam, ABBASID al-Amin, double-weight Dirham, al-Khayzuraniya 194h, obv margin: muhammad rasul allah arsalahu ..... (to kullihi), rev field: li'l- khalifa / al-amin abaqa / allah, mint and date formula in margin, 5. 85g (Lowick 1087; cf Ilisch, Munsterische Numismatische Zeitung XIV 3 1994, no. 1). 

Traces of mounting at top otherwise good very fine, extremely rare, the second known example.

al-Khayzuran was the wife of al-Mahdi, the mother of al-Hadi and al-Rashid, and the grandmother of Muhammad al-Amin, the caliph for whom this commemorative dirham was struck; she was also the maternal aunt of Zubayda, the mother of al-Amin. The mintname al- Khayzuraniya probably refers to a palace complex built by and named after her, probably near Baghdad. This location was the site of an important ceremony which took place in 194h, when this special coin was distributed to those in attendance. The ceremony may have marked the moment when al-Amin modified the wording of the khutba to add the name of his own son al-Natiq bi'l-Haqq Musa after that of al-Ma'mun, the official heir to the caliphate. This act widened the rift between the two brothers and set the stage for the full break which took place early in 195h, when al-Amin set aside the Makkan settlement and made al-Natiq Musa his direct heir. It may be noted that the interjection abaqa allah, which appears on both this coin and on lot 73, is found nowhere else in the coinage record; perhaps it was a favourite one in Zubayda's household.

18339.description:
Ex Baldwin's Islamic Coin Auction 10:
ISLAMIC COINS, Gold and Silver Coinage of the World of Islam, UMAYYAD REVOLUTIONARY, Anonymous, Dirham, Gharshistan 137h, struck by partisans of Abu Muslim, 2.57g (Klat Codrington, NC 1894 p88, & NC 1902 p269; recorded in Zambaur as 'unique'). This is the only recorded issue from the mint of Gharshistan, a district in northwestern Afghanistan around the headwaters of the Murghab river in the Harat division of Khurasan. It is of the style of an Umayyad dirham, and is similar to the post-revolutionary issues struck at Marw in 131h, 132h, and 133h; Wurtzel attributes these issues to Abu Muslim, who ruled over Khurasan from 130h until his death in late 137h Although the success of the Abbasid revolt can largely be attributed to the leadership of Abu Muslim, his elimination was seen by al-Mansur as a necessary step in order to establish full political and military power in the east. Against his better judgement, Abu Muslim allowed himself to be lured to the court of al-Mansur who then promptly had him put to death. Perhaps this coinage was struck to pay troops loyal to Abu Muslim while he was on his way to meet his doom. Cleaned, very fine and of the highest rarity. Estimate - 6000-8000

ISLAMIC COINS, Gold and Silver Coinage of the World of Islam, UMAYYAD temp 'Abd al-Malik, Dirham, Dasht Maysan 79h, 3.89g (Klat 318 [same dies]). Maysan was an area on the eastern banks of the Tigris in southern Iraq; it was divided into several districts, one of which was known as Dasht Maysan. Dasht or desht is a Persian word meaning wilderness, steppe, or desert, while dast is an Arabic word meaning seat of honour or office. It is difficult to determine whether the unpointed mint name refers to the plain of Maysan or the capital of Maysan, because the early historians and geographers themselves were not consistent in their writings. For further discussion on the subject see EI2, Maysan, vol VI, pp 918-921. Good very fine and very rare. Estimate - 1,400-1,600

18438.description:
Ex Islamic Coin Auction 10:
ISLAMIC COINS, Gold and Silver Coinage of the World of Islam, ABBASID al-Mu'tadid, Dirham, al-Shash 281h, single marginal legend on obv, 2 96g. The year 281h saw a transition from Abbasid to Samanid coinage at the mints of al-Shash and Samarqand. As part of this transition a new design of dirham, with a single marginal legend on the obverse, was introduced. The fact that this type is only recorded for this year suggests that it was not well-received; production soon reverted to traditional-style dirhams. The new-style dirhams normally have the name of the Samanid ruler Isma'il b. Ahmad on the reverse, so the present coin is presumably a mule of a new-style obverse and an older, purely Abbasid, reverse. Very fine and very rare. Estimate - 100-120

Coins of 281h were previously believed to be the last purely Abbasid issues from the mint of al-Shash; the present coin is believed to be the first known example dated 282h. As with the previous lot, this coin is likely to be a mule, struck with an older, purely Abbasid, reverse die. Centres weak, very fine, very rare. Estimate - 150-200

18444.description:
Ex Islamic Coin Auction 10:
ISLAMIC COINS, Gold and Silver Coinage of the World of Islam, FATIMID al-Mu'izz (341-365h), Dinar, Filastin 359h, 4.12g (Miles 28; BN 98). This coin is a witness to the Fatimid 'drive to the east' which began the previous year, 358h/969. The Fatimid advance was prompted by the challenge posed by the Qarmatids who occupied Syria and Palestine in the same year. After he founded Cairo, the Fatimid general, Jawhar, sent one of his commanders to invade Palestine and Syria. In 359h Fatimid forces took Ramla, Tabariya and laid siege to Damascus. It was during this campaign that this dinar was struck in Ramla, the chief town of Filastin. For the next ten years the Fatimids contested the province with the Qarmatids, with each side striking coins whenever they held one of these areas. These form a valuable historical record of the ebb and flow of the conflict. Graffiti in centre of obverse, otherwise extremely fine, very rare. Estimate - 3000-4000

One of the major independent dynasties, ruling from their capital at Bukhara from 864-1005 (and earlier as governors under the Abbasid Caliphate). 23385.description:
Image source: http://www.angelfire.com/ny3/vaguebrit/longlist2.html#DABIL
DABÎL

The capital of Umayyad Armenia, also called Dwîn, Dabîl lay to the north of the Aras river to the south of the modern capital of Yerevan. Nearby, on the southern bank of the river, stood Mount Ararat.

The site of Dwîn has been occupied since the third or fourth millenium B.C., and was possibly fortified under the Arsacid rulers of Armenia. Following the defeat of the Arsacids by the Sasanians Dwîn was established as the capital of Persian Armenia in 428 A.D., and Sasanian coins were struck there soon afterwards. Dwîn was frequently embroiled in warfare between Byzantium and the Sasanians, and in 623 A.D. it was taken and sacked by Heraclius. The Muslims captured the city seventeen years later in AH 19, and it remained the seat of the caliph’s governor until AH 173.

Walker states that (pace Codrington) this is not the same place as Ardabîl.

Dirhams are recorded for the following dates: 84-87

24147.description:
CNG, Inc.:
Sale: Triton IX, Lot: 1804. Closing Date: Jan 09, 2006. EARLY ISLAMIC, Umayyads. temp. Sulaiman. 715-717 AD. AV Solidus/Dinar (4.16 gm, 1h). Dated AH 98 (716/7 AD). al-Andalus mint (Spain). 
EARLY ISLAMIC, Umayyads. temp. Sulaiman. 715-717 AD. AV Solidus/Dinar (4.16 gm, 1h). Dated AH 98 (716/7 AD). Al-Andalus mint (Spain). FERITOS SOLI IN SPAN ANXCI (Feritos Solidus in Spania Anno XCI); eight-pointed star / "Muhammad rasul Allah" in two lines across fields, "bismillah struck was this dinar in al-Andalus in the year eight and ninety" in outer margin. Balaguer 49; Miles, Umayyads, 1e; Gomez 7; cf. Walker, Arab-Byzantine, p. 79, C.17; Kazan -; cf. Album 122. Good VF, good strike on large flan. A very rare and early bilingual dinar of Muslim Spain. ($7500)
A similar example appeared in Sotheby's 12 July 1993, lot 171 where it realized £19,800.
The eight-rayed star on the obverse of this coin is similar to an earlier all-Latin dinar struck in Spain and dated by its reverse indictional formula to 712/713 AD, and fractional dinars struck in North Africa with a Byzantine-style reverse (see lot 1797 above). Unlike these other examples, however, the blundered Christian legend on the obverse is accompanied by a well-executed Arabic legend on the reverse, and shows a Muslim celator unfamiliar with the Latin. The presence of the first two types show that as the Umayyads were expanding their control over North Africa and into the Iberian Peninsula during the first two decades of the eighth century AD, the Umayyads struck coins on these earlier models to facilitate their control over the local Christian population. Like a similar one struck in Africa at the same time, our bilingual coin, struck for only two years and with a specifically Islamic reverse, suggests that such facilitation was was becoming unnecessary as the Umayyads were quickly beginning to assert their control of their newly-won territories and replacing such issues with standard Umayyad types. 
Estimate $7500
Sold for $15000

Ex CNG, Inc.:
Sale: Triton IX, Lot: 1787. Closing Date: Jan 09, 2006. EARLY ISLAMIC, Arab-Byzantine. In the style of Justin II. After 641 AD. Æ Follis (6.57 g, 7h). Scythopolis (Beth Shan) mint. 
EARLY ISLAMIC, Arab-Byzantine. In the style of Justin II. After 641 AD. Æ Follis (6.57 g, 7h). Scythopolis (Beth Shan) mint. CKVQO POLHC, Justin II and Sophia enthroned facing, holding cruciform sceptres; cross between / Large M; cross above, ANNO (N's retrograde) U/II across field, A/NIKO below. APBQ A1; Walker, Arab-Byzantine 1; SICA 1 594; Album 98; Berman, Islamic 16. VF, desert patina with contrasting sandy encrustation. Sharp example of the type. ($750)

The important town of Scythopolis-Beth Shan struck an extensive series of imitative folles in the period between the collapse of Byzantine authority in Syria-Palestine in the 640s AD and the introduction of pure Islamic types around 695 AD. This is the earliest issue, having purely Byzantine types with Greek legends. It is not known why Scythopolis and other cities like Gerash struck heavy folles imitating coins of Justin II while other mints were striking small copies of the contemporary coins of Constans II. It has been noted that several large hoards of regular folles of Justin II have been found in the Jordan River valley area. This was an important frontier for the empire, and was well supplied with legionary outposts and fortified settlements which would have required quantities of coinage. 
Estimate $750

27860.description:
Die axis is 140 degree.

Metal composition of the coin is: Ag 93.4498, Cu 2.8386, Sb 2.4630, Bi 0.5028, Pb 0.4691, Sum 99.7233 %, XRF data. So it is AК ~934 because its surface is enriched with silver due weathering. Point microprobe analyses gave: Ag 91.16/97.41, Cu 8.84/2.21, Sb 0.0/0.38, Sum 99.25/99.96 %.
So we can state sufficient admixture of antimony in the alloy. It seems to me, that it is the reason of specific features of the coin surface - abundant sinuous microcrackes of stretching. Obviously addition of antimony made metall too tough.

Point microprobe analyses of the coin surface are: Ag 86.91/88.31, Cu 1.17/0.91, Zn 0.0/0.0, Cd 4.14/3.38, Sn 3.66/4.25, Sb 3.22/2.56, Bi 0.0/0.0, Pb 0.0/0.0, Hg 0.77/0.58, Sum 99.87/99.99 % what are correspond to AR 870 and AR883. 

Here we can see enrichment of the surface with silver and minor constituents (Cd, Sn, Sb) and loss of copper during weatering of the alloy in oxidizing conditions.
It is very possibly, that metal of such composition was too fragile for strucking (we see abundant small radial sinuous cracks). So apparently this coin was strucked with addition of some mercury as plastificator. And for strucking amalgam was used. Now main part of the mercury was dessipated with minor relicts on outer surface of the coin. Also it is possible, that mercury was specially eliminated by heating after strucking.
Now metal of the coin is porous and fragile. Some part of these pores apparently were formed after mercury elimination, other part during weathering and copper dissolution.

So we can observe here evidences of using complex special technology of producing such coins, which were unusually large for this times and this region. From other side we can see, that unexpected and rare metals present in the alloy in significant concentrations. It can indicate presence of unusual types of ore deposits in this region.

31259.description:
Mamluk, probably al-Salih Salah al Din Hajji II, first reign (783-784 H/ 1381-3 AD), Balog 516.

Unfortunately my Balog is a photocopy, and the illustration is not too clear, but everything I see on Levon's coin seems to fit with Balog's illustration. Also, the inscription on the reverse fits well with Hajji II's gold as illustrated in Balog and in the BMC (Vol. IV, 616), though the arrangement of the kalima on the obverse differs.

The 2nd and 3rd lines on obverse appear to read "al-sultan al-malik salah al-dunya wa" similar to Balog 516 (Hajji II, 1st reign), including the two ornaments (like twin lam-alif ribbons) above "salah". Balog gives the top line as "al-ashraf" but your coin reads differently. However, Balog states that dirhams of this reign are "very scarce and difficult to read". The legends he gives are "reconstructed" and he suggests there is but one variety for this reign, minted at Halab. There are also other Mamluk rulers named "Salah al-Din", so I would say Hajji II is likely but not 100% certain.

Yes, probably it belongs to Hajji first reign issued at Halab, Cf. Balog 516

32451.description: ARAB-BYZANTINE, Anonymous, early imitation of a Solidus of Heraclius and Heraclius Constantine, obv facing busts of the emperor on left and his son on right, pellets in place of crosses atop crowns, rev capital I on three steps, K in right field, VICTORIA AUGY around, officina I, CONOB below, 4.42g (Miles, 'The Earliest Arab Gold Coinage', ANS Museum Notes 13, pp. 207-209, 2-3 var [no. 2 was sold in Spink-Taisei Zurich Auction 18, 18 February 1986, lot 85]; cf Sear, Byzantine Coins, 745 [prototype]). Crude, very fine with spade scuff on reverse, unpublished and of the highest rarity. The I on steps reverse is invariably found on the early Islamic coinage of North Africa in both gold and copper. The cataloguer suggests that this variety of early Arab solidus may have been the first type of non Byzantine coinage struck in North Africa.
32451.keywords: Early Arab/Umayyad AV solidus/dínár 7th cent /1st AH

32452.description: Umayyad, Copper Token, issued by al-Hajjaj b. Yusuf to the value of six mithqals, obv: bism allah a / mr al-amir al-hajja / j bin yusuf / bi'l-wafa hadha / mizan sitta, rev two rows of three dots, waf across centre, 2.38g (unrecorded but see Walker for a coin weight in the British Museum with similar obverse legends but reverse bism allah / 'adl between the two lines of three dots, weight 25.14g). Virtually extremely fine and of the highest rarity. This remarkable piece forms part of the currency reform introduced by 'Abd al-Malik b. Marwan and al-Hajjaj b. Yusuf in the middle of the 70s h. The British Museum specimen appears to be an actual coin weight for six mithqals, the six dots on the reverse being placed there for the benefit of the illiterate. This piece, however, is a token to be exchanged for a measure of six, whether of mithqals or dirhams is unclear, but certainly well known to the original holders. It appears likely that these pieces were used in conjunction with one another, the British Museum weight to receive metal from the public and the token to be given to a recipient to redeem for coin at an issuing office. The inscriptions bear this out. On the obverse both read, "In the name of God, the Amir al-Hajjaj bin Yusuf ordered honesty this is the measure of six". The reverse of the weight reads, "in the name of God, just ( weight) and the reverse of the token, "redemption' or "payment in full " The token was engraved by hand, as only a small number would have been needed to facilitate the transactions of the mint in receiving old and issuing new coin to the public.
32452.keywords: Umayyad AE in value of 6 units issued by al-Hajjáj b Yúsuf

There are mint Tabriz (?) or Siirt (?) or Shahr (?) (by Lutz Ilish) on coins, but by Steve Album opinion it's "rare type, local imitations issued in Erzerum area".

At first these coins are very heavy for Anatolia. Of course they are in the name of Abu Sa'id. I saw this kind of coins before and the mint is inscribed certainly as Tabriz. And their carats are not normal. They use silver less than other coins of the period of Abu Sa'id. This type coins are rarely. But I don't think that they minted at Erzerum. 35125.description:
Ex. Dr.Busso Peus Nachf
Auction 378-379. 
1304. SAMANIDS AHMAD IBN ISMA'IL 295-301 H./907-914 AD. Dinar 300 H., ash-Shash, of elaborate style with double crossed lam-alifs. cf. Kazan 969 for a dinar 304 H. of the same style, this date probably unpublished. 3.62 g. GOLD Very fine
 The monetary history of the Samanids is still full of mysteries One is the extreme scarcity of gold coins minted in as-Shash (with anexception at the end of the Tahirid governorship in the 250s H), where at that period the World's most important mines for silver were operated.It is however well established that the ore from the area contains both silver and gold and in fact present day mining in the area is gold mining. There cannot be any doubt that also during the Samanid period substantial quantities of gold were produced there, but unlike the silver they were not turned into coins. The present dinar adds a little bit of evidence to this problem. The dies were probably cut in Samarqand as they differ considerably from the style of contemporary ash-Shash dies and also the spelling of the mint name without a long letter alif shows a peculiar unfamiliarity. The coin may well have been struck in Samarqand with metal from ash-Shash.
Schätzung (estimation): 4500,-- EUR Zuschlag (result): 0,-- EUR

35432.description:
Ex CNG, Inc.: Sale: 73: 1089. 
ARAB-SASANIAN, Bishapur. al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf. 691-714. Æ 18mm (0.60 g, 7h). Struck after 699. Crowned facing Sasanian style bust; “hc’cywsp’n” in blundered Pahlavi / Horse advancing right. Gyselen Type 62. VF, brown patina. 
Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf was an important administrator during the Umayyad Caliphate. Appointed Governor of Iraq in 691, he replaced the administrative language of the area from Pahlavi to Arabic during his governorship. Renowned for the apparent severity of his rule and his crushing of a local Khwarij uprising, he was appointed in 699 as governor of of several districts in Persia with the goal of suppressing rebellions in those areas. Included in his control was the important Sasanian city of Bishapur, at which time this coin was struck

36380.description:
ARAB-BYZANTINE, Abasis in Egypt mint? Circa 640-675. Æ 12 Nummi (17mm, 6.71 g). Crowned and cuirassed facing bust, holding palm; star in right field / I B with M between; ABLZ. Fustat 29. VF, red-brown patina, some encrustation. 
This type copies the Alexandrian 12 nummi of Heraclius, continued into the transitional period between the ouster of the Byzantines and the imposition of full Muslim Arabic rule. The tentative identification of the mint as Abasis is an attempt to reconcile the corrupted ALEZ mintmark. Abasis does not appear as a place name in the authoritative gazetteers of ancient Egypt, although there is an Avaris in the Delta, the ancient Hyksos capital. A mint at Abila in the Dekapolis has also been suggested; coins of this type having been found in the region of the province of Palestine. See Gorny & Mosch 153 (11 October 2006), lot 4910 for a similar piece with an estimate of 400 euros (which remained unsold).

Ex Stephen Album rare coins: Sale 10: Lot 343
UMAYYAD: Anonymous, ca. 705-715, AE fals (2.98g), Qaysariya, ND, A-A184, W-—. SNAT-199, Bone-1, superb strike, no weakness whatsoever, RRR, from an American collection. 
The interpretation of the mint name has been questioned, as the spelling is peculiar for the Arabic name of Qaysariya (Ceasarea), closer to Qaythara, which might have been a local pronunciation of the city name during the Umayyad period. Most scholars, including Bone, Ilisch and myself, are convinced that Qaysariya is the likely location of this mint. The coins are stylistically very similar to contemporary fulus of Bayt Jibrin, Ludd, and Saffuriya, especially Saffuriya, which also bears the mint name at the top of the reverse. Thus a location at Qaysariya is geographically sensible. Note that the final letter of wahdahu has been omitted. Qaysariya, aka Qaythara, is the rarest of the Palestinian mints for the post-reform Umayyad copper coinage.
(The coin was uploaded 2011-05-02.)

36952.description:
Ex Stephen Album rare coins: Sale 10: Lot 236
ARAB-BYZANTINE: Standing Caliph, ca. 690-698, AE fals (3.08g), Ayla, A-3545A, 6-point star above cursive m on reverse, crescent below, RRR, from an American collection. 
There has been a long debate over whether the mint name on this coin refers to Ayla, now Eilat at the southern edge of Israel, together with Aqaba directly across the border in Jordan, or is simply an engraver's typo for Iliya (Aelia Capitolina), then the current name for Jerusalem. Surprisingly, the form Ayla appears on both these pre-reform Arab-Byzantine coins and the post-reform fulus. In both cases, the style is identical to the regular issues of Iliya, except for the 8-point star above the cursive m on the pre-reform issues. One may argue that the identical style and calligraphy suggest a single mint, where ayla was merely a typo. Contrarily, one can argue that the stylistic similarity occurred because the dies were produced by the same engravers, or even that the coins were struck at a single location, then distributed to the named cities. In the early Islamic period, an important copper smelting factory was located at or near Ayla, which would suggest some sort of commercial relationship between the two locations. At present, the dilemma remains unresolved, but current opinion seems to favor the separation of Iliya and Ayla as two separate locations, irrespective of where the dies or the coins were produced.
(The coin was uploaded 2011-05-02.)

Third dinar, al-Andalus 102h, 1.44g (Miles, The Coinage of the Umayyads of Spain, 2c; Walker HSA.12 = Miles, RIC 65, same dies; Ties. 497), very fine and extremely rare. 
This is the earliest year that post-Reform gold coins were issued in Muslim Spain, replacing the earlier bilingual Arab-Latin coinage. Full dinars, half-dinars and third-dinars are all known dated 102h, but while small numbers of dinars were struck intermittently thereafter, the issue of halves and thirds seems to have been confined to this year.

37159.description: Samanid, Isma'il b. Nuh (390-395h), dinar, Naysabur 391h, obv., al-malik al-Muntasir, rev., al-Qadir billah / Isma'il bin Nuh, 3.43g, small scratch on reverse, otherwise very fine to good very fine and extremely rare, apparently unpublished. Samanid rule in Central Asia was finally brought to an end by the Qarakhanids, who captured Bukhara. Isma'il b. Nuh was a younger brother of the last Samanid ruler, 'Abd al-Malik b. Nuh, who managed to escape the Qarakhanids. Raising an army in Khwarezm, he managed to drive them from both Bukhara and Samarqand, but the approach of the main Qarakhanid army forced him to flee once again to Khurasan. Here again he was initially successful and took control of Naysabur in 391h (as this coin attests), but was again obliged to abandon his conquests in the face of superior forces. This time, he returned to Transoxiana where he obtained help from the Oghuz Turks, but although he continued to inflict defeats on the Qarakhanids he was unable to strike a decisive blow. In 394h he was comprehensively beaten by the Qarakhanids and abandoned by the Oghuz. Isma'il and a few followers escaped to Khurasan, and after one last failed attempt to raise support in Transoxiana he took refuge near Marw, where he was killed by a tribal leader in 395h.

ISLAMIC, Umayyad Caliphate. temp. al-Walid I ibn 'Abd al-Malik, AH 86-96 / AD 705-715. Pashiz (Bronze, 20 mm, 0.46 g, 4 h), anonymous Arab-Sasanian type, derived from the 'Anahita' issue of Khosrau II, without mint name, circa AH 81-101 = AD 700-720. Draped bust resembling Khosrau II facing, wearing elaborate and winged mural crown; to left, AFZUT GDH ('may his kingship increase' in Pahlawi); to right, HWSRWD ('Khosrau' in Pahlawi). Rev. Draped bust of Anahita wearing a flame nimbus around the head; to left, illegible legend; to right, HWSRWD ('Khosrau' in Pahlawi). Album N41. Gyselen 65. SICA I, -. In exceptional condition for this very difficult issue. Minor edge crack and with light deposits, otherwise, good very fine.

R. Gyselen questions the widely accepted identification of the bust on the reverse as a representation of the goddess Anahita. In his opinion, it is much more likely 'a male divinity with a strong relationship to the Holy Zoroastrian Fire' (Gyselen, Arab-Sasanian, p. 32).

38176.description:
The coin came from a small hoard of Samanid dinars struck on Afganistan territory, some Khorezmshakh and Gurid dinars.

Metal composition of the coin is: Au 85.0823, Ag 7.3145, Cu 1.4330, Sn 2.1383, Sb 1.4922, Fe 0.6215, Cl 0.3202, J 1.4972, Zn,As,Bi,Pb,Co,Ni and Br all are under detection and error limits, Sum 99.8992 %, XRF data. Such composition corresponds to AV852 fineness. Tin and antimony contents are high and they are strange impurities for gold alloys, but typical regional (Afganistan-Kashmir-Nepal) components of silver alloys, which I'd check before. 

Halogenides contents are connected with microfilms of AgCl and AgJ covering surface of the coin. Green copper nodular mineral is malachite. Redish-brown films are composed by cuprite.

Dies axis 345.

Condition of the coin isn't too high, but its calligraphy is very nice. Is it possible to read inscriptions? What may to means these out circle inscriptions on obverse at 14-00 & 19-00 and on reverse at 23-00? Thanks in advance!

Ex Dr. Busso Peus Nachf.: Auction 378: 1209
SISTAN REGIONAL COINAGE 'AWN, UNKNOWN LATE UMAYYAD GOVERNOR, EARLY 2ND CENTURY H. Drachm with barbarized date, SK for Sijistan. In obv. margin: allah wali 'awn / bismi llah / rabbi. Rev. unusual additional Arabic legend in 3rd quarter of margin: darb al-muharraq. Shams Eshraq 138. 3.95 g. Very rare Very fine.
A-76.2.
The term muharraq means litterally "burnt" and with regard to silver refined. On coins it reappears on fine silver dirhams of the Hamdanids and 'Uqaylids, when it was necessary to qualify and discern the good silver from previously and elsewhere struck alloyed silver. The regional drachm coinage of Sistan underwent a noticeable but unresearched process of debasement, which may have started around the period when the otherwise unknown 'Awn was governor.
Sold for 975 euro

39356.description:
The coin was cut by knife or something similar, very specific traces are well visible on its edge.

Dies angle 140.

Metal composition in two obverse points (worned letters/ more weathered plane place) is: Au 80.2180/86.9537, Ag 15.0824/10.1186, Cu 1.6786/1.4898, Zn 0.0000/0.3345, Sn 2.0840/0.000, As 0.2279/0.0000, Fe 0.4890/0.8703, Ni 0.1223/0.1668, Sb,Bi,Pb,Hg,Pt,Co all are under error and detection limits, Sum 99.9022/99.9337 %, XRF data. Such compositions are correspond to AV803 and AV870 fineness. So we can to appreciate grade of weathering, which the coin had undergo. It is interesting and unusual, that leaching of silver was predominate over copper one. It is very probably, that iron contents in both cases are connected with surface pollution. Arsenic admixture is typical for gold from Egypt.

40196.description:
Image Property of Nassif

Dear members;
This coin as the Arab-sassanian coin already posted and a third one [will be posted later],have been acquired recently by me from old collector.For the arab-Sassanian i haven't received any answer from S.Album yet..
Here the description of this COIN:
Obv:
-center:Kalima
-marginal legend:"in the name of God this Dirham was strucked at Wassit in the year seventy five"[khams wa sab'in] sic
PS;Already the arabic calligraphy is unusual with word "wahdahou" and "shairka"
Rev:
-center:"Surath 112 "th of Holy Kuran.
-marginal legend:"the prophetic mission" ,also with very curious calligraphy,without errors but with unusual way to write some words.[Arabic is my maternal language...].
The mystery is that Wassit started strucking coins in 84-85 H.So where this dirham was strucked?by whom?and why??this fatidic and unrecorded date??75H??.....
S.Album answered:"looks to me like a contemporary North African imitation,circa AH100-150"
I am not convinced at all by this response,for multiple reasons:calligraphy is very different from north african coins,the weight also:2,7 g,and the shape.Other major reason is that Umayyad ruler in spain :Abdel Rahman I[138-172 H] issued completely different coins and he didn't need to do imitation because of his own regular issue...
My opinion is that Dirham is among the first islamic dirham prototype and because of the unusual calligraphy it was probably left for more regular issue[look also at the trasversal signs on Obv.]
This coin was seen by several experts and look really ancient and authentic with a lot of weak signs on both side.
Please help to identify this major coin.
Thanks in advance.
nassif

Can anyone make sense of this?

43123.description:
ISLAMIC, Anatolia & al-Jazira (Post-Seljuk). Zangids (Sinjar) Qutb al-Din Muhammad. AH 594-616 / AD 1197-1219. Æ Dirhem (29mm, 16.46 gm). Sinjar mint. Dated AH 600 (AD 1203/4). Helmeted bust of Athena Promachos right, the names and titles of Muhammad and reference to his heir around/ Five line legend with the name and titles of the Abbasid Caliph and the Ayyubid sultan; tamgha below, mint and date around. S/S 82.1 (same dies as the “exceptional style” piece illustrated on p. 104). VF, brown patina. 

Wayne G. Sayles has presented a remarkable hypothesis linking this type with one of the most important artistic achievements of the classical world. The bronze and ivory monumental statue of Athena Promachos, created around 460 BC by Pheidias of Athens, became one of the most admired art works of the ancient world. Except for an abortive effort by Caligula to remove it to Rome, it was a protected treasure of Athens for 750 years, until Constantine removed it to his new capital of Constantinople in 330 AD. The statue faded from view for nearly 900 years, until 1203, when Constantinople was beseiged by the forces of the Fourth Crusade. A superstitious populace, believing the mammoth statue was somehow beckoning the invaders, pulled it down and destroyed it. This wanton act of destruction would have appalled the few scholars still conversant with classical history, quite a number of whom were attached to the courts of Islamic rulers. Muhammud, educated by such scholars, would have struck this coin to mark the loss of an important work of art at the hands of what the Turks would regard as barbaric westerners.

Obv. male head in profile r., surrounded by kufic legend citing ruler’s name and title. 
Rev. Five lines kufic legend citing names of Ayyubid ruler Al-Kamil, caliph and Artuq Arslan; date on rim: year 620.

From my point of view, the male portrait on obverse belong to Constantine I (Great) rather than to Tiberius or Claudius. Compare with portrait on Roman AE2 of Antioch mint issued by Constantine I. It seems to me, that he was more known and popular person in this region in XIII century as founder of Constantinople/Byzantium/Stambul, then any Roman ruler of I century.

48618.description:
al-Amin (193-198h), Silver Dirham, al-Muhammadiya 197h, in the names of al-Amin and his mother Zubayda, wife of Harun al-Rashid, rev: al-sayyida / muhammad rasul allah / mimma amira bihi al-khalifa / muhammad amir al-mu'minin / umm al-khalifa, 2.84g (Lowick -). Weakly struck but very fine and of the highest rarity, believed unpublished.

This is a mystery coin that should not have any reason to exist. It is, however, undoubtedly a genuine, contemporary issue, purportedly from the most important Iranian mint under al-Ma'mun's control at a time when the only other mint striking coins in the name of al-Amin was Madinat al-Salam. There is only one other reverse similar to this, which is found on a Silver Dirham of Ma'dan Bajunays 195h (Lowick 924). Lowick does not record any Silver Dirham of al-Muhammadiya 197 with six single annulets, as is found on the obverse of this coin. It is therefore unlikely that this piece is an accidental muling of two incompatible dies, but rather that it was a deliberate creation intended for propaganda on behalf of al-Amin, the son of Zubayda, to undermine the authority of his half-brother, her stepson al-Ma'mun, in a town which was securely under the latter's control. Where it was actually struck is unknown, but the cataloguer believes that it may have come from a North African mint.

53888.description:
Zanzibar AH1304 (1887) 1 Pysa Coin.

Struck during the reign of Sultan Sir Barghash bin Said,whom you can read about here; http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barghash_bin_Said_of_Zanzibar .

This Zanzibari 1 Pysa was the very last coin to be struck when Zanzibar was an independent state under British influence prior to becoming a British protectorate in 1888.

The design of this coin was used as a source design for the Mombasa AH1306 (1888) 1 Pice coin.

The silver & gold Ryal coins of AH1299 (1882) are extremely rare,as is the coins of the 1908 coinage.

53904.description:
Mombasa AH1306 (1888)H 1 Pice Coin.

The design of this coin is derived from the Zanzibari AH1304 (1887) 1 Pysa coin.

The 'H' mintmark is located on the lower part of the reverse,just inside the circle.

63520.description:
Ex. http://www.vcoins.com/ancient/saylesandlavender:
Ikhshidid/Hamdanid. Nasr al-Thamali, Governor of Tarsus. Fl. ca. 335/946. Cast Æ fals. NM (Tarsus), ND. VF/Fine, quite nice for this crudely cast series.

Ikhshidid/Hamdanid. Nasr al-Thamali, Governor of Tarsus. Fl. ca. 335/946. Cast Æ fals (22 mm, 2.92 g). NM (Tarsus), ND. O: al-Amir / Nasr Thamali. R: la ilah / illa Allah. Nasr al-Thamali, 'Amir of the Syrian Marches'. Cf. Shamma p. 101, 17 (but with nisba 'al-Thamali' on obverse); cf. Album 300 for immediately preceding issues under 'Abbasid governors. VF/Fine, quite nice for this crudely cast series. Very rare. 

Nasr al-Thamali is known to history only in connection with an exchange of prisoners with the Byzantines while he was governor of Tarsus under Muhammad b. Tughj known as 'the Ikhshid' and founder of the Ikhshidid dynasty. The Ikhshid died during the course of the negotiations in July A.D. 946. The remaining delegation returned to Tarsus where they found that Nasr had switched his allegiance to the Hamdanid ruler Sayf al-Dawla, who then completed the negotiations with the Byzantines in September of that same year.

67329.description:
Ex CNG, Inc.: Nomos 2: 230. 
ISLAMIC, Umayyad Caliphate. Pseudo-Byzantine types. Dinar (Gold, 4.26 g 6), uncertain mint in North Africa, circa 695-705/715. [NON] EST dS NISI IPSE SO[... Two imperial busts facing (based on those of Heraclius and Heraclius Constantine), both draped and wearing crowns with a triple ornament; the one on the left larger and bearded, that on the right beardless and smaller. Rev. dE d NO CIAS MA ET OMN AN Pillar, with cross bar on top, on base and two steps; to right, pellet. BMC (Arab-Byzantine) 143. Extremely rare. Minor nicks and scrapes, otherwise, nearly extremely fine. 

This very rare dinar (it was struck on a slightly lower standard than the Byzantine gold solidus) was produced based on Byzantine prototypes at some point towards the end of the 7th century. The curious fact is that the types are those used on coins minted at Carthage under Heraclius, which were last struck in 641, even though Carthage itself was only captured by the Arabs in 695. In the winter of 697/8 a Byzantine fleet was able to recapture the city, but the Byzantines were driven out later in 698 by a very much superior Arab force that retook the city. At that point our sources differ: most say that the city was destroyed during the final attack, but others suggest that the city was deliberately dismantled in 705 to prevent any further foreign occupations. In any case, after the city was destroyed it was replaced by the nearby town of Tunis, to which much of the old population of Carthage was transferred. The minters of this coin chose to produce a Byzantine-looking coin that would be familiar to local users, but not from a prototype that was so recent that it would imply Byzantine overlordship. The legends on both the obverse and reverse relate to the Islamic profession of the faith (the shahâda) but are not in fully canonical form; they are in Latin and can be expanded to: NON EST DeuS NISI IPSe SOLus CuI Socius Non est and DEus Dominus NOster CIAS MAgnus ETernus OMNiA Noscens. The most recent discussion of this coinage is in Michael Bates’ Roman and Early Muslim Coinage in North Africa, North Africa from Antiquity to Islam, edited by M.Horton and T. Wiedemann (Bristol, 1995) pp. 12-15 (a more expanded version is in preparation): he suggests that the North African Arab-Byzantine issues were produced in the period running from c. 695 to 715/718. They were replaced by completely Arabic issues, albeit using typically local thick flans in 718, and by broader, flatter coins in a style close to that used in Damascus and the other main mints of the caliphate in 719/720. He also suggests that the figural types were struck in Carthage while those with Latin inscriptions but no images were produced in the purely Islamic city of Kairouan, which had been founded in 670. This makes sense, especially since the inscriptions used on the coins seem to run in parallel and make it very likely that two mints were involved. If, however, the sources that state that Carthage was destroyed in 698 are correct, this makes the minting history of the figural types rather complicated. The possibilities are as follows: 1. all the figural issues were produced in Carthage from 695 through the Fall of 697 and then ended; 2. figural types began to be produced in Carthage 695, stopped with the Byzantine occupation, and then resumed in 698, either in Carthage if a) the city was only destroyed in 705 as some sources suggest, or b) in Tunis, if Carthage was dismantled in 698 and its population, and mint, removed to that nearby city. This would be an intriguing possibility; and it might also be where the issues of Hasan ibn al-Nu’man that are dated to A.H. 80 (699/700), as BMC 164 ff., were produced (though they bear only a single bust and have inscriptions that are only in Arabic) or c) in Tripolis, where a whole series of bronzes were struck (c. 699-704) in the name of Musa ibn Nusair, who was the governor of Africa from 698 and was soon to be the conqueror of Visigothic Spain (these coins seem marginally different in style from those in the main series and probably should be seen as a parallel issue).

The mint of Qubadhkhuirra was first published by Gyselen in 2000 with reference to a copper coin. Stephen Album found the abbreviated mint name on drachms of Ziyad ibn Abi-Sufyan dated 52 H. Auction 6: Stephen Album Rare Coins
Lot 360

ILKHANS: Ghazan Mahmud, AR 6 dirhams (12.55g), Jalalabad, 8 Ramadan AH700. A-2171. Full bold strike, remarkably attractive, Very Fine, RRR.
Estimated Value$1,000 - 1,200.

The location of Jalalabad, "city of victory", is undetermined, and its reading remains uncertain, and there are several typos in the Arabic inscriptions on this coin. The location may be some sort of administrative center or gathering retreat, probably in southern Azerbaijan or adjacent Kurdistan. It is known only from this type, always dated to the 8th of Ramadan AH700, on which some important event must have taken place. Has anyone searched through Rashid al-Din Tabib's history of Ghazan Mahmud for an explaination?

Our item number 80384

Ex Baldwin´s Auctions.: Islamic Coin Auction 16:322
 al-Muqtadir, Ornamental Dirham, no mint undated, 2.94g (unrecorded by Ilisch in Donative Coins). Ex-mount, good very fine and extremely rare. £6000-8000.
This and #76037 are examples of the very rare “personal” coinage of the caliph. Both obverse bear identical designs and legends which begin with the caliph’s ism, Ja’far, and continue with his caliphal title al-Muqtadir billah. The central designs on the first coin resembles a flamboyant “W” and on the second the design is reminiscent of a swastika. The first is known to have been struck in both gold and silver, which is also possibly the case for the second. As these pieces do not carry any mark of denomination it is likely that they were intended as
pièces de plaisir which were usually mounted for suspension and displayed (in the harem?) as a mark of caliphal favour.

The calligraphy of this year (AH144) is still similar to that of the late Umayyad dinars, which terminated in AH132. The silver mint at Dimashq (Damascus) was transferred in AH138 to a tentative Iraqi mint known as al-Hashimiya, finally to Madinat al-Salam (Baghdad) in 146. All dirhams of al-Hashmiya and those of Madinat al-Salam dated 146 retain the Dimashq calligraphy.

77719.description:
Ex Stephen Album rare coins: Auction 7: Lot 120
ABBASID: al-Mu'tadid, 892-902, AV dinar (3.65g), Samarqand, AH281. . A-241. Arabic "s" below reverse field, probably unique, clipped on one side.
The letter "s" in of undetermined meaning. It appears in the same location on the unique Samarqand 280 dinar (SNAT-696), as well as silver dirhams 279-281 and coppers dated 280-288. The gold and silver coins dated 280-281 are purely Abbasid, but the contemporary coppers cite the Samanid ruler in the marginal legend, as had already been the case for several decades. Later in 281, the name of the Samanid ruler, Isma'il, was added to both the silver and gold (both Samarqand and al-Shash mints), and retained thereafter. Thus 281 is the last possible year for a purely Abbasid coin of Samarqand.

85649.description:
Please help understand this coin. It can be read as Astarabad, (6)81, which is a problem because Arghun's ascension (and Ghazan's appointment as Governor of Khorasan) happened in 683.
Alternately it could be read as (6)91, which would make it a posthumous issue, struck by Ghazan as governor under Gaykhatu's reign, but honoring his father Arghun.
Any interpretative help will be appreciated.

89970.description:
http://www.stevealbum.com/cgi-bin/viewlota.php?site=2&sa...
Lot 286

SAMANIDS: Nuh III, 976-997, AR multiple dirham, NM, AH363, A-1469.2, SNAT-375var, 8.56g, clear inscription …hadha al-dirham sana thalath wa sittin wa thalathmi'a in inner obverse marginal legend, but very important for dating the entire series of multiple dirhams, as this cites Nuh III in reverse as usual and Nuh II below the obverse field, vf-ef, lustrous Extremely Fine, RRR. 

This is the earliest confirmed date on a multiple dirham, very neatly engraved. My interpretation is that this must be one of the very earliest multiple dirhams, and that any issues citing earlier rulers on obverse or reverse must actually have been struck later, i.e., after AH363 (probably at least a decade later). Although the 363 dated type was unknown at the time, Nicholas Lowick came to a similar conclusion in his article published in Spink's Numismatic Circular. May 1977.

90824.description:
`Abd al-Malik bin Marwan, AH 65-86 (685-705). Solidus AH 72-73 (691-692), sans mention d’atelier (Damas). Trois personnages debout de face / Légende coufique autour d’une haste terminée par un globe. Lettres B – I de part et d’autre. 4,52g. Foss p. 65; Miles “The earliest Arab gold Coinage” in “Museum Notes” 13, New York 1967, 10 pl. XLV. 

La première apparition de la profession de foi musulmane (Kalima) sur une monnaie d’or, et peut-être sa première apparition écrite sur un objet. Bism Allah la ilah illa Allah wahdahu Muhammad rasul Allah (« Au nom de Dieu. Il n’y a de dieu que Dieu Seul, et Muhammad est Son Prophète ») : cette légende purement musulmane fait de cette monnaie la première pièce d’or du Monde musulman. Dans le souci de fournir à leurs sujets une monnaie adaptée à leurs besoins, les dirigeants musulmans de Syrie avaient commencé par imiter les solidi byzantins, largement répandus et utilisés dans la région. Ces imitations reprenaient la légende et l’iconographie byzantines du prototype, en omettant toutefois les symboles chrétiens apparaissant tant à l’avers qu’au revers. Le remplacement de la légende byzantine par une légende arabe fait de cette monnaie une pièce originale et non plus une imitation. Déterminé à supprimer toute iconographie de son monnayage, ‘Abd al-Malik introduisit une nouvelle monnaie d’or purement épigraphique quelques années plus tard, en AH 77. Les solidi portant des représentations humaines furent alors retirés de la circulation, ce qui explique leur extrême rareté aujourd’hui. Le présent exemplaire est le premier à apparaître dans une vente aux enchères depuis 24 ans, le précédent ayant été vendu par Spink à Zurich en 1986. 

The earliest appearance of the Muslim profession of faith (the Kalima) on a gold coin, and perhaps its first written appearance on any object. Bism Allah la ilah illa Allah wahdahu Muhammad rasul Allah («In the name of God. There is no god but God alone; Muhammad is the Prophet of God”) : this purely Muslim legend makes this piece the very first gold coin of the Islamic world. In their efforts to provide their subjects with a coinage that was suited to their needs, the Muslim rulers of Syria began by striking imitations of Byzantine solidi which circulated widely in the region. These prototypes bore Byzantine legends and iconography, but omitted any Christian symbols on either obverse or reverse. The replacement of the Byzantine legends with an Arabic legend is witness to the moment at which the faith of Islam became the religion of state. ‘Abd al-Malik was determined to remove any form of imagery from his coinage. In AH 77, only a few years after the Three Standing Figures solidus was struck, he introduced a new gold coin which bore only the denomination and date of striking, with the Kalima and words from the Holy Qur’an. At this time all the old gold coins, such as the Three Standing Figure solidi, were withdrawn from circulation, and as a result they are virtually impossible to find today. This piece is the very first to appear in an auction sale for 24 years, the last one having been sold by Spink in Zurich in 1986. 

Emission arabo-sassanide Le plus bel exemplaire au monde en mains privées. Superbe.

The date for the mint unrecorded by Klat. Bardasir was the capital of Kirman province. Its mint is known only from the year 79h, one reference, and now this coin from 82h. In 90h the provincial name Kirman supplanted that of Bardasir on the coinage.

90869.description: Umayyad. temp ‘Abd al-Malik, Dirham, Fil 81h, 2.67g (Klat -). Good very fine and extremely rare . The date for the mint unrecorded by Klat. Fil is one of the Umayyad mystery mints. It has been given the convenient name Fil (meaning ‘elephant’) because no other plausible reading has been accepted. There was a town of this name located in Khwarazm, but it is said to have been conquered by the Muslims after this coin was struck. Examples are known from 79h, 80h, 81h (this coin) and 82h. With four dates recorded, it should not be long before the identity of this mint is revealed.

90879.description: Umayyad. temp ‘Abd al-Malik, Dirham, al-Mawsil 82h, 2.76g (Klat 626.a, but an unrecorded die variety). Good very fine and extremely rare. Mosul was the principal town of Diyar Rabi‘a. Somewhat surprisingly Mosul is an extraordinarily rare Umayyad silver mint. Three examples are recorded of the year 82h (including this coin) and one of 83h. Mosul was, however, a prolific copper mint with the names of governors under the Caliph Hisham and Marwan II being regularly recorded. This coin has a distinctive pattern of pellets which links it to the die-sinker of Klat 626a.

91065.description:
Ex Baldwin´s Auctions.: Islamic Coin Auc 19: lot 53.
al-Ma’mun (104-218h)/Tahir, Gold Dinar, no mint name 198h, rev inner margin: mimma amira bihi ‘Abd Allah ‘Abd Allah amir al-mu’minin (“among those things ordered by the servant of God ‘Abd Allah (al-Ma’mun), Commander of the Faithful”), field fourth line: Tahir, 4.18g (Bernardi 87, 4 refs; Album 222.6T).Slightly clipped, good very fine and rare. Tahir bin al-Husayn was the general in command of the caliphal troops which invested Madinat al-Salam in the closing year of al-Amin’s reign.This coin was presumably struck in the city’s mint after the defeat or death of al-Amin in 198h.It should be noted that Tahir does not give al-Ma’mun his caliphal name, but only his personal name, ‘Abd Allah, in the inner marginal legend on the reverse of this Dinar.Tahir was the founder of the Tahirid dynasty of semi-independent governors of Central Asia and this coin provides evidence of his lukewarm loyalty to the Abbasid dynasty.

93439.description:
Ex. Forum Ancient Coins
Islamic, Zangids of al-Jazira, al-Mu'azzam Muhmud, 605 - 648 AH, 1209 - 1251 A.D.

Perhaps an unpublished Mongol imitative of the last coin type issued by the Zangids of al-Jazira? Worthy of study by a specialist of these types.
IS47245. Bronze dirham, unpublished in references examined; see Spengler and Sayles 89, Album 1884, Edhem 177 for a similar tamgha obverse dirham, F, al-Jazira (Mesopotamia) mint, weight 10.337g, maximum diameter 23.8mm, obverse Zengid tamgha in the form of a stylized fulmen (thunderbolt symbol), Kufic script around; reverse uncertain lobed shape with pellets and symbols; $300.00

93440.description:
Ex. Item number: 270675872542
Arab-Sassanian Coin Of Al-Ḥajjāj Bin Yūsuf, 77 AH / 69
Starting bid: US $1,500.00
 Obverse field: Typical late Arab-Sassanian bust with the name "al-Ḥajjāj bin Yūsuf" written in Arabic on the right hand side of the bust. Obverse margin: bism Allāh / lā-ilaha il- / Allāh waḥdahu Muḥammad / rasūl Allāh ("In the name of God. There is no god but God alone. Muḥammad is the Messenger of God").

 Reverse field: Typical Arab-Sassanian fire-altar with attendants with mint (Bīshāpūr).

Comments

 Weight = 3.95 gms.

This is a very unique coin. The shahāda is arranged in striking fashion radially in the obverse margin. As far as we are aware, no other coin from 1st century of hijra shows this feature.
