Umayyad Caliphate, Silver coinage. AR Dirham (26mm, 2.69 g, 7h). Tustar mint. Dated AH 79 (AD 698/9). Klat 196 (same obverse die); al- 'Ajlan p. 92, no. 21. Minor graffiti in fields. VF, lightly toned. Excessively rare.

Tustar, the modern Shushtar, was located in Khuzistan, about sixty miles north of Ahwaz. It was watered by the Dujayl river, and mediaeval accounts speak of it as being surrounded by gardens where fruit including grapes, oranges, dates, pomegranates and pears grew plentifully. Tustar was also the location of the celebrated Band-i Kaisar, a dam and arched bridge built across the river in Sasanian times. Its name, which translates as 'Caesar's Dam', refers to a tradition that this remarkable structure was built by Roman prisoners of war captured after the defeat of Valerian by Shapur I in AD 260. 
Price realized: 9500 USD

332392.description:
Fatimids. al-Mustansir billah. AH 427-487 / AD 1036-1094. AV Dinar (20.6mm, 3.26 g, 4h). Madinat Rasul Allah (Medina) mint. Dated AH 450 (AD 1059), month of Dhu'l-Hijja. Obverse margin: Bismillah al-rahman al-rahim duriba hadha al-dinar bi-Madinat Rasul Allah min Dhu'l-Hijja sanat khamsin wa arba' mi'at.
In field: al-Imam / Ma'add Abu Tamim / al-Mustansir billah / amir al-mu'minin / Reverse margin: Muhammad rasul Allah arsulahu bi'l-huda...al-mushrikun (Qur'an ix:33).
In field: 'Ali / la ilaha illa Allah / wahdahu la sharik lahu / Muhammad rasul Allah / wali Allah. Nicol -; cf. Morton & Eden auction 92 (26 April 2018), lot 97 = Baldwin's Islamic Auction 19 (25 April 2012), lot 106 (same dies). Minor marks, slightly wavy flan. Good VF. Excessively rare, an historically important coin.

Madinat Rasul Allah, 'The City of God's Messenger' is perhaps the rarest mint-place in the entire Fatimid series. Only three or four dinars from this mint are known today. It is generally accepted that the name is an honorific title for Madina al-Munawara itself, and writing more than seventy years ago George Miles simply stated Madinat Rasul Allah (=Medina)', without qualification or any mention of alternative suggestions (Miles, G.C., (Fatimid Coins: ANS NNM 121, 1951).

We can only conjecture why Fatimid dinars should have been struck at Madina al-Munawara in the year AH 450, but there is probably a connection with the activities of the founder of the Sulayhid dynasty in Yemen, 'Ali b. Muhammad al-Sulayhi. Born a Sunni, al-Sulayhi became an Isma'ili convert and it seems that by the late 420s he was already the amir al-hajj,, responsible protecting pilgrims travelling through Yemen en route for Makka. In AH 439 al-Sulayhi summoned his followers to the mountain of Jabal Masar, where he announced his intention to establish a Shi'ite state in Yemen. Unsurprisingly, the Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir gave his endorsement to the new movement, and al-Sulayhi embarked on a series of campaigns against other Muslim rulers in the region. By AH 454 the whole of Yemen was under al-Sulayhi's control – including Makka, which al-Sulayhi visited personally when undertaking the Pilgrimage. It is also known that al-Mustansir was named in the khutba in Mecca in this year, by which time the local nobility of the city had already acknowledged Fatimid overlordship. Thus while this remarkable dinar cannot be linked to any single historical event, there is ample evidence for Fatimid influence in the Holy Places around the time of its striking.

From CNG Islamic Auction 5. Lot 148. Price realized US$ 55000 plus commission.
332392.keywords: Fatimid al-Mustansir AV Dinar AH 450 Madinat Rasul Allah

334015.description:
ISLAMIC, Ayyubids. Egypt. al-Salih Ayyub, AH 636-647 / AD 1238-1249. Dirham (Silver, 22 mm, 2.91 g, 3 h), square-in-circle type, Dimashq, AH 636 = 1238/9. Citing the ʿAbbasid caliph al-Mustansir billah (AH 623-640 / AD 1226-1242) within a square, 'al-imām al-Mustanṣir / billāh Abū Jaʿfar / al-Manṣūr amīr al-muʾminīn' ('Imam al-Mustansir billah Abu Jaʿfar al-Mansur, Commander of the Believers' in Arabic); in the margin, 'lā ilāha illā / Allāh waḥdahū / lā sharīka lahū / Muḥammad rasūl Allāh' ('There is no deity but Allah, the One, there is no partner to Him. Muhammad is the messenger of Allah' in Arabic). Rev. Within a square, 'al-malik al-Ṣāliḥ / Najm al-Dunyā wa al-Dīn / Ayyūb ibn Muḥammad' ('King al-Salih Najm al-Dunya wa al-Din Ayyub son of Muhammad' in Arabic); in the margin, 'bism Allāh / ḍuriba bi Dimashq / sana sitt wa / thalāthīn [wa] sitta miʾa' ('In the name of Allah. Struck in Dimashq in the year 636' in Arabic). Album 823.1. Rare. Somewhat rough, otherwise, very fine.

From an important collection of Byzantine and Islamic coins and seals, formed over the past 25 years.
334015.keywords: Ayyubid al-Salih Ayyub AR dirham Dimashq 636AH SNAT #787

334285.description:
WOW CRUSADERS, Type of Dirhams. Mid to late 13th century AR Dirham Medieval Coin
CRUSADERS, Pseudo Dirhams. Mid to late 13th century. AR Dirham (18mm, 2.62 g, 4h). Copying a Damascus mint issue in the name of the Ayyubid al-Salih Isma’il and the ‘Abbasid caliph al-Mustansir. Uncertain mint in Levant. Dated [12]5[...] (in Arabic), though possibly struck later. Legend in blundered Arabic citing al-Salih Isma’il; [mint formula] and partial date in outer margin / Legend in blundered Arabic citing al-Mustansir; partial pseudo-mint formula and date in outer margin. Bates Type 5 and 6 ; Metcalf, Crusades 238-9; CCS 9. VF, a bit of spotty toning, areas of flat strike at periphery. From the estate of Thomas Bentley Cederlind.
334285.keywords: Ayyubid al-Salih Isma'il AR dirham Dimashq 64xAH rev as SNAT #861

334288.description:
VERY RARE CRUSADERS. Crusader Imitations of Islamic Dirhams. Dirham Silver Coin.
CRUSADERS. Crusader Imitations of Islamic Dirhams. Dirham (Silver, 20 mm, 3.00 g, 6 h), imitating an Ayyubid dirham, date illegible. Citing the Ayyubid al-Nasir Yusuf II (AH 634-658 / AD 1236-1259) within a square, ‘al-malik al-Nāṣir / Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn Yūsuf / … ibn Muḥammad’ (‘King al-Nasir Salah al-Din Yusuf … son of Muhammad’ in Arabic); marginal legend effaced. Rev. Citing the ʿAbbasid caliph al-Mustaʿsim billah (AH 640-656 / AD 1242-1258) within a square, ‘[al-I]mām al-Mustaʿṣim / billāh Abū Aḥmad / [amīr] al-muʾminīn’ (‘Imam al-Mustaʿsim billah Abu Ahmad, the Commander of the Believers’ in Arabic); margin off flan. Album -. Very rare. Areas of weakness, otherwise, extremely fine.

ISLAMIC, Anatolia & al-Jazira (Post-Seljuk). Zangids (al-Mawsil). Saif al-Din Ghazi II, AH 565-576 / AD 1170-1180. Heavy Dinar (Gold, 28 mm, 7.91 g, 6 h), al-Mawsil, AH 568 = 1172/3. Citing the ʿAbbasid caliph al-Mustadi bi-amr Allah (AH 566-575 / AD 1170-1180), 'lā ilāha illā Allāh / waḥdahū lā sharīka lahū / al-Mustaḍī bi-amr / Allāh amīr / al-muʾminīn' ('There is no deity but Allah, the One, there is no partner to Him. al-Mustadi bi-amr Allah, Commander of the Believers' in Arabic); to right, above and left, 'Ghāzī ibn – Mawdūd – ibn Zangi' ('Ghazi son of Mawdud son of Zangi' in Arabic); in the inner margin, 'bism Allāh ḍuriba hādhā al-dīnār bi al-Mawṣil sana thamān wa sittīn wa khamsa miʾa' ('In the name of Allah. This dinar was struck in al-Mawsil in the year 568' in Arabic); in the outer margin, 'li-llāh al-amr min qabl wa min baʿd wa yawmaʾidhin yafraḥu al-muʾminūn bi naṣr Allāh' ('To Allah belongs the command before and after, and on that day the believers will rejoice with the help of Allah' in Arabic; Qurʾān 30: 4-5). Rev. Within a dotted circle, 'Muḥammad / rasūl Allāh / ṣalla Allāh ʿalayh' ('Muhammad is the messenger of Allah. May Allah bless him' in Arabic); citing the Zangid ruler of Syria Nur al-Din Mahmud (AH 541-569 / AD 1146-1174) on the four sides, 'al-malik – al-ʿādil – Maḥmūd – ibn Zankī' ('The just king, Mahmud son of Zangi' in Arabic); in the margin, 'Muḥammad rasūl Allāh arsalahū bi al-hudā wa dīn al-ḥaqq liyuẓhirahū ʿalā al-dīn kullih wa law kariha al-mushrikūn' ('Muhammad is the messenger of Allah. He sent him with guidance and the religion of truth, so that He may make it overcome all religions, even though the unbelievers may dislike it' in Arabic). Album 1859. Very rare. Slightly clipped and with light areas of weakness, otherwise, very fine.

339803.description:
Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 6 9 Aug 2024; lot 46.
Estimate: 5000 USD
Pre-reform issues, Arab-Sasanian. Abdallah b. Harith (or b. 'Ali). fl. late 60s / 680s. AR Drachm (31.9mm, 2.97 g, 3h). SK (Sistan) mint. Dated AH 66 (AD 685/6). Obverse margin: - / bin 'Ali ∵ / ∵ ✶ - / -. Malek,Arab-Sasanian p. 255; SCC 1752; cf. Weber, Arabo-Sasanidische Drachmen 195 (dated AH 65); SICA 1, -; Album 26N (as 'Abdallah b. 'Ariq). VF, small portion of edge repaired. Extremely rare.

The identity of the governor on this coin remains the subject of scholarly debate. His first name, 'Abdallah, is unambiguous, but the Pahlawi form of his patronymic is ambiguous. It can be read either as ALYKAN or HLYKAN, which would equate to 'son of 'Ariq' or 'son of Harith' respectively. Malek notes that an 'Abdallah b. Harith was dismissed from his post as governor of Basra in AH 65, but found no evidence to connect this individual with the province of Sistan where these coins were issued (Malek, Arab Sasanian p. 255, s.vv. 'Abd Allah b. 'Ali and 'Abd Allah b. Harith). However, this is not quite correct: the local history of Sistan records that 'Abdallah b. al-Zubayr 'gave Basra, Khurasan and Sistan to Harith b. 'Abdallah (sic)...[who], in turn, dispatched 'Abd al-'Aziz b. 'Abdallah b. 'Amir to Sistan.' That being so, it would be hardly surprising that drachms from Sistan struck in AH 65 and early 66 should have named 'Abdallah b. al-Harith himself, with those struck from later AH 66 onwards issued in the name of his viceroy, 'Abd al-'Aziz b. 'Abdallah b. 'Amir.

But this does not explain the presence of the remarkable legend bin 'Ali in the obverse margin, which was only read when a new and better-preserved example of this extremely rare coinage came to light. This coin (SCC 1752) led Shams-Eshragh to propose the alternative reading of the governor's name as 'Abdallah b. 'Ali. While attractive, this requires a certain amount of special pleading to explain by the Pahlawi form of 'Ali should be rendered as ALYKAN with an unexpected letter K. Weber's suggestion that that this individual might have been an 'Abdallah b. 'Ali b. Husayn, a great-grandson of the fourth caliph 'Ali, is tantalising but speculative. 
Price realized: 3250 USD

341424.description:
Ex Leu Numismatik AG: Web Auction 31 7-8 Sep 2024, lot 1737.
Starting price: 50 CHF
ISLAMIC, Umayyad Caliphate. Uncertain period (pre-reform), AH 41-77 / AD 661-697. Drachm (Silver, 34 mm, 4.11 g, 3 h), ART (Ardashir-Khurra), (probably not a genuine date), struck circa AH 36-50 = AD 656-670. Draped bust resembling Khosrau II to right, wearing elaborate mural crown; behind head, AFZUT GDH ('may his kingship increase' in Pahlawi); before head, HWSRWD ('Khosrau' in Pahlawi); in outer margin, either APD / ('excellent' in Pahlawi) or 'lillah' ('for God' in Kufic). Rev. Fire altar with ribbons flanked by two attendants; in upper left field, six-pointed star; in upper right field, crescent; to left, date; to right, ART (name of the mint in Pahlawi). Album A6. Beautifully toned. Struck from a slightly worn reverse die, otherwise, extremely fine.

From the collection of J. Knudsen, formed from the late 1970s to the late 1990s, Leu Web Auction 16, 22-24 May 2021, 4311. 
Price realized: 170 CHF

342026.description:
'Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Qa'im. AH 422-467 / AD 1031-1075. AV Dinar. Madinat al-Salam mint. Dated AH 455 (AD 1063). Obverse field: elaborate ornament above, other ornaments below and to sides of legend / Reverse field: Muhammad rasul Allah / al-Imam al-Qa'im / bi-amr Allah amir / al-mu'minin, 'Uddat - al-Din - Abu'l-Qasim above, to right, and to left of field. Jafar A.MS 455A; Album 265Q. Excessively rare and historically important.

This is the first purely 'Abbasid gold dinar struck in Baghdad since the forced abdication of al-Mustakfi in AH 334 (AD 945/6), more than a century before this coin was issued.

Following the death of Tughril Beg, the Seljuq Sultan, the 'Abbasid caliph al-Qa'im found himself in a delicate position while two rival claimants, Sulayman and Alp Arslan, fought for the Sultanate. Before Alp Arslan emerged victorious, al-Qa'im struck dinars in Baghdad which named neither of the two Seljuq rivals. On the one hand, this can be interpreted as prudent caution: without knowing which of the two claimants would emerge victorious, it would have been unwise for the caliph to be seen to favour one over the other by naming him on the coinage. But the addition of the name of al-Qa'im's heir, who appears on the reverse with the honorific title 'Uddat al-Din ( 'Promise of Faith'), suggests that the caliph may have been making a grander and more ambitious statement on these coins. Tughril Beg had harboured ambitions to establish marriage links with the caliph, and this dream of a caliph with Seljuq blood in his veins was to persist throughout the Seljuq period. By reinforcing the claims of his own choice as heir to the Caliphate, al-Qa'im was able to take this opportunity to counteract Tughril Beg's schemes.

In the event, Alp Arslan emerged victorious. Preoccupied with his own military campaigns, he never visited Baghdad during his ten-year reign, and he kept his involvement with the caliph's affairs to a minimum. 'Uddat al-Din, named here on the coinage for the first time, duly succeeded to the caliphate as al-Muqtadi billah in AH 467.
342026.keywords: 'Abbasid al-Qaim AV Dinar AH 455 Madinat al-Salam

Umayyad dirhams of Ifriqiya are known dated 124, 125, and all years 128-132, all of them extremely rare. The last year that is reasonably common is AH118, with 119 very rare and 120 extremely rare. It is believed that taxation funding from North African ceased to reach the Umayyad centers, such as Damascus and Basra. As a result, the post-120 dates are only found in hoards from North African and Spain, whereas pre-119 dirhams are often found as frequently in eastern hoards as western hoards. 342115.description:
Ex Stephen Album Rare Coins Auction 50 19-22 Sep 2024, lot 169.
Start Price:7,000.00 USD
ABBASID: al-Muqtadir, 908-932, AV donative double dinar (8.58g), Madinat al-Salam, AH299, A-Y245, standard design as on the normal dinar (A-245.2), but produced with larger dies on a broader planchet (29mm), which is the same for silver dirhams of Madinat al-Salam around AH299; trace of mount at the top, light scrape on reverse; a most important issue of al-Muqtadir, apparently unknown for any mint or date and unique, NGC graded UNC details. The weight is correct for a double dinar, with the single dinar standard at 4.26g, though individual specimens of Madinat al-Salam show considerable deviations, typically weighing between about 3.25g and 4.75g by the time of al-Muqtadir. Twice that standard would be 8.52g, and the weight of this piece, with a few hundredths of a gram added by the remaining portion of the mount, is indeed correct. The style and arrangement is identical to the contemporary silver dirhams of Madinat al-Salam, but the denomination is boldly al-dinar rather than al-dirham, with no evidence that the denomination had been altered. The calligraphy and arrangement are identical to both silver dirhams and gold dinars of Madinat al-Salam dated AH299 and for others dated between 297 and the early 300s. While there are surprisingly heavy normal dinars, sometimes up to 7 grams, such heavy dinars are not known for Madinat al-Salam, observed mainly for the mints around al-Ahwaz. Furthermore, the gold dinars are struck with much smaller dies, typically in the range of 21.5mm to 24.5mm. This difference confirms that this was struck from special broad dies meant for this special type, which might have been produced for a normal circulating double dinar, though given its exceeding rarity it must have been produced as a donative or presentational piece.See Baldwins ICA 24, lot 4488 for the silver dirham, also 29mm diameter, and CNG E-Auction 450, lot 469, for the ordinary gold dinar.

342306.description:
'Abbasid Caliphate. AV Dinar, AH 255 (868/69). al-Ahwaz Mint. Al-Muhtadi. NGC AU-55.
A-237 (RRR). Weight: 4.51 gms. An EXTREMELY RARE issue of Al-Muhtadi, as evidenced by being the finest of only two examples of a Dinar of Al-Muhtadi being encapsulated by NGC. There is some strike weakness at the peripheries as is typical, though this is actually quite a bit lesser than normally encountered for this issuer. al-Ahwaz is even less common than other mints for this ruler, with us being able to find only three other examples trading in the past several decades. As perhaps the nicest example one could hope to find of this ruler and mint combination, we are assured that there will be many excited bidders for this remarkable specimen.

From Stacks September 2024 auction. Lot 76153. Price realized USD 950 plus commission.

343279.description:
ALMORAVID: Abu Bakr b. Yahya, fl. 1147/48, AV dinar (4.17g), Dar'a, AH542, A-476J, traditional Almoravid design and legends, with the name abu bakr bin / yahya below kalima in obverse field, the mint and date in the reverse margin, likely issued during the chaos following the death of the last Almoravid ruler Ishaq b. Ali in AH541/1146, bold XF, RRRR. Nothing seems to be known about Abu Bakr b. Yahya, though given the relatively short distance between Sijilmasa and Dar'a, it is possible that he was related to or was the son of Yahya b. Abi Bakr, who struck dinars at Sijilmasa in 543. No other coins are known from the city of Dar'a. According to Yaqut (vol. 2, p. 567), Dar'a lay about 4 farsakh (about 15 miles) southeast of Sijilmasa in Morocco. The demise of the Almoravids in AH541 led to numerous local rulers issuing their own coins before the Almohad expansion in the 540s and 550s in both Spain and North Africa, known as the Taifas de los Almoravides.

From SARC auction 50. Lot 204. Price realized USD 4750 plus commission.
343279.keywords: Almoravid Abu Bakr bin Yahya AV Dinar AH 542 Dar'a

ABBASID: al-Muqtadir, 908-932, AR medalet (5.25g), 19mm, a special decorative silver piece in the caliph's name, al-muqtadir on the reverse, billah on the obverse, with a raised outer border on each side; the silver blank was probably cast, the legends hand-engraved and dozens of tiny circles hand-punched after the initial engraving, as a few of these circle overlap the engraved letters, VF, RRR. The same punch was used to create the center of the "m" in al-muqtadir and the "h" of billah. The side with billah was considered the obverse, as the attached mount kept billah lever but al-muqtadir sideways. The purpose of these pieces is not known, though the mount suggests that it was attached to an object where both sides could be read.Another example was offered in the CNG Islamic Auction 4, lot 82, with a different suggestion for this items' purpose.

From SARC Auction 50. Lot 172. Price realized USD 2400 plus commission.

AYYUBID. al-‘Aziz ‘Uthman.(1193-1198).al-Iskandariya 592 AH.Dinar.

Obv : ثمان بن يوسف.
Arabic inscription in field

Rev : لمام / احمد.
Arabic inscription in field.

Condition : The coin is in excellent condition with a bright gold patina. The inscriptions and designs are clear and sharp, with minimal signs of wear, and the patina enhances its vibrant appearance.Extremely fine.

Material : Gold.
Axis : 6h

Weight : 5.65 gr
Diameter : 19 mm

Al-‘Aziz ‘Uthman (1171–1198 AD) was a prominent figure in the Ayyubid dynasty a Muslim dynasty founded by the famous military leader Salah al-Din (Saladin). The Ayyubids played a central role in the defense of Islamic territories during the Crusades and were key players in the political and military history of the medieval Middle East.The Ayyubid dynasty was established by Saladin in the late 12th century after he rose to power following the dissolution of the Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt. Saladin is best known for his leadership during the Crusades, especially for his victory at the Battle of Hattin (1187), which led to the Muslim recapture of Jerusalem from the Crusaders. Under Saladin's leadership, the Ayyubid dynasty expanded its control over large portions of the Middle East, including Egypt, Syria, Yemen, and parts of Mesopotamia.After Saladin's death in 1193, the Ayyubid dynasty was divided among his heirs. His sons and nephews ruled various Ayyubid territories, often independently, but they maintained loose connections as a family-based empire.

Al-‘Aziz ‘Uthman ibn Salah al-Din was one of Saladin’s sons, and he became the second Ayyubid sultan of Egypt following his father’s death. Al-‘Aziz ‘Uthman ruled Egypt from 1193 to 1198 AD inheriting a critical region that had become the economic and political center of the Ayyubid empire. His rule marks a transitional period in Ayyubid history, where the powerful and unified empire of Saladin began to fragment as different branches of the family ruled separate territories.Al-‘Aziz ‘Uthman’s rule in Egypt was relatively stable, and he is often credited with continuing his father's policies of maintaining a strong military defense against the Crusaders, while also strengthening the internal administration of Egypt. Though he did not lead large military campaigns like his father, Al-‘Aziz ‘Uthman played a key role in consolidating Ayyubid power in Egypt and stabilizing the region.One of his notable military undertakings was an unsuccessful attempt to demolish the pyramids of Giza. According to historical accounts, Al-‘Aziz ‘Uthman sought to dismantle the pyramids, possibly as a demonstration of his power or a rejection of the pre-Islamic past. However, the scale of the task proved too great, and he abandoned the effort after only causing minor damage to the Pyramid of Menkaure.

During his reign, Al-‘Aziz ‘Uthman was involved in managing the delicate balance of power among the Ayyubid princes. The Ayyubid empire, while formidable under Saladin, was largely decentralized after his death, with different members of the family ruling over regions such as Syria, Aleppo, and Damascus. Al-‘Aziz worked to maintain peaceful relations with his relatives, although tensions and power struggles were common among the Ayyubids.Al-‘Aziz ‘Uthman also focused on internal development in Egypt, ensuring the smooth operation of the government and continuing to support the military forces that protected the region from external threats. His reign saw continued economic prosperity in Egypt, which had become the heart of the Ayyubid empire under his father.Al-‘Aziz ‘Uthman died in 1198, just five years after assuming power. His untimely death marked the beginning of a period of instability in Egypt as his young son, Al-Mansur, succeeded him. Al-Mansur was still a minor, and power effectively fell into the hands of the regent Al-Adil I (Al-‘Aziz’s uncle), who eventually took control of the Ayyubid empire and reunited much of the fragmented territories under his rule.Al-‘Aziz ‘Uthman’s legacy is often overshadowed by the monumental achievements of his father, Saladin. However, his reign is significant for the consolidation and stabilization of Ayyubid Egypt during a critical period in the dynasty's history. He managed to uphold the internal stability of Egypt, fend off external threats, and maintain the integrity of the Ayyubid territories despite the growing internal divisions within the family.

344817.description:
Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 7 24-25 Oct 2024; lot 42.
Estimate: 25 000 USD
Umayyad Caliphate, Silver coinage. AR Dirham (25.8mm, 2.36 g, 3h). Bukhara mint. Dated AH 84? (AD 703). Obverse: margin reads bism Allah db (sic, for duriba) hadha al-dirham bi-Bukhara fi sanat arba't thamanin; five small annulets in outer border / Reverse: wa at beginning of third line of field. VF, minor losses to edge and some flan delamination . Unpublished, believed unique, and the first Umayyad dirham known from the mint of Bukhara.

Two other extremely rare Eastern dirham mints, both similarly unknown to Klat, were also briefly active at this time. These mints are Tukharistan, known from two specimens dated AH 80 (CNG Triton XXI, 9 January 2018, lot 947) and AH '8' (Morton & Eden 69, 10 April 2014, lot 20), and Balkh, known from a specimen with the date read as either AH 87 or 82 (Morton & Eden 79, 21 April 2016, lot 36). The coin offered here exhibits a number of striking similarities with these three pieces, and the style and fabric are clearly close to the Balkh and the Tukharistan '8' dirhams in particular. It is noteworthy that these two coins also have illegible or incomplete dates, which are difficult to read and interpret, much as on the present piece. The year as been tentatively read as AH 84 here; the decade is certain, but the unit is not clearly engraved. AH 82, which would of course fit with the Balkh dirham mentioned above, is another possibility.

The first Muslim armies reached Bukhara during the caliphate of Mu'awiya, when a force led by 'Ubaydallah b. Ziyad crossed the Oxus in AH 53/4. 'Ubaydallah was able to demand tribute from Khatun, who was ruling in Bukhara as regent for her young son Tughshada, and further tribute was exacted two years later by 'Ubaydallah's successor, Sa'id b. 'Uthman. But our sources are clear that the Muslims were not able to establish permanent control of Bukhara until the mid-80s, when Qutayba b. Muslim led a series of campaigns into Sogdiana and finally overcame Bukharan resistance in AH 87. For two decades before this, the Arab settlers in the neighbouring province of Khurasan had squabbled and fought among themselves while also launching occasional raids across the Oxus - with varying degrees of success. A few years before this coin was struck, the governor Umayya b. 'Abdallah had been abandoned by his main commander while campagining beyond the Oxus, forcing him to conclude a swift and humiliating peace with Bukhara. His successors, including the celebrated warrior al-Muhallab b. Abi Sufra and his son Yazid, achieved little more than Umayya. But during the early 80s, when this coin was struck, the situation finally began to shift in the Arabs' favour. Feuding between the local rulers in Transoxiana left them less able to mount a cohesive resistance, while the defeat of the Arab rebel Musa b. 'Abdallah helped clear the way for Qutayba b. Muslim to launch the sustained assault which would finally see Bukhara securely in Muslim hands. 
Sold: $ 16.000

Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 7 24-25 Oct 2024; lot 51.

Umayyad Caliphate, Silver coinage. AR Dirham (25.9mm, 2.73 g, 12h). Khusraw Shadh Hurmuz. Dated AH 97 (AD 715/6). Klat 284; Al-'Ajlan p.213, no. 16. Good VF, minor peripheral hornsilver. Very rare.

Khusraw Shadh Hurmuz is one of the rarest Umayyad dirham mints, known only from a small number of specimens dated AH 97. Its name is that of a district in Iraq located between the Tigris and the Nahrawan canal, to the east of the future site of Baghdad.

Three other extremely rare Umayyad dirham mints were located within the district of Khusraw Shadh Hurmuz. Two of these, Nahrbuq and Radhan, are only known for the year AH 90. The third, al-Madinat al-'Atiqa, is only recorded for AH 97 - the same date as the present coin. Bahurasir, another Umayyad mint active only in the year AH 97, lay opposite al-Madinat al-'Atiqa on the western bank of the Tigris.
Price realized: 6500 USD

345286.description:
Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 7 24-25 Oct 2024; lot 7.
Estimate: 7500 USD
Pre-reform issues, n/a. Arab-Sasanian. Abu Hadhir b. Hajan. fl. AH 77 / AD 696/7. AR Drachm (25.9mm, 2.66 g, 12h). WYHC (Arrajan) mint. Dated AH 77 (AD 696/7). Obverse margin: - / Abu Hadhir billah (?) / - / -. Cf. Morton & Eden 48, lot 9; Malek, Arab-Sasanian p. 271. Near VF, clipped and creased, some light scratches. Extremely rare.

The name and identity of the governor on this excessively rare coin remains uncertain. Several suggestions have been made, some of which seem more likely than others:

Shams Eshragh published a coin with similar legends dated AH 76 (SCC 1758). He read the Arabic legend in the obverse margin as Abu Hadhir billah, which he interpreted as a personal name. On this basis, he proposed to read the Pahlawi name before the bust as ABW HAJL Y HAJAN, for 'Abu Hadhir b. Hajan'.

In 2011, a second coin of this governor appeared at auction, dated AH 77. On this specimen, the Arabic marginal legend was tentatively read as 'Abu Nasr' (sic), and the Pahlawi interpreted as a version of the name Abu Sa'id b. Numayla. Because a governor named Numayla b. Malik had struck drachms at the same mint four years previously, it was conjectured that this hypothetical individual might have been his son. But 'Abu Sa'id' cannot be the correct reading of the first part of the governor's name, since the final letter is clearly 'L' or 'R' (this cannot be 'Y', meaning 'son of', which appears at the beginning of the following line). Having originally proposed this reading myself, I now have no hesitation in retracting it.

Malek, having cautiously accepted Abu Sa'id b. Numayla as a 'possible but uncertain' reading for the Pahlawi governor's name, nevertheless preferred Shams Eshragh's reading of Abu Hadhir billah for the Arabic legend in the margin. 'Abu Hadhir' certainly fits the Arabic letter-forms, and as the first line of the Pahlawi name-legend appears to read ABW [...]TR it is not clear why Malek rejected Shams Eshragh's suggestion that this was the Pahlawi equivalent of Abu Hadhir. There is no reason why the two names should be the same - on another unique drachm struck at Arrajan in this year we find the name of al-Hajjaj b. Yusuf before the bust and that of al-Hakam b. Nahik in the margin (Malek Fig. 9.25.12). But there are plenty of Arab-Sasanian drachms where the Arabic marginal legend does indeed correspond to the Pahlawi governor's name, and there seems no good reason to exclude the possibility in this case.

In any case, the identity of Abu Hadhir remains mystifying. The governor of Arrajan at this time appears to have been the al-Hakam b. Nahik mentioned earlier, and who is also recorded as having begun building the mosque there in AH 75. Might al-Hakam have been ousted during the Kharijite incursion into Iraq under Shabib al-Shaybani during AH 76, and temporarily replaced by our mysterious Abu Hadhir? 
Price realized: 10 000 USD

345287.description:
Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 7 24-25 Oct 2024; lot 53.
Estimate: 3000 USD
Umayyad Caliphate, Silver coinage. AR Dirham (26.6mm, 2.88 g, 9h). Dard mint. Dated AH 93 (AD 711/2). Klat 303; Al-'Ajlan p.172, no. 20; ICV 263. Near EF, some peripheral hornsilver. Very rare.

'Dard' was once thought to be a blundered version of the well-known mint-name Darabjird. In Arabic, bi-Darabjird, 'at Darabjird', would be written with two visually similar triplets of joined consonants before the final d, and it was suspected that the engraver might have omitted the second in error. But in 2008 an Umayyad dirham dated AH 79 came to light on which the mint-name was unambiguously written as 'Dard' (Baldwin's Islamic Auction 14, lot 25), which supports the view that 'Dard' represents a different locality, yet to be identified. Further support for this view comes from the fact that that all surviving dirhams of Dard dated AH 93 appear to have two pellets below fi in the obverse mint/date legend; these are not found on dirhams from Darabjird, although similar pellets are known on other Umayyad dirhams, including issues of Marw struck in AH 99, 100 and 101.
Price realized: 3250 USD

345370.description:
Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 7 24-25 Oct 2024; lot 64.
Estimate: 20 000 USD
Umayyad Caliphate, Silver coinage. AR Dirham (27.9mm, 2.87 g, 8h). 'Maziyan' mint (uncertain location in Caucasian Albania). Dated AH 93 (AD 711/2). Klat –; Al-'Ajlan –. Good VF. Extremely rare, believed to be an unpublished date.

This is a new date for this enigmatic mint-name, which was previously only known for the year AH 92.

The reading 'Maziyan' is a conjectural one. The first letter of the mint-name is clearly 'M', and is connected to what can only be a 'Z' or 'R'. This is followed by a single 'tooth' linked to an 'A', and then another isolated 'tooth'. It has not been possible to construct a plausible version of the mint-name which can be matched to either ancient or modern geographical sources. There is a place called Marnab in present-day East Azerbaijan (Iran), but this is only a hamlet.

While the mint-name on this dirham cannot be read securely, let alone identified with a known town or city, it can nevertheless be attributed with confidence to a location in Caucasian Albania. This is because the distinctive calligraphy on dirhams from 'Maziyan', as well as the numerous points around the mint-name itself, are characteristic of a series of dirhams struck on the Northern frontier of the Umayyad lands. These coins have been studied in detail by Michael Bates ('The Dirham Mint of the Northern Provinces of the Umayyad Caliphate,' Armenian Numismatic Journal, XV (1989), pp.89-110). He argues convincingly that, while at least ten different Umayyad mint-names referring to locations in this area appear on the coinage, only one mint was normally active at any one time. He concludes that this was a mint which 'moved from place to place as the governor moved his headquarters, taking the name at any time of the city of province where he was.' (op. cit., p.91). Thus when two different mint-names are known for a particular date, this shows that the governor himself had moved from one location to another during that year.

Bates produced a table listing the sequence of dirham mints active in the region during the Umayyad period, which can now be supplemented by a few more recent discoveries. Dirhams with the mysterious mint-name 'Maziyan' are known for AH 92 and 93, for which we also have stylisticaly similar coins from the mints of Janza (AH 92) and Barda'a (AH 92 and 93). These two cities, both located in present-day Azerbaijan (ancient Caucasian Albania), are barely fifty miles apart and so 'Maziyan' can be assigned with confidence to a location in the same area (so Bates, op cit., p. 103). 
Price realized: 15 500 USD

345371.description:
Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 7 24-25 Oct 2024; lot 66.
Estimate: 10 000 USD
Umayyad Caliphate, Silver coinage. AR Dirham (26.2mm, 2.83 g, 3h). Mihrjanqudhaq mint. Dated AH 94 (AD 712/3). Klat 625; Al-'Ajlan p.186, no. 50. Minor edge damage, otherwise EF. Extremely rare.

Mihrjanqudhaq was the name of a district in Jibal, close to the border with Iraq. Its chief town was Saymara. One of the rarest Umayyad dirham mints - Mihrjanqudhaq was completely unknown to Walker - the mint-name is not otherwise found in the Islamic coinage record.

After the foundation of Wasit and the opening of its mint in AH 84, production of dirhams elsewhere in Iraq and the East virtually ceased for several years. This policy was abruptly reversed in AH 90, when dozens of mints began to strike silver in this part of the Islamic world. Some of these had previously issued Arab-Sasanian or early post-Reform silver, while others completely new foundations, and it is clear that their output could vary dramatically. Given their extreme rarity today, it is difficult to see any economic benefits from opening a new mint at Mihrjanqudhaq as they could hardly have made a noticeable contribution to the coinage stocks in circulation. But they might hint at a change in how taxes were raised and collected, or perhaps even a wider and more decentralised approach to provincial administration.
Price realized: 9500 USD

345375.description:
Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 7 24-25 Oct 2024; lot 67.
Estimate: 3000 USD
Umayyad Caliphate, Silver coinage. AR Pattern or Trial (18mm, 6.58 g, 12h). Without mint or date. Obverse: la ilaha illa / Allah wahdahu / la sharik lahu, five simple annulets in outer margin, double linear border around field and outer margin / Reverse: Muhammad / rasul / Allah, five simple annulets in outer margin, double border of dots around field and outer margin. Unpublished. Test marks on edge and below reverse field. VF. Apparently unpublished and believed unique.

This enigmatic piece could be Umayyad or early 'Abbasid. The presence of Muhammad rasul Allah on the reverse recalls early 'Abbasid dirhams, but the five plain annulets are a characteristic of Umayyad post-Reform silver, and are also occasionally found on Umayyad fulus. Its status is unclear, but it has been carefully made on an exceptionally thick flan (2.4mm) and was presumably intended as a pattern or trial of some kind. Both test marks suggest that the piece is made of solid silver. 
Price realized: 1900 USD

345500.description:
Zanj Rebellion. 'Ali b. Muhammad. AH 258-271 / AD 872-884. AR Dirham (24.6mm, 2.99 g, 3h). Al-Madinat al-Mukhtara mint. Dated AH (263) (AD 876/7). Obverse field: la ilaha illa / Allah wahdahu / la sharik lahu / Muhammad ibn / amir al-mu'minin / Reverse field: 'Ali / Muhammad / rasul / Allah / al-Mahdi 'Ali ibn Muhammad. Album 1432; ICV 1424; cf. Morton & Eden 92 (26 April 2018), lot 113 (same dies). Good Fine. Extremely rare.
The name 'Zanj' survives in the modern place-name Zanzibar. They were Black African slaves, brought into southern Iraq to improve agricultural land by clearing away salt. Their living and working conditions were appalling, and in AH 255 they revolted under the leadership of the 'Ali b. Muhammad mentioned on this coin. He was a Persian 'Alid, who proclaimed himself the Mahdi and waged a vicious campaign against the caliph, which saw great destruction and loss of life.
The town of al-Madinat al-Mukhtara was founded by the Zanj downstream from Basra. It was completely destroyed in AH 270 when the revolt was finally quashed by the caliph's brother, al-Muwaffaq, so that its location is not certain.

From CNG Islamic Auction 7. Lot 197. Price realized USD 2625 plus commission.

345651.description:
'Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Mu'tadid. AH 279-289 / AD 892-902. AV Dinar (23.2mm, 4.11 g, 11h). Amid mint. Dated AH 288 (AD 900/01). Cf. CNG Islamic Auction 3 (27 April 2023) lot 108 (dated AH 289); Bernardi type 211 (not recorded for this mint); Album 241. Near VF, buckled flan. Excessively rare.
Amid is one of the rarest mints for 'Abbasid gold. This coin was struck in the first recorded year when dinars were issued there.

Amid was besieged and captured by al-Mu'tadid's forces in AH 286, and the caliph himself remained in the city for a few weeks thereafter. Having taken the city, one of al-Mu'tadid's first actions was to order the destruction of Amid's defensive walls, which suggests that he may not then have envisaged holding the city permanently. However, it appears that only a portion of the wall was damaged, and in the event Amid remained an 'Abbasid city until the advent of the Hamdanids.

From CNG Islamic auction 7. Lot 95. Price realized USD 10000 plus commission.

Independent Emirate of Spain 132-138 H. Anonymous.
Silver Dirham 135 H., al-Andalus. Standard Umayyad silver dirham type. 2,87g. Tawfiq Ibrahim/Alberto Canto, Moneda andalusi en la Alhambra, Granada 1997, p. 101 n° 14; Miles CUS -; Klat -.
Extremely rare. Extremely fine.

This and the following coin are among of the greatest rarities in Muslim Spanish coins. Published for the first time in 1948 in an article by Casto del Rivero, El arte monetario de la Espana musulmana, in Revista de Archivos, Bibliothecos y Museos, LIV, pp.53-72, doubted by George C. Miles, when he published his Coinage of The Umayyads of Spain in 1950, p. 126, who had only seen bad illustrations and regarded it as an isolated emission. 348087.description:
ex Leu Numismatik auction 7, lot 2076

Original description:

ISLAMIC, 'Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Mu'tadid, AH 279-289 / AD 892-902. Dirham (Silver, 23 mm, 2.81 g, 10 h), citing the caliph al-Mu'tadid billah. al-Mawsil, AH 2[8]8 = 900/1. Album -. Unique and of great historical interest. Somewhat crystallized and with areas of weakness, otherwise, very fine. From the Tabib Collection, formed over the past 40 years.

In the year 288 AH, the city of al-Mawsil was in turmoil and fiercely contested between different tribes fighting each other. Unfortunately, the name in the third line of the inner legend on the reverse of this coin is illegible, leaving the identity of the head of the clan who struck the issue in the dark. The appearance of al-Mu'tamid's name in the fourth line, on the other hand, shows that the contestant pledged public allegiance to the caliph in an attempt to legitimate his own claim to power. The turmoil eventually ended five years later, when Abu'l-Hayja' Abdallah, a member of one those families, the Hamdanids, was appointed governor of Mosul by the Abbasid caliph al-Muktafi.

349841.description:
Bought in Morocco, this qirat is not easy to identify...
In the picture on the right we find the classic sentence with Allah in the 3rd line.
In the left photo, I think we have "Ali" at the bottom and at the end of third line I think we have "ibn".
If my reading is correct, then it would be either "Tashfin ibn Ali" or "Iskhaq ibn Ali", but the beginning of the third line "Yusuf" instead of Tashfin or Iskhaq....
I checked Tonegawa photos or Vives catalog and I did not find similar writing.
So I need help from arabic readers or Almoravid specialists; thanks in advance

351019.description:
This Artuqid of Halab BI dirham which was offered on a major auction house as a coin of Najm al-Din Il- Ghazi I is in fact belonging to different Artuqid ruler. 
After deep research and closer look, and thanks to Dr. Hasan al-Halabi, this coin belongs to the Artuqid ruler of Halab Fakhr al-Din Balak Ghazi , A-B1820. We can see his name clear on the right image : فخر الدين بلك غازي 
There is another coin on Zeno which is wrongly attributed to Najm a-Din Il-Gazi # 243034. Please move it to the certain ruler : Balak Ghazi.

351038.description:
Ex Stephen Album Rare Coins Auction 51 23-26 Jan 2025, lot 60.
Starting price: 550 USD
ARAB-ARMENIAN: Muhammad, ca. 690-700+, AR zuzun (3.06g), "ShY", year "37", A-H97, with Muhammad in Arabic in ObQ2 & awsrwy (Khusro) in Pahlavi before the obverse bust, pleasing F-VF, RRR. This type is believed to have been issued within the regions of Armenia or Azerbaijan. The mint name is derived from a prototype from the Shiraz mint, and the date, while convincingly 37, is probably just a copy from the prototype. Also of considerable interest is the Greek letter Ph instead of a star within the right crescent in the obverse margin. Other types have a different Greek letter in one of the crescents in either the obverse or reverse margin. These Greek characters are of undetermined meaning, but the use of Greek does support the assignment to the Caucasian lands, where Byzantine silver coins were circulating throughout the 7th centuries, first introduced by Heraclius circa 615 AD. This type is currently assigned to the very last years of the 7th and early 8th century. The weight of 3.00-3.25g corresponds quite accurately to half the weight of the Byzantine hexagram (about 6.0-6.5g). Another example was sold in our Auction 14, lot 98, back in 2012.
Price realized: 700 USD

351748.description:
Mamluk AE fals, Sha'ban II AH764-778, Halab, undated. Balog 471. Legend "al-Malik al-Ashraf". See Zeno #248449 for a clear example. 
Coin is an overstrike associated with another type, which I believe is Balog 527. Legend of Balog 527 is "al-Malik al-Salih" and current attribution of Balog 527 is as follows:
Mamluk AE Fals, Hajji II 1st reign, AH783-784 , Hamah, undated. See Zeno #295319 for a clear example. 

Now of course a coin from AH764-778 can't be overstruck on a coin from AH783-784. But looking at this coin, I think it is Balog 471 on top of 527. 

Possibilities:
A) Balog 527 is mis-attributed, not from Hajji II but from an earlier ruler, for example Salih AH752-755 
B) I am wrong, it is not 471 on 527, but instead 527 on top of 471 or I am wrong about this coin representing of one of these types.

353890.description:
Balog 507 Plate XIX 507; Album 954; SNAT Hamah 538-546

AE fals; Hamah mint, undated; 2.10 g., 15.73 mm. max., 270°

Obv.: Circular line border. Legend in three lines, apparently ضرب(= duriba = struck at) / الملك المنصور (al-malik al-Mansur = the king al-Mansur) / بحماه (= Hamah).

Rev.: Circular line border. Two interwoven linear tetralobes. In the center, a crescent. Pellets in the free spaces.

The single specimen recorded by Balog reads الملك ا (= al-Malik a / لمنصور (= Mansur). It is attributed to `Ali II (al-Mansur `Ala al-Din Ali) (778-783 A.H. = 1377-1381 A.D.). It was tentatively attributed to the Trablus/Tripoli mint by analogy to Balog 506, which bears a similar crescent (per Zeno # 68065). SNAT Hama attributes the emission to Muhammad II and Hama, presumably based on specimens with more complete legends. According to Balog, there is no circular line border on either side. However, while most of SNAT Hama 538-546 do not contain such a border, 541 has an obverse border and 546 has a reverse border. The full legend is per Zeno # 294628.

May Allah bless him and grant him peace' in Arabic); in the margin, 'Muḥammad rasūl Allāh arsalahū bi al-hudā wa dīn al-ḥaqq liyuẓhirahū ʿalā al-dīn kullih wa law kariha al-mushrikūn' ('Muhammad is the messenger of Allah. 354471.description:
BYZANTINE EMPIRE. ARAB-BYZANTINE, UMAYYAD CALIPHATE.
Gold Solidus - Dinar, circa AH 65-86 = AD 685-705. Uncertain North African mint (Carthage?).
Struck under 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, imitating the types of Heraclius. Obv: NON EST DEUS NISI IPSE SOLOL CIS ET (truncated and garbled version of 'Non est Deus nisi ipse solus cui socius non est'), crowned and draped facing male busts (Heraclius and Heraclius Constantine), the left bearded, each crown topped by trefoil ornament (originally crosses). Rev: L... T(?) OMMINNAV (truncated and garbled version of 'Deus dominus noster sapiens magnus eternus omnia noscens'), T (truncated cross) on three steps.

Mint State; wonderfully bright and lustrous.

In the mid-to-late 7th century AD, after the final and longest of the Roman-Persian Wars (602–628) had exhausted both great powers of antiquity, a new force emerged from Arabia. Within fifty years, the armies of Islam had forged a multi-continental empire under the Umayyad Caliphate, swiftly absorbing territories once essential to Roman wealth, including Egypt and - crucially for this coin - Carthage in North Africa. Contemporary observers, witnessing the speed of these conquests, might be forgiven for believing the end times had arrived.

It was in this extraordinary context that the so-called “Arab-Byzantine” or “Pseudo-Byzantine” coinage was created, typically dated to circa 695–715. The present gold piece (struck to a slightly lower standard than the Byzantine solidus) draws heavily on earlier prototypes minted by Emperor Heraclius (AD 610–641). The obverse features two confronting imperial busts - resembling Heraclius and his son - whose diadem crosses have been replaced by trefoil ornaments, while the reverse modifies the familiar cross-on-steps into a T-bar or “mutilated” cross. Inscriptions on both sides transliterate the Islamic shahada into Latin, albeit in a truncated and garbled manner, effectively merging Islamic religious doctrine with the visual vocabulary of Byzantine coinage.

Carthage itself fell to the Arabs in 695 and changed hands twice more before being decisively retaken in 698. Some sources say the city was destroyed immediately, while others suggest it lingered until 705. The precise mint location for coins bearing these figural motifs remains debated; they may have been struck in Carthage before or after its destruction, or possibly in nearby Tunis or the newly founded city of Kairouan. Whatever the specific site, these coins reflect the Caliphate’s pragmatic approach: rather than introduce entirely new coin designs, they adapted well-known Byzantine types to reassure local users, subtly eliminating overt Christian symbols and proclaiming Islamic faith in Latin script.

Rarity further elevates the significance of this dinar - and the next lot, a corresponding tremissis (1/3 dinar). Both were issued in limited quantities during the transitional period between the last days of Byzantine authority in North Africa and the establishment of fully Arabic coinage. Together, they offer a fascinating glimpse into a world in flux, marking the twilight of Roman influence and the meteoric rise of an Islamic empire - one that, in a single generation, redrew the map of the Mediterranean and left contemporaries convinced they were witnessing the dawn of a new age.

Reference: Wilkes-143; 
Dr. Busso Peus Nachf., Auction 428, 28-29 April 2021; Lot 620 (same dies, hammer: 22,000 EUR); 
Heritage World Coin Auctions, NYINC Signature Sale 3061, 7-8 January 2018; Lot 32117 (var. legend, hammer: 22,000 USD);
Nomos 2, 18 May 2010; Lot 230 (hammer: 27,000 CHF).

Rarity: An issue of the utmost rarity and historical significance.
Die Axis: 8h.
Diameter: 14 mm.
Weight: 4.39 g.

Dirham Kekhalifahan Bani Umayyah masa AL-Walid bin Abdul Malik. Dicetak pada tahun 96 Hijriah di Kota Wasit.

Al-Walid bin Abdul Malik merupakan seorang khalifah ke-6 Bani Umayyah. Ia memerintah pada tahun 86 - 96 Hijriah (705-715 Masehi). Ia berkuasa menggantikan ayahnya, Abdul Malik bin Marwan.

Pembangunan2 yg dilakukan Al-Walid bin Abdul Malik. Dari merenovasi MASJID NABAWI, hingga Membangun MASJID UMAYYAH di DAMASKUS :

Pada tahun 88 Hijriah (707 Masehi) Al-Walid memerintahkan perluasan Masjid Nabawi di Madinah. Untuk pertama kalinya, menara masjid dibangun dengan empat menara di Masjid Nabawi. Al-Walid juga memerintahkan pembangunan jalan dan sumur-sumur di Hijaz.
Ia juga memugar dan membangun kembali bekas bangunan basilika kristen yang terletak di Damaskus dan mengubahnya menjadi Masjid. Sebelum dilakukan pemugaran, bekas basilika itu memiliki dua buah menara. Al-Walid membiarkan menara tersebut dan tidak merusaknya. Ia bahkan membangun satu menara lagi di sisi utara pelataran. Masjid tersebut dikenal dengan nama MASJID UMAYYAH.

354476.description:
ABBASID DIRHAM reign Al-Muqtadir Billah citing Abu Al-Abbas, Mint Surra man ra'a, 317 AH (year hajar Aswad Missing because Syiah Qaramitha)

●Weight : 2,61 gram
●Diameter : 26 mm

(Indonesian language)
Al-Muqtadir Bilah, atau Abu Fadhl. Berkuasa 908-932 Masehi / 295-320 Hijriah. Ia khalifah abbasiyah ke-18. Belum pernah ada seorang khalifah yang diangkat sebelumnya yang lebih muda darinya. Ia memerintah dari usia 13 tahun.

Peristiwa Kudeta Yang Dialami Al-Muqtadir :

Kudeta 1 : Tahun 296 Hijirah 
Pejabat negara & militer yang tak puas diangkatnya Al-Muqtadir, mencoba untuk mengkudeta al-Muqtadir. Imam Thabari mencatat nama-nama mereka: Muhammad bin Dawud al-Jarrah, Abu Mutsanna bin Abi Ya’qub. Mereka ingin membunuh al-Muqtadir & mengangkat Abdullah bin al-Mu’tazz. Akan tetapi Abdullah bin al-Mu’tazz berkuasa hanya sehari-semalam. Al-Muqtadir & pasukan setianya berbalik melawan sehingga kudeta itu gagal.

Kudeta 2 : Tahun 317 Hijirah Al-Muqtadir mencopot Mu’nis dari pemerintahan & mengganti dengan Harun bin Ghalib. Mu’nis yg tak terima melancarkan pemberontakan & membawa pasukannya. kekhalifahan kemudian diambil oleh Muhammad bin Al-Muhtadhid bergelar “Al-Qahir Billah”. Tapi ia tak memenuhi bayaran tentara istana. Maka para tentara istana menuntut Al-Muqtadir kembali menjadi khalifah.

TRAGEDI BERDARAH, DICURINYA HAJAR ASWAD DAN PEMBANTAIAN PARA JAMAAH HAJI PADA ERA AL-MUQTADIR :

Tahun 317 Hijriah atau 930 Masehi, ada kelompok yang mencuri Hajar Aswad. yaitu kelompok syiah bernama Qarmatian/Qaramitah yang dipimpin oleh Abu Tahir Al Qaramithiy. Mulanya, Abu Tahir & pengikutnya berpura-pura menunaikan haji agar diperbolehkan masuk ke Mekkah. ia bersama sekitar 600 penunggang kuda dan 900 pasukan. Pada 8 Dzulhijjah 317 Hijriah, ia membuat rusuh di sekitar Mekkah. Ia berdiri didepan pintu Ka'bah dan menyeru kepada para pasukannya untuk menghabisi para jamaah haji, ia banyak membunuh jamaah haji. Pembantaian terjadi di sekitar Ka'bah, Mayat mayat mereka lempar kedalam sumur zam-zam, ia menjarah harta benda jamaah haji, lalu kain kiswah ia robek, dan ia mengambil paksa Hajar Aswad, ia memukulnya dengan palu sampai Hajar Aswad terlepas dari sisi Ka'bah. lalu ia simpan di masjid Al-Dirar (yaitu masjid mereka sendiri). Al-Muqtadir sebenarnya tidak diam saja mendengar kejadian itu. Ia mencoba menawarkan 50 ribu dinar kepada kelompok Syiah Qaramitah, tapi ditolak. Barulah sekitar 20/22 tahun berselang pada masa khalifah Al-Muthi’ Hajar Aswad berhasil dikembalikan tetapi dengan keadaan rusak parah dan dengan tebusan yang besar. Hajar Aswad kembali dengan keadaan menjadi 7 bagian, lalu ia dibingkai dengan perak agar menjaga bentuknya lalu ia dikembalikan ke posisinya semula yaitu disisi Ka'bah.

354478.description:
ISLAMIC. UMAYYAD CALIPHATE. temp. Yazid II.
Gold Dinar, dated AH 102 = AD 720/1. Ifriqiya.

About Extremely Fine; an impressive example.

Yazid II was the ninth Umayyad caliph, ruling from AH 101–105 (AD 720–724). He inherited a vast empire stretching from Spain to Central Asia but faced internal unrest and economic challenges. The son of Caliph Abd al-Malik, he is particularly noted for issuing the iconoclastic edict, which ordered the destruction of Christian images in the Levant, possibly as a response to rising tensions between Muslims and non-Muslims. His reign also saw continued frontier conflicts, including battles against the Byzantines and unrest in Khorasan. Unlike his father and brother, al-Walid I, Yazid was criticised for his indulgent lifestyle, and some sources, including al-Tabari, suggest that his death was hastened by excess.

His dinars are relatively rare today and remain highly prized among collectors of Islamic coinage.

Reference: Album-134A; Bernardi-44Ca; NGSA 16, lot 75 (hammer: 20,000 CHF).
Rarity: Extremely Rare and desirable issue.
Die Axis: 12h.
Diameter: 19 mm.
Weight: 4.31 g.

(Indonesian language)
Al-Qahir Billah, berkuasa dari 932-934 Masehi atau 320-322 Hijriah. Nama aslinya Abu Mansur Muhammad bin Mu’tadhid. khalifah ke-19 Abbasiyah. Ia saudara sebapak dgn Al-Muqtadir beda ibu.

Pada tahun 932 Masehi atau 320 Hijriah, Mu'nis dan para pasukannya kembali menuju Baghdad. Mereka mencoba merebut Kekuasaan yang saat itu dipegang oleh Khalifah Al-Muqtadir. setelah pada tahun 317 Mu'nis dan pasukannya gagal mengambil alih kekuasaan, akhirnya pada tahun ini mereka sukses menggulingkan Al Muqtadir. Mereka membunuh Al-Muqtadir. Setelah berhasil, Mu'nis menunjuk Al-Qahir. Al Qahir yang sudah berambisi langsung naik takhta kekuasaan menggantikan Al muqtadir.

Al-Qahir menjelma menjadi pemimpin yang amat ditakuti dan tidak segan membunuh dan menyiksa orang yang tak sependapat dengannya. Menurut buku karya ulama seperti Imam As-suyuthi dan Ibnu Katsir. Bahkan Menteri Agama indonesia yang pertama yang sekaligus Ulama yaitu Buya Hamka menulis kisah tentang Al-Qahir dengan jelas. Menurut catatan sejarah, Al-Qahir menambahkan gelarnya dengan AL-MUNTAQIM MIN A’DA’ALLAH LI-DINILLAH yang mempunyai arti (YANG MELAKUKAN BALAS DENDAM KEPADA MUSUH-MUSUH ALLAH). Gelar itu pula yang dia cantumkan PADA MATA UANG DIRHAM & DINAR yang dicetak khusus spesial hanya pada tahun 322 Hijriah. Akan tetapi pada tahun itulah juga ia diturunkan dari kursi khalifah.

Turunnya Al-Qahir Dari Kursi Kekhalifahan dan Peristiwa Pencongkelan Mata :

Kekejaman demi kekejaman yg dilakukan AL-Qahir membuat tentara istana mulai muak. Mereka berhasil menangkap al-Qahir. Mereka kemudian membai’at Al-Radi (anak dari Al-Muqtadir). Al-Qahir dipaksa untuk menyatakan pengundurannya. Namun, Al-Qahir ngeyel dan menolak mundur karena merasa dia masih Khalifah yang sah. Menurut Imam Suyuthi, sang khalifah baru (Al-Radi) lalu mencungkil kedua mata Al-Qahir dengan paku yg panas sehingga berakibat ia Buta. Al-Qahir pun di penjara.

Naik tahta khalifah pertama kali :
Ia naik takhta pertama melalui konflik al muqtadir dengan Menteri Mu'nis al-Mudzaffar. Ia terpilih sebagai Khalifah 929 Masehi atau 317 Hijriah, ketika Mu'nis melancarkan kudeta & menggulingkan al-Muqtadir. Tetapi kudeta itu gagal dan al muqtadir kembali ke kursi khalifah

932 Masehi atau 320 Hijriah, Mu'nis dan pasukannya kembali ke Baghdad. Al-Muqtadir & pasukannya mencoba menghadapinya, tapi ia terbunuh terkena tombak pasukan Mu’nis.
Al-Qahir terpilih kembali menjadi khalifah. Tetapi saat berkuasa, Al Qahir malah mencoba membunuh Wazirnya yaitu Ibnu Muqlah. Tetapi Muqlah berhasil bersembunyi dan membalik menghasur agar Al Qahir turun takhta.

Para tentara dan petinggi istana ingin menurunkan khalifah. Mereka berhasil menangkap al-Qahir yg mencoba melarikan diri. Mereka kemudian membai’at Al-Radi (anak dari Al-Muqtadir). (Indonesia Language)
Al Mu’tasim Billah, yang bernama asli Abu Ishaq al-Mu'tasim bin Harun Arrasyid, ia adalah Khalifah Bani Abbasiyah ke-8. ia memerintah pada tahun 218-227 Hijriah (833 - 842 Masehi). Ia menggantikan Saudaranya yaitu Al-Ma’mun. Julukan Al Mu’tashim Billah berarti ‘Yang berlindung kepada Allah’. Al Mu’tashim adalah seorang yang dikenal memiliki tubuh yang kuat. Badannya kekar, dan ia memiliki sikap militer dengan kedisiplinan yang tinggi. Ia juga dikenal karena membentuk pasukan militer Budak Turki yang sangat kuat, sehingga sangat membantu saudaranya Al-ma’mun saat memerintah.

Pemindahan ibukota dari BAGHDAD ke SURRA MAN RA’A :

Pada tahun 220 Hijriah Ibukota yang sebelumnya di Baghdad dipindahkan oleh Al-Mu’tasim ke Surra Man Ra’a yang memiliki arti “Menyenangkan bagi yang melihat/menyaksikan”. Beberapa sejarawan mengatakan penyebab pemindahan ibukota kekhalifahan itu karena penduduk Baghdad pada saat itu mengeluhkan tentang tingkah laku bala tentara yang dibawa oleh Al-Mu’tasim yang berasal dari keturunan turki. Karena bala tentara turki tersebut sering mengganggu ketenangan dan sering menaiki kuda di sekitar Baghdad, hingga kota tersebut penuh sesak. Saat pembangunan kota baru itu Ia mendatangkan arsitek pilihan dari berbagai negeri Islam untuk membangun kota itu dan mendirikan istana. Ia juga membangun pemukiman para pedagang, buruh, tentara, panglima, pegawai, dan masyarakat pada umumnya. Akan tetapi kota ini lama kelamaan tidak berkembang dan ibukota kembali ke Baghdad pada masa Khalifah ke-15 yaitu Al-Mutamid.

Kisah dibalik peristiwa penakhlukan kota AMMURIYAH(AMORA) dan Menjaga martabat Muslimah :

Terdapat sebuah kisah yang menunjukkan kepedulian Khalifah Al-Mu'tashim kepada kaum muslimah. Peristiwa ini tercatat dalam kisah penaklukan Kota Ammuriyah (Amoria) Tahun 223 Hijriah. Dikisahkan, pada Tahun 837 Masehi atau 223 Hijriah, ada seorang muslimah yang dilecehkan oleh kaum Romawi. Ketika ia tengah lewat, muslimah ini dilecehkan oleh sekelompok kaum Romawi. Kainnya dikaitkan ke paku sehingga ketika berdiri, terlihatlah sebagian auratnya. 
Wanita muslimah itu berteriak memanggil nama Khalifah Al-Mu'tashim billah dengan kalimat yang legendaris: "WAA MU'TASHIMAA" yang artinya "Tolong aku, Di mana engkau wahai Mu'tashim Billah". 
Kabar ini lantas tersebar dan sampai ke telinga Al-Mu'tashim. Hal ini membuat sang khalifah menerjunkan puluhan ribu pasukannya untuk menyerbu Ammuriyah. Adapula yang meriwayatkan bahwa tentara berbaris dengan sangat panjang. Barisan ini tidak putus dari gerbang istana khalifah di Baghdad hingga Ammuriyah. Mereka mengepung Ammuriyah selama lima bulan. Pada pertempuran itu, pasukan muslim berhasil membebaskan kota tersebut dari tangan Romawi. Sebanyak 30 ribu tentara Romawi terbunuh dan 30 ribu lainnya dijadikan tawanan.
Al-Mu'tashim mencari laporan tentang wanita yang memanggil namanya itu. Kemudian berkata "Wahai Saudariku, apakah aku telah memenuhi seruanmu atasku?". Sang wanita itu pun mengangguk terharu.

354483.description:
ARAB-BYZANTINE. Imitating Heraclius (ca. AD 695-710 / AH 65-92). AV solidus (16mm, 4.35 gm, 6h). NGC Choice MS 4/5 - 5/5. Uncertain North African mint (likely Carthage). [NON EST DEUS NI]SI IPSЄ SOLOL CIS ЄT (truncated and garbled version of Non est Deus nisi ipse solus cui socius non est), crowned and draped facing male busts (Heraclius and Heraclius Constantine), the left bearded, each crown topped by trefoil ornament / d' (or pellet) Є SNCIPIAS MN ЄT OMNNA N (truncated and garbled version of Deus dominus noster sapiens magnus eternus omnia noscens), T (truncated cross) on three steps. Wilkes 143. Extremely rare! Sharply struck on a compact flan, with lustrous fields.

The early decades after the Islamic conquest of Arabia, the Levant, and North Africa witnessed a transitional era wherein the burgeoning Umayyad Caliphate experimented with various forms of coinage based upon that of the new-conquered territories. The East Romans had long maintained a mint at Carthage in North Africa that produced gold solidi and fractions of a peculiar thick fabric. In the mid-seventh century the mint had produced vast numbers of solidi depicting Heraclius and his son Heraclius Constantine in a frontal pose, with the familiar Cross Potent on the reverse. Carthage fell to the Arabs in AD 695 and switched hands twice again over the next five years before the city's final destruction circa 698. Although half a century had passed since Heraclius ruled, his solidi remained in wide circulation and the new Arab masters produced their own version of this ubiquitous coin. Bearing a Latinized version of the Islamic statement of faith (the shahada) slightly different than the "canonical" form later adopted on the coinage of Caliph 'Abd al-Malik (the legends translate to There is no god but He alone who has no associate / God, our wise Lord, the Great, the Eternal, the All-Knowing), it represents a fascinating period in early Islamic history. The use of Latin in place of Arabic at once evinces the Arab conquerors' interest in preserving a familiar coinage - indeed Roman officials were likely retained to mint these new pieces - while at the same time "de-Christianizing" it through removal of blatant Christian symbolism (the crosses on the emperors' helmets have been reduced trefoil ornaments and the cross-on-steps on the reverse is now a "T-bar on steps" or a "mutilated cross"). It also relates the Umayyads' concern to distance their claim to caliphate from the foundational role of Muhammad, whose name does not appear on the coin (the Umayyad caliphs certainly recognized the role of Muhammad as the founder of their faith, but they did not utilize him as the chief legitimizing pillar of their rule). Surviving examples of this type are extremely rare, numbering in the high single digits or low teens, presenting historically minded collectors a unique opportunity to acquire what is likely the best specimen extant.

354490.description:
Islamic Dynasties

Umayyad Caliphate. Abd al-Malik (AH 65-86 / AD 685-705). AR drachm (30mm, 3.51 gm, 9h). VF. Uncertain mint, possibly Damascus. AH 75 (ca. AD 693-694). Bism illah la i-laha illa Allah wa-hdahu Muhammad ra-sul Allah (In the name of God, there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the Messenger of God) (Arabic), bust right, wearing armor with crosshatch pattern and domed headdress topped with pellet in annulet, sheathed sword in right hand; may his sovereign glory increase! (Pahlawi), Khusru (Pahlawi) double border, star-in-crescents in margin / Amir al-mu'minin (Commander of the Faithful), kh-l-f-t Allah (Deputy of God), nasr-Allah ("Victory of God" or "May God give assistance") (all in Arabic), arch supported by columns, grounded spear between columns with ribbons floating to left; praise (Pahlawi), triple border, stars-in-crescents in margin, all within dotted border. Cf. Treadwell (2005), cat. no. 1 (reverse, same die) and cat. no. 2 (obverse, same die). Cf. Morton & Eden, Auction 85 (27 April 2017), lot 3 for same dies. Gaube 2.2.2.5 (obverse) & 2.3.2.4 (reverse). An exceedingly rare and perplexing issue, represented by a mere three examples in sales archives in the past 20 years. A lovely specimen in hand with light toning around the devices.

Most early Islamic coinage imitates Sasanian types by featuring a ruler on the obverse that exudes religious authority with a reverse that has long-standing religious symbolism of the region, not Islamic symbolism. The "Mihrab and 'Anaza" coin is unique in that the ruler on the obverse demonstrates his military prowess with a reverse that is much more overtly Islamic. This issue has been of much debate for many years, partly because it deviates from the norm in many of its features and partly because it lacks any mintmarks or dates that would help explain why it is so different.
The ruler on this obverse cannot be confirmed, as the name in the legend is that of earlier Sasanian ruler Khusru II, but it is reasonable to assume that it is Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, as he marked a crucial transition point in the early Umayyad Caliphate. He was of the first generation of born-Muslims and was the last caliph to issue gold coinage that imitated Sasanian coinage and featured a ruler on the coin. Treadwell notes that coins must have consistent imagery in order to be trustworthy as holding a particular value, especially through changes of government.

In trying to date this issue and explain its elements using similar coins, Treadwell and Bates both argue that the Standing Caliph issue of AH 74-77 was an immediate precursor to the Mihrab and 'Anaza. While the Standing Caliph issues do have a sheathed sword, that is where the commonalities end – the abnormal headdress and crosshatch pattern on the chest are not reflected in the Standing Caliph. Gaube concludes that the headdress may be a mixture of Persian, Byzantine, and Visigoth headdresses, signifying that al-Malik is ruler of the East and West. However, the differences in the pattern on the chest may not be relevant. Miles concludes that the headdress is a helmet, which would explain the crosshatch pattern as being chainmail. Morton & Eden propose that the Arab-Hephthalite issue struck by Yazid b. Muhallab in AH 84 also has a figure in chainmail and with a sheathed sword, and as the headdress also bears remarkable similarities to that of this issue, this ruler is probably wearing a helmet.

The reverse is what gives the Mihrab and 'Anaza issue its name, but it is not without its own debates. The 'Anaza is the clearest – it is a spear like the one that the prophet Muhammad used to indicate the direction in which to pray. However, it is uncertain when Mihrabs became so common in mosques that the symbolism would have been recognizable on a coin, so some scholars doubt that the archway on this coin is a Mihrab. This coin is supposedly the first evidence of a Mihrab, but because archways like this are featured in architecture of all three Abrahamic religions, Treadwell concludes that this is not actually a Mihrab. Abd al-Malik b. Marwan also had coinage that clearly imitated Byzantine types, so while some have suggested that this is specifically a niched Mihrab, others are not certain that it is a Mihrab at all.

For such an experimental transitional issue, and with such few surviving examples, there were quite a few dies. Treadwell's examples consist of seven obverse dies and six reverse dies, and others have come to market since the publication of his paper. There is also at least one example that was countermarked in Hephthalite territory, far from Damascus where many assume that this coin was struck. When this is considered along with the lack of mint mark or date, the sword, and the armor and helmet on the portrait, one might conclude that this coin could have been struck for some military campaign.

The mixture of Sasanian and Islamic elements makes this a perplexing instance in isolation, but when taken into a broader context, it may be the missing link in a time rife with cultural diffusion and changing state religions. Among the myriad questions about its meanings and origins, there is no doubt that it is a physical representation of a critical inflection point in the culture wars of its time.

ABBASID DIRHAM reign AL-MA'MUN mint Madinat Al-Salam(Baghdad) Year 198 AH

●Weight : 2,5 gram
●Diameter : 23 mm

Khalifah Abdullah Al Makmun merupakan khalifah ke-7 dari Bani Abbasiyah. Ia berkuasa selama 20 tahun pada tahun 198-218 Hijriah (813 sampai 833 Masehi). Ia bernama lengkap Abdullah Abu Abbas bin Ar-Rasyid. Khalifah Al-Ma'mun dikenal sebagai pemimpin yang jenius dan gigih dalam mempelajari ilmu pengetahuan. Bahkan, masa pemerintahannya merupakan puncak kejayaan dari Bani Abbasiyah. Ia menggantikan khalifah sebelumnya sekaligus saudaranya sendiri yaitu Al-Amin 

Jalaluddin as-Suyuthi dalam bukunya menggambarkan sosok putra Harun ar-Rasyid ini sebagai pribadi yang istimewa karena memiliki sejumlah karakter seperti memiliki ambisi yang kuat, kesabaran, pengetahuan yang luas, cerdik, berwibawa, dan toleran.

Tidak seorang pun dari khalifah Abbasiyah yang lebih pintar darinya. Dia juga pembicara yang fasih dan lantang. Tentang kefasihannya dia berkata "Juru bicara Muawiyah adalah 'Amr bin Ash, juru bicara Abdul Malik adalah Hajjaj, dan juru bicara saya adalah saya sendiri". Disebutkan juga dalam Bani Abbas itu ada Fatihah (pembuka) , Wasithah (penengah) dan Khatimah (penutup). Adapun pembukanya ialah Khalifah As-Saffah (khalifah pertama), penengahnya adalah Al-Ma'mun dan penutupnya adalah Al-Mu'thadid.
Disebutkan juga bahwa saat bulan Ramadhan Al-Ma'mun bisa menghatamkan Al-Quran hingga 30 kali.

Beberapa Kejadian masa pemerintahan Al-Ma'mun :

Pada tahun 201 Hijriah dia mencopot saudara Al-Mu'taman dari putra mahkota dan memberikannya kepada Ali Ar-Ridha bin Musa Al-Kazhim bin Ja'far Shadiq. Al-Ma'mun jugalah yang memberi gelar Ar-Ridha dan ia juga mencetak Dirham dengan menggunakan nama Ali Ar-Ridha. 

Pada tahun 215 Hijriah Al-Ma'mun berangkat untuk menakhlukkan romawi. Dalam penyerangan itu dia berhasil membuka benteng Qurrah lewat sebuah pertempuran sengit. Dia juga berhasil menahlukkan benteng Majidah.

Pada Tahun 216 Hijriah dia kembali menahlukkan beberapa benteng romawi dan menuju mesir lalu menetap disana. Dengan demikian dia adalah khalifah pertama dari kalangan bani abbasiyah yang memasuki mesir.

Pada tahun 218 Hijriah sekaligus tahun terakhir dia memerintah, ia menguji para Ulama tentang pendapat mereka mengenai Al-Quran. Untuk itu dia menulis kepada pembantunya yang ada di Baghdad agar meminta Ishaq bin Ibrahim Al-Khuzai untuk menguji para ulama. Peristiwa tersebut dikenal dengan MIHNA.

Pada tahun 218 Hijriah, disebuah wilayah yang disebut Badidun Al-Ma'mun wafat.

Beberapa ulama dan tokoh besar wafat saat Al-Ma'mun berkuasa diantaranya adalah : Sufyan bin 'Uyainah, Imam As-Syafi'i (SALAH SATU IMAM MAZHAB), Yunus bin Bakir (orang yang banyak mengisahkan tentang peperangan di zaman Rasulullah), Ma'ruf Al-Karkhi (seseorang yg terkenal dengan kezuhudannya), Ali-Ridha bin Musa Al-Kazim (Salah seorang imam Syiah).

●Video 1 : Dirhan Bani Abbasiyah masa Al-Ma'mun Abdullah bin Harun Arrasyid, dicetak pada tahun 198 Hijriah (813 Masehi), di kota Madinat Al-Salam (Baghdad).

Dirham ini ditemukan di SUMATERA. Merupakan jejak sejarah yang sangat berharga karena merupakan saksi bisu bahwa masuknya Islam di Nusantara sudah sangat lama yaitu sekitar 1200-1400 Tahun yang lalu.

354708.description:
Pre-reform issues, Arab-Byzantine. North Africa. AV Solidus (13.9mm, 4.39 g, 7h). Without mint-name (struck in Carthage). Undated (struck circa AH 80-85 / AD 700-705. NON EST dS NISI IPSE [...] S E I (for NON EST DEUS NISI IPSE SOLUS CUI SOCIUS NON EST, 'There is no God but He Alone, to whom there is no associate'), Two facing Imperial busts, wearing trifoliate crowns, the left bust bearded, the right bust clean-shaven / [DEUS MAGNUS] (?) ET OMNI IN MANVS, for 'God is Great, and everything is in His hands', Cippus set on three steps. Cf. Bernardi 8 (no point below or to right of cippus); Album 115 . AU, a superb example with full lustre and die-polish lines visible. Extremely rare.

The first part of the reverse legend is coarsely engraved and difficult to read, but ET OMNI IN MANVS is extremely clear. Bernardi interpreted a similar inscription which he read as OMN N IN M A NO (p. 101, the fifth example) as a highly abbreviated version of 'Omnia Noscens Ingenitus Magnus Alius Non est', but this is perhaps more ingenious than plausible. It seems more likely that this, like the legend on the coin offered here, is in fact a version of 'God is Great, and everything is in His hands'.

355632.description:
ARAB SASANIAN DRACHM, ABD ALLAH BIN ZUBAIR (rival caliph) , Year YE-60 (71-72 AH), Mint DA+P (Fasa).

•Weight : 4,12 gram
•Diameter : 29,5 mm

Beautiful condition, extremly fine

(INDONESIAN LANGUAGE)
Wahyu islamic ancient ~ 15 April 2025

Abdullah bin Zubair bin Awwam yang juga dikenal sebagai Ibnu Zubair adalah salah seorang sahabat Nabi Muhammad. Ia dijuluki dengan (sahabat kecil) karena saat itu Abdullah bin Zubair masih anak-anak. Ia juga merupakan pemimpin kekhalifahan yang berbasis di Makkah yang menyaingi Kekhalifahan Umayyah dari tahun 62 – 72/73 Hijriah (680-692 Masehi). Dia adalah putra dari Zubair bin Awwam dan Asma' binti Abu Bakar. Ayahnya adalah sahabat nabi dan 10 orang yang dijamin masuk surga oleh Nabi. Ibunya adalah anak sahabat Nabi sekaligus Khalifah pertama yaitu Sayyidina Abu Bakar AS-Shiddiq.

Ibnu Zubair juga merupakan anak pertama yang lahir saat Rasulullah dan para pengikutnya Hijriah ke Mekkah pada tahun 1 Hijriah. Dalam kitab imam as-suyuti di Tarikh Khulafa, Pada saat ia lahir Rasulullah men-tahnik-nya (mengolesi langit-langit mulut) dengan sebiji kurma yang telah beliau kunyah. Kemudian beliau memberinya nama Abdullah, dan menjulukinya Abu Bakar, sesuai dengan nama kakeknya. Nenek dari ayahnya adalah Shafiyah, bibi Rasulullah. 

SIKAP ABDULLAH BIN ZUBAIR PADA MASA KEKUASAAN UMAYYAH HINGGA DI BAI'AT MENJADI KHALIFAH HIJAZ :

Saat gejolak fitnah begitu kuat antar kaum muslimin, beliau sebenarnya tidak setuju penunjukkan kekuasaan dari Mu’awiyah kepada putranya yaitu Yazid. Banyak sahabat Nabi dan para tabi’in yang hidup pada masa itu juga tidak setuju. Meski tidak setuju, mereka juga tidak memprovokasi untuk memberontak. Tetapi semua berbalik arah ketika peristiwa Karbala terjadi yang mengakibatkan syahid/wafatnya Husain bin Ali (anak dari ali bin abi Thalib sekaligus cucu Nabi Muhammad S.a.w) . Tragedi itu menyebabkan kekecewaan dan luka bagi umat muslim terhadap kekuasaan Bani Umayyah. Di sisi lain dukungan datang terhadap Abdullah bin Zubair meliputi Hijaz, Mesir,
Yaman, Irak, Khurasan, dan sebagian wilayah Syam (Suriah). Yazid bin Muawiyah mencoba menghentikan pemberontakan Ibnu Zubair dengan mengirim pasukan ke Mekkah. Yazid mengirim utusannya dan berencana menyerang Abdullah bin Zubair di Mekkah. Pada 26 Muharram 64 H (683 M), pasukan Al-Hushain bin Numair mengepung Abdullah bin Az-Zubair selama 64 hari. Terjadi saling serang menggunakan Manjaniq ke Kakbah dari Gunung Qubais, sampai menimbulkan kebakaran di Masjidil Haram. Ditengah pengepungan itu, pemimpin Umayyah yaitu Yazid wafat pada 64 Hijriah. Al-Hushain bin Numair meminta Abdullah bin Az-Zubair untuk berdiskusi. Al-Hushain bersedia membaiat Abdullah dan memintanya untuk datang ke Syam seraya berdamai.

KEMBALI MUNCULNYA KEKUATAN BANI UMAYYAH DIBAWAH KOMANDO ABDUL MALIK BIN MARWAN :

Di Damaskus (Ibukota Umayyah), ketika muawiyah II wafat, ditunjuklah Marwan bin Al-Hakam memegang komando Bani Umayyah yang sudah carut marut pada saat itu. Penunjukan ini tak lepas dari dorongan Gubernur Irak, Ubaydillah bin Ziyad. Akan tetapi kubu Umayyah dan Abdullah bin Zubair memanas. hingga akhirnya keduanya berhadapan dalam Pertempuran Marj Rahith pada 64/65 Hijriah (684 Masehi). Akan tetapi kekuasaan Marwan bin Al-hakam tidak berlangsung lama hanya sekitar 10 Bulan, ia meninggal secara mendadak pada 65 Hijriah (685 Masehi). Sebelum meninggal ia menunjuk putranya yaitu Abdul Malik bin Marwan menjadi penerusnya. Disinilah titik balik menguatnya Bani Umayyah. upaya menundukkan Abdullah bin Zubair menjadi target utama. Taktik Abdul Malik cukup cerdik. Ia tidak langsung menyerang pusat kekuatan Abdullah bin Zubair yang berada di Mekkah dan Madinah, tapi melumpuhkan dulu Persia (Irak, Iran, Khurasan dan Bukhara) yang menjadi lumbung perekonomian Ibnu Zubair. Setelah berhasil, Abdul Malik memerintahkan Hajjaj bin Yusuf untuk menyerbu Abdullah bin Zubair di Hijaz.

SUASANA MENCEKAM SAAT PASUKAN UMAYYAH DAN PASUKAN ABDULLAH BIN ZUBAIR BERTEMU :

Hajjaj bin Yusuf lalu berangkat menuju Mekkah, namun ia tidak melalui jalur biasa, melainkan menggunakan jalur ke Irak lalu memutar ke arah Mekkah. Dan pada bulan Sya’ban 72 H, dia tiba di Tha’if. Pada kesempatan yang sama, kekuatan Abdullah bin Zubair bersiap menyambut serangan ini di Madinah, harus bergerak menunju Tha’if. Di Thaif perangpun tak dapat dihindarkan. Dalam pertempuran ini, pasukan Abdulah bin Zubair hancur. Di sisi lain, Hajjaj bin Yusuf juga mengalami kerugian yang besar. Setelah pertempuran ini, Hajjaj bin Yusuf mengirim laporan ke Abdul Malik tentang kemenangan dan kerugian yang dialaminya. Mendapat laporan ini, Abdul Malik mengirimkan pasukan tambahan 5000 personil dari Damaskus untuk menggandakan kekuatan. Pasukan ini baru tiba pada bulan Zulqaidah atau hanya satu bulan sebelum bulan haji. Mereka langsung bergabung dengan pasukan sebelumnya dan membombardir kota Mekkah dengan ketapel (Manjaniq). Mereka menghentikan penyerangan hanya pada musim haji, itupun atas permohonan Abdullah bin Umar.
 Salama proses haji berlangsung, pasukan Hajjaj bin Yusuf tidak mengenakan kain ihram dan berkeliling kota Mekkah dengan menghunus pedang. Pada tahun 73 H, akhirnya pasukan Damaskus berhasil membunuh Abdullah bin Zubair. Cucu khalifah Abu Bakar ini ditusuk dengan pedang dan kepalanya dipenggal.

KOIN SISI DEPAN :
• Wajah yang menyerupai Khusro II menghadap kanan
• Tertulis dengan bahasa persia kuno. "AFZUT GDH “semoga kemakmuran rajanya bertambah”
• Dibagian bawah sebelah kanan terdapat tulisan “Bismillah” (ini yg membedakan koin Arab sasanian dan koin persia (sasanian) .
•Tertulis disisi sebelah kanan koin dalam tulisan bahasa Persia 
“apdwla-i zubiran amīr-i -wurrishnikān”
Artinya : Abdullah bin Zubair, Pemimpin orang orang beriman

KOIN SISI BELAKANG :
• Posisi bulan sabit & bintang di arah jam 3,6,9 dan 12
• Disebalah kiri bertuliskan Tahun koin itu dicetak yaitu YE-60
(dalam koin ini menggunakan penanggalan Yazdegird era(tahun ke 60) dalam Hijriah, 71-72 Hijriah)
• Disebelah kanan bertuliskan tempat koin ini dicetak yaitu DA + P (Fasa)

356164.description:
Ex NBJ Auction 14 16 Apr 2025, lot 219.
Starting price: 200 USD
Umayyad: Sulayman b. Abd Al-Malik, 96-99AH / 715-717AD. AR Dirham, Mint: al-Timara, Date: 97h. Two rare contermarks. (2.75gm, 28mm), Good Very Fine & Rare.
Price realized: 255 USD
Stuart Sears attributes this countermark (cm 150a, beast head), and (cm 23c, tamgha), to the time of the revolt of al-Harith b Surayj, 116 AH / 734-740s CE in Khorasan. Both cm share some common technical features, which indicate they were products of the same, or related, workshop. He lists six beast head cm:s, the latest on a Marw dirham AH 100 / 718/19 CE, and four tamgha cm:s, the latest on al-Mubaraka AH 107 / 725/26 CE. The motifs might indicate that the countermarks was applied by some of al-Harith’s Hephthalie allies, probably around 734-35 CE. In Zeno we have a dirham of al-Mubaraka AH 117 / 735 CE with the tamgha cm!
