356402.description:
ISLAMIC, Umayyad Caliphate. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, AH 65-86 / AD 685-705. Drachm (Silver, 32 mm, 3.42 g, 2 h), Arab-Sasanian 'Miḥrāb and ʿAnāza' type, without mint, possibly struck in Dimashq, around AH 75 = AD 694/5. Draped and armoured Sasanian-style bust of the Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan to right, wearing a helmet surmounted by korymbos, chain mail tunic and holding a sheathed sword in his right hand across his chest; behind head, 'GDE / ʾp̄zwt' ('[may his] glory increase' in Pahlavi); before, 'hwslwb' ('Khosrau' in Pahlavi); in the outer margin, divided by stars and crescents at 3, 6 and 9 o'clock, 'bism Allāh lā ilāha – illā Allāh wa–ḥdahū Muḥammad ra–sūl Allāh' ('In the name of Allah. There is no deity but Allah, the One. Muhammad is the messenger of Allah' in Arabic). Rev. Vertical barbed spear (ʿAnāza) with two pennants floating to the right, positioned beneath an arch supported by two columns, resembling a prayer niche (Miḥrāb mujawwaf); to left and right of the spear, 'naṣr – Allāh' ('The help of Allah' in Arabic); to left and right of the columns, 'amīr al-muʾmin[īn] – khal[ī]fat Allāh' ('Commander of the Believers. Caliph of Allah' in Arabic); in the outer margin, four crescent-and-star motifs, each with a pellet on either side; to the right of the uppermost crescent and star, distorted 'ʾp̄', standing for 'ʾp̄d' = 'abd' ('wonderful' in Pahlavi). CNG Mail Bid Sale 107 (2020), 3 = Malek 2019, p. 298, Fig. 9.32.27. L. Treadwell: Mihrab and ʿAnaza or Sacrum and Spear? A Reconsideration of an Early Marwanid Silver Drachm, in Muqarnas 22 (2005), pp. 1-28 (2005), p. 6, no. 5 (same dies). Extremely rare and of great historical importance. A key rarity in the early Islamic series with intricate iconography. Pierced and with minor traces of mounting, otherwise, very fine.

From a European collection, formed before 2005.

This coin is undoubtedly one of the most important issues of the early Islamic period. With its rich symbolism and extreme rarity, it quickly attracted the attention of scholars of religion and numismatics alike. While it draws inspiration from Sasanian prototypes - as is typical of early Islamic coinage - it diverges in several remarkable ways from the standard Arab-Sasanian types.

The obverse bust, for instance, displays a number of highly distinctive features: unlike the images of Khosrau II with his winged crown, the figure here wears a conical helmet and a coat of mail. He also holds a sword in both hands - a striking motif that recalls the 'Standing Caliph' found on contemporary fulus. These elements suggest that the figure is not, as the Pahlavi legend implies, Khosrau himself, but rather ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, the Caliph.

This interpretation is further supported by the reverse, which breaks even more decisively with Sasanian models. Instead of the familiar Zoroastrian fire altar, it depicts a spear adorned with pennants blowing to the right - the so-called ʿAnāza (عَنَزَة) - positioned within an arch. According to George Miles, this is almost certainly the Prophet's spear, possibly shown within a Miḥrāb (مِحْرَاب), the prayer niche in a mosque oriented toward Mecca. Interestingly, the cataloguer of Morton & Eden Auction 107 (2020), lot 3 - a note later reappearing in CNG's Islamic Auction 3 (2023), 13 - offered a more imaginative reading: he perceived a stylized face formed by the arch, legends, spear, and surrounding dot motifs. While this interpretation may be speculative, it does not detract from the coin's iconographic significance.

The type marks a pivotal moment in the transition from Sasanian to Islamic coinage - a period in which inherited imagery was being reinterpreted, transformed, and gradually replaced. The likely depiction of the Caliph is a revolutionary innovation and underscores the extent to which early Islamic art remained rooted in the visual language of Late Antiquity, especially its imperial portraiture. One of the most striking features is the substitution of the Zoroastrian fire altar with the Prophet's spear - an act of symbolic appropriation and religious transformation. A direct depiction of the Prophet was already inconceivable at this time, even though the Islamic prohibition of images had not yet been universally or rigidly applied. All the more remarkable, then, is this visual gesture that draws so close.

The precise historical context of this extraordinary issue remains unknown. Its extreme rarity suggests that it may have been an experimental series. The coins name neither a mint nor a date. Although long attributed to Damascus, both their unusual iconography and the presence of a Hunnic countermark on at least one specimen suggest an origin further east.

The considerable stylistic differences among the known dies may suggest a mobile mint - perhaps one operating in the context of a military campaign. This interpretation is supported by the coin's martial imagery: the Caliph appears in arms, while the Prophet's weapon evokes both spear-won territory - a concept deeply rooted in Hellenistic and Roman imperial ideology - and religious legitimacy.

Also notable is the stark imbalance between the number of known dies and the very limited number of surviving coins. The most plausible explanation is that the struck pieces were later withdrawn and melted down, whether for religious or political reasons. The iconography may ultimately have been deemed too provocative. As a result, only a handful of examples have endured - making them among the most compelling and enigmatic numismatic testimonies of early Islam.

Pars Coins E-sale 34, Lot 199.

Description from the auction house: 
ILKHANS of PERSIA, Hulagu, 1256-1265 AD. Natanz mint. AR Dirhem (2.87 gm; 22 mm). obverse, "Munaka qa'an/ Hulagu Khan/ Padshah dar/ zamin/ al-A'zam" (Hulagu great king on earth), reverse at the center "Ahmad/Ishaq/zarb-e Natanz"(name: Ahmad Ishaq, minted in Natanz), outer ring Shahadah and Shahdah for Prophet Mohammad. Extremely rare variation of Hulagu's coinage from an unrecorded mint city of Natanz (near present day Isfahan). Ilkhanid grand vizir Zain al-Din Mastari, created a major monument dedicated to his Sufi teacher Sheikh Abd-Al-Samad in Natanz. Another interesting variation is the coin's description of the king's title is in Persian and not standard Arabic. Not in Omer Diler's monumental reference, thus extremely rare. Some minor weakness, otherwise well struck. Choice Good VF.

Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 9 24-25 Apr 2025; lot 2.
Estimate: 1500 USD
Pre-reform issues, Arab-Byzantine. Imperial Image coinage. Æ Fals (25.9mm, 5.67 g, 6h). Without mint-name (probably struck at Gerasa/Jerash). Undated (probably struck in AH 65 / AD 685). Modified cross or spear on three steps, flanked by two standing figures, each wearing long robes and Arab headdress, their right hands on their sheathed swords / Large M with cross above and A below; ANNO - NIKO around. Foss p. 61; Amitai-Preiss et al. D11a . Good Fine, obverse cleaned. Extremely rare.

Foss suggests that 'the type apparently represents the caliph Abd al-Malik and his brother Abd al-Aziz, who were jointly proclaimed as successors to their father Marwan in 684/85. It is probably an accession issue of Abd al-Malik, who assumed supreme power, with his brother recognised as his successor, in April 685.'

357677.description:
Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 9 24-25 Apr 2025; lot 13.
Estimate: 5000 USD
Pre-reform issues, Arab-Sasanian. al-Hajjaj b. Yusuf. AH 75-95 / AD 694-713. AR Drachm (32.4mm, 3.98 g, 9h). TART (Tawwaj) mint. Dated AH 77 (AD 696/7). Obverse margin: bism Allah / la i- laha i- la A- / llah wahdahu Muhammad ra- / sul Allah, with the la -i and la A- in the second quadrant arranged vertically. Malek, Arab-Sasanian p. 225 = Morton & Eden 48 (4 April 2011), lot 8, same obverse die; SICA 1, –; Album 35.1 var. (this transitional type not mentioned). Near EF, toned. Extremely rare.

The earliest drachms of al-Hajjaj b. Yusuf, struck in AH 76 and 77, have their obverse marginal legends arranged radially (see the previous lot). During AH 77, this attractive design was abandoned in favour of a reversion to the standard linear legends familiar from previous Arab-Sasanian drachms, written clockwise. This appears to be an extremely rare transitional type, on which the lam-alifs and the alif following them are written vertically, as on the radial drachms. 
Price realized: 3250 USD

357680.description:
Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 9 24-25 Apr 2025; lot 6.
Estimate: 7500 USD
Pre-reform issues, Arab-Sasanian. Ubaydallah b. Ziyad. AH 54-64 / AD 673-683. AR Drachm (27.8mm, 2.89 g, 4h). KRMAN-NAR (Narmashir) mint. Dated AH 61 (AD 681/2). With Pahlavi PYRWČ (pērōz, 'Victorious') before usual name legend, Obverse margin: – / bism Allah ∴ / – / –. Malek, Arab-Sasanian 737; SICA 1, –; Album 12. Dark toning, clipped to the weight of a post-Reform dirham (but with all legends complete). VF. Extremely rare.

This remarkable issue has been described as 'perhaps the earliest Islamic commemorative coin'. Adding the word pērōz to the normal name-legend in this way proclaims the governor as 'The Victorious 'Ubaydallah b. Ziyad'. This feature is unique to these extremely rare drachms of 'Ubaydallah struck at KLMAN-NAR in this year, and has no parallel on the Arab-Sasanian coinage.

It has been suggested that the victory alluded to here was the tragic battle of Karbala, which took place in this year. Following the death of the caliph Mu'awiya I in AH 60, the sons of some prominent Companions of the Prophet disputed Mu'awiya's choice of his son Yazid as his successor. These included Husayn, the son of the fourth caliph, 'Ali, who refused to give his allegiance to Yazid. Encouraged by promises of support from the inhabitants of Kufa, Husayn marched from Mecca to Iraq in AH 61, but was intercepted by a much larger Umayyad force under 'Ubaydallah b. Ziyad. 'Ubaydallah refused to give Husayn safe passage to Kufa, and battle ensued on the plain of Karbala on 10 Muharram AH 61. Hopelessly outnumbered, Husayn was killed along with most of his relatives and companions. Both Sunni and Shi'a Muslims acknowledge Karbala as an historical tragedy, and one which cemented the enduring divisions between these two branches of Islam. 
Price realized: 5500 USD

357682.description:
Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 9 24-25 Apr 2025; lot 51.
Estimate: 25 000 USD
Umayyad Caliphate, Silver coinage. AR Dirham (26.9mm, 2.79 g, 2h). Maskin mint. Dated AH 90 (AD 708/9). Obverse margin: bism Allah duriba hadha al-dirham bi-Maskin fi sanat tisa'in . Klat –; al-'Ajlan –; The Shah Firzan Heritage of Islamic Coins p. 13 (this piece). VF, some double-striking. Of the highest rarity, believed unique, and the only Islamic coin recorded from this mint.

In the year AH 90, dozens of silver dirham mints were opened or reopened throughout the Eastern Islamic lands. This was a radical departure from the previous five years, when almost all Umayyad dirhams had been struck at Wasit and Damascus, supplemented by a handful of rare and often ephemeral mints active in the Umayyad North. The scale of the change becomes apparent when one compares the number of active mints for the years AH 89 (six) and AH 90 (at least forty). The reasons for this change are not fully understood, but may well be connected to other, broader changes in provincial administration and taxation.

Some of these mints were very prolific. From others, including Maskin, only a tiny number of dirhams have survived today, and it seems unlikely that these rare mints ever produced silver in quantity. Perhaps a decision was taken to establish one dirham mint in every administrative district, only for it to become clear that not all of these would be needed equally?

Le Strange (The Lands of the Eastern Caliphate, Cambridge, 1905, pp. 51 and 80), describes the district of Maskin as follows:

'The Dujayl Canal...meaning "the Little Tigris", watered all the rich district of Maskin lying to the north of West Baghdad beyond Katrabbul.... The district of the Dujayl, otherwise called Maskin, included a great number of villages and towns, lying westward of 'Ukbara and the Tigris channel, the chief of which was Harba, which was visited by Ibn Jubayr in 580 (1184) and still exists. Here may be seen at the present day the ruins of a great stone bridge across the canal which, as the historian Fakhri records and the extant inscription still testifies, was built by the Caliph Mustansir in 629 (1232). Near Harba was Al-Hazirah (the Enclosure), where the cotton stuffs called Kirbas were manufactured, being largely exported. Yakut further names a considerable number of villages - there were over a hundred in all - which were of this district, and many of these, as for example Al-Balad (the Hamlet) near Hazirah, are still to be found on the map. As late as the 8th (14th) century the Dujayl district, with Harba for its chief town, is described by Mustawfi as of amazing fertility, and its pomegranates were the best to be found in the markets of Baghdad.' 
Price realized: 17 000 USD

Ex Stephen Album Rare Coins, Auction 37, lot 484

BURJI MAMLUK: Barsbay, 1422-1438, AV ashrafi (3.38g), al-Qahira, AH835, A-998, VF to EF, ex Gamal Amer Collection, ex Morton & Eden Auction, 23-24 November 2004, part of Lot 461. The ashrafi was introduced as the reform gold coinage by Barsbay, and drew its name from the kunya of al-Ashraf Barsbay. Unlike the failed gold coin reforms by Faraj and Shaykh, Barsbay's reform, introduced in AH829, was successful, maintained by all later Mamluk rulers, then transferred to the Ottoman, who maintained it until the early 19th century. The term ashrafi as "asarfi" is still used for the gold coinage of Nepal in the 21st century!

358581.description:
https://www.biddr.com/auctions/savoca/browse?a=5893&l=726375...

Lot 463

"Umayyad Caliphate. Wasit. Classic Early Umayyad Post-Reform Issue AH 690-750. Anonymous (Time of Marwan II, AH 127–132 / AD 744–750)
Dirham AR

25 mm, 2,88 g

lā ilāha illā Allāh / waḥdahū / lā sharīka lahū — “There is no deity but Allah alone, He has no partner.” bism Allāh ḍuriba hādhā al-dirham bi-Wāsit fī sana thamāniyah wa ʿishrīn wa miʾah — “In the name of Allah. This dirham was struck in Wasit in the year 128.” / Allāh aḥad / Allāh al-ṣamad / lam yalid / wa lam yūlad / wa lam yakun lahū kufuwan aḥad — “Allah is One. Allah is Eternal. He neither begets nor is born. And there is none like unto Him.” Muḥammad rasūl Allāh arsalahū bi-l-hudā wa dīn al-ḥaqq li-yuẓhirahū ʿalā al-dīn kullih wa law kariha al-mushrikūn — “Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, whom He sent with guidance and the religion of truth, so that He may make it prevail over all religion, even though the polytheists may dislike it.”

Good Very Fine

Album 137

The dirhams presented here belong to the final phase of Umayyad silver coinage, struck between AH 127 and 129 (AD 744–747), during the reign of the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II. These coins reflect the enduring impact of the great coinage reform of Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, who had introduced uniform Islamic epigraphy and Qur’anic inscriptions to replace earlier Sasanian and Byzantine imagery. Struck at key eastern mints such as Wasit and Marw, these anonymous dirhams — bearing no caliphal names — represent a period of mounting political instability. As the Abbasid revolution gathered strength in the east, the Umayyad administration focused on reinforcing legitimacy through religious formulas rather than naming rulers."

خمس (five) and ثمن (eight) get mixed up frequently.

This is the earliest purely Ilkhan coin of Kazirun, better known for Shiraz. Kazirun is much rarer than Shiraz, with no example of Kazirun on CoinArchives.

361211.description:
Arab-Sasanian, ‘Abd al-Rahman b. Muhammad (AH 80-84 / 700-703 AD), silver Drachm, AH 83 / 702 AD, BYŠ (Bishapur), 3.97g (SICA unlisted; Malek 356 var.). Good Very Fine. Some corrosion to surfaces and scratches. Extremely rare, this variation is unique so far on the market.

Excessively rare Arab-Sasanian Drachm – unique variant

The silver Drachms of ‘Abd al-Rahman b. Muhammad are notable for their varied legends in different writing systems and languages. Like the coins of al-Hajjaj b. Yusuf his name is found in both Kufic and Pahlavi such as on this coin. On the obverse, the name ‘Abd al-Rahman bin Muhammad in the field and bismallah in the margin, both in Kufic. On reverse, date and mint name are featured in Pahlavi, while in the margin the name of Mansur is written in Kufic, which is unique to this coin. 

This particular combination of legends with the additional inscription in the reverse margin is thus far the only example known to have come to the market. In the past, Baldwin’s has sold one similar example in Islamic Coins Auction 8, May 2004, lot 32. It was the Malek type 356, however, without the additional inscription on the reverse which makes this a unique variation. This type overall was unrecorded until our 2004 auction and the subsequent publication in the reference book by Hodge Malek in 2019. This particular variant, however, is still unrecorded in literature.

https://www.vcoins.com/en/stores/solidus_numismatik/303/prod...

Ilkhans - Mongols of Persia. Uljaytu (703 - 716 H. / 1304 - 1316). Donative (gold) in the weight of 4 Dinars

Golden Donative in the weight of 4 Dinars. Madinat as-Salam Baghdad, 709 H.
Obv: In the middle within two circles: Shahadah with Shia addition (Ali wali Allah). Below ornament. Outer legend, surrounded by circle and circle of dots: Names of the twelve Imams.
Rev: Within quadrilobe the title of the sovereign, followed by blessing formula: Duriba fi / ayyam dawla al-mawla / as-sultan al-a'zam malik riqab / al-imam Uljaytu sultan Ghiyath / al-Dunya wa'd-Din Kuhdabanda Muhammad / khallada Allah / mulkuahu.
In corners between surrounding circle of dots and quadrilobe: Top right: Uljaytu Sultan (in Uigur); top left: li-llah al-amr min qabl wa-min ba'd; bottom right: darb madinat as-salam Baghdad, bottom left: sana tis' wa sab' mi'at.

33 mm. 18,23 g.

Diler Ul-365.
 
Extremely rare in this size and with this weight. Well centered, slight weakness of strike towards the edge, minimal fault on edge (testing track?),extremely fine.

The exceptional high weight of the coin corresponding to four dinars of 4,5 g,is carefully centered and its calligraphy is very refined. The piece has been produced for donative purposes and not as regular currency. Items of this type are known from several mints. Donative issues of this size and in this excellent state of preservation, however, are distinct rarities.
361516.keywords: Ilkhans Uljaytu Donative Gold in weight of 4 Dinars Madinat as-Salam Baghdad 709 AH

361517.description:
https://www.vcoins.com/en/stores/solidus_numismatik/303/prod...

Ilkhans - Mongols of Persia. Abu Sa'id (716 - 736 H. / 1316 - 1335). Donative (gold) in the weight of 6 Dinars

Golden Donative in the weight of 6 Dinars. Baghdad, 709 H.
Obv: In the middle within two circles: Sunni Shahadah Below names of the four. rightly guided Caliphs. Between this central inscription and the outer legend around the rim (Qur'an Surah XLVIII, 29) a calligraphy in the shape of a prayer niche: Fasika fi kuhum, darunter: Allah wa huwa / al-sami' al-'alim.
Rev: Within a quadrilobe with protruding angles in the corners the title of the sovereign, followed by blessing formula: Duriba fi / ayyam dawla as-Sultan / al-a'zam Abu Sa'id / khallada Allah mulkuahu.
In the fields between quadrilobe and surrounding circle place and year of minting: darb / Ba'dad / fi / sana / tis' / 'ashr / sab' / miat.
Outer legend, surrounded by circle and circle of dots: Qur'an Surah XLVIII,4.

39 mm. 26,75 g.
 
Diler Ab-487 (Typ C, Mihrab-Type), no item made of Gold listed.
 
Extremely rare, probably unique. Well centered, slight weakness of strike on the averse, extremely fine. 
 
The exceptional high weight of the coin corresponding to six Dinars of 4,5 g,is carefully centered and its calligraphy is very refined. The piece has been produced for donative purposes and not as regular currency. Other coin types of Abu Sa'id occur rarely as heavy gold coins with a weight of 2 Dinars. The donative issue presented here can probably be regarded as unique as regards its size in gold for this sovereign and is in an excellent state of preservation. It may rightly be regarded as a masterpiece of Ilkhanid die cutting.
361517.keywords: Ilkhans Abu Sa`id Donative gold in weight of 6 Dinars Baghdad 719 H

Within a square, ‘lā ilāha illā / Allāh Muḥammad / rasūl Allāh’ (‘There is no deity but Allah. Muhammad is the messenger of Allah’ in Arabic); the names of the four Rashidun Caliphs in Arabic in the four surrounding panels: ‘Abūbakr / ʿUmar / ʿUthmān / ʿAlī’. Rev. Within a central circle, ‘ḍarb / Jimishkizāk / sana / 758 [retrograde]’ (‘Struck in Çemişgezek, year 857’ in Arabic); in the margin, barely legible, ‘al-sulṭān al-malik al-ẓāhir Jaqmaq khallada Allāh taʿālā mulkahū’ (‘The Sultan and King al-Zahir Jaqmaq. May Allah, the Exalted, perpetuate his kingdom’ in Arabic). Album A1016 (mislisted under Aynal, AH 857-865 / AD 1453-1461). Extremely rare. Minor deposits and some doubling on the reverse, otherwise, very fine.

362839.description:
A Complete Set of Fifty-Six Post-Reform Umayyad Dinars, comprising an example of each year from 77h to 132h inclusive, generally in excellent condition, including the celebrated Year 77 dinar (56) 

The famous year 77 dinar, issued by the caliph 'Abd al-Malik b. Marwan, is the first purely Islamic gold coin. Its design and inscriptions set a pattern for Islamic dinars which lasted until the fall of the Umayyads and whose influence can be seen on coins issued centuries later. Apart from the date on the reverse, the legends remain unchanged throughout the fifty-six years these coins were struck, but examination of a set such as this reveals many subtle changes in style and calligraphy with a gradual change from a small, rounded script with clear Pahlawi influence to a more angular form of Iraqi Kufic. From an historical perspective, the establishment of a uniform and distinctively Islamic coinage system represents a key stage in the creation of a stable Islamic state. During the early years of conquest and expansion, the victorious Muslims had wisely left existing social and political institutions largely untouched. Over time, however, priorities inevitably shifted towards settlement and government, and it became important that the Islamic lands should become administered in a distinctively Islamic way which followed the precepts of the Holy Qur'an. With its central role both in taxation and in the payment of troops, the coinage had a prominent part to play in this process. 

Monetarily, the territory controlled by the Muslims at this time comprised two distinct areas. The erstwhile Byzantine provinces in the West had maintained a bimetallic system based on the gold solidus and the copper follis. The Sasanian empire had issued only small quantities of gold and copper coins, relying instead on a plentiful supply of silver drachms which the Muslims had continued to strike in a modified form. Establishing a single coinage system for both areas was a highly visible statement of unified Muslim control: a symbolic as well as a practical measure. 'Abd al-Malik's coinage reforms are still not fully understood, but it appears that in the early 70s he began to issue experimental gold and silver coins. Several different types of solidi were struck, all clearly based on Byzantine issues but with minimal modifications to remove obviously Christian symbols. Indeed, these 'transitional' dinars give a strong impression that the Muslims were still trying to copy Byzantine solidi as closely as possible. Few of them survive today, and it seems unlikely that they were ever produced in large quantities. This conservative approach to coinage design was dramatically reversed in the year 77h, when 'Abd al-Malik introduced a dinar of a radically new type. Purely epigraphic, the new coin replaced modified crosses and images of emperors or caliphs with verses from the Qur'an rendered in austere Kufic script. The weight of the coin was also changed from that of the Byzantine solidus to the mithqal of approximately 4.25g. As dinars of the earlier Byzantine type dated 77h are also known, this gives the impression of an abrupt change in policy for reasons which remain unclear. Mediaeval Arab writers stress the religious aspects of 'Abd al-Malik's coinage reforms rather than their economic significance, while ancient and modern authors have suggested a link between these reformed dinars and a new series of Byzantine solidi, issued at approximately the same time, which were the first to depict the facing bust of Christ. 

The extremely rare 77h dinar in the present set is struck from the same dies as the specimen in the Penn Museum, Philadelphia (accession number 29-231-148, wt. 4.21g, published by Giulio Bernardi in the Schweizerische Numismatische Rundschau, 80, 2001, 133, 9 (dies e/D) and earlier by George Miles, Some Early Arab Dinars, ANS Museum Notes III, 1948, 2). The other key dates in terms of rarity are the dinars dated 107h (very rare), 127h (extremely rare) and 132h (very rare). 

Provenance: Years 77-96 and 114-132 ex Morton & Eden 18, 7 March 2006, lot 14.

Original description:

'Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Muqtadir. AH 295-320 / AD 908-933. AV Dinar (25.2mm, 4.08 g, 5h). Al-Muhammadiya mint. Dated AH 302 (AD 914/5). Bernardi 302Mh (this date not recorded); cf Miles, Rayy 149 (dated AH 301). Good Fine. Of the highest rarity, apparently unpublished.

While Miles records standard 'Abbasid dinars from al-Muhammadiya for the years AH 301 and 303, the only gold coin known to him dated AH 302 additionally bore the name of Muhammad b. 'Ali, the Sa'lukid governor of Rayy who held the city at various times between AH 302 and 314. It is recorded that Muhammad b. 'Ali led an army from Rayy in AH 301 or 302 (our sources are inconsistent) against an 'Alid rebel, al-Hasan b. 'Ali al-'Utrush, but was defeated and forced to return to Rayy. Whether the present coin, which is purely 'Abbasid in its legends, was struck during Muhammad b. 'Ali's absence on campaign or in the aftermath of his defeat is not clear, but when writing about the dinar dated AH 303 Miles comments: 'There is no record in the chronicles of Rayy having been reoccupied by the central 'Abbasid authorities, but this would seem to have been the case, if we are to judge by the numismatic evidence.'

363506.description:
This gold dinar was minted in Samarqand in AH 309 (AD 921–922), during the reign of Nasr II ibn Ahmad (AH 301–331 / AD 914–943). Apparently only three examples from this mint and year are recorded by Bernardi (269Qe), making it a rare date for this ruler and mint. Minor edge marks noted. Fine condition. Album 1449.

In AH 308–309, Khorasan witnessed several major disturbances, including the end of Ahmad ibn Sahl’s rebellion (AH 303–309 / AD 915–921) and the uprising of Layla ibn Nuʿman in Nishapur, specifically dated to AH 309 (Ibn Athir, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh; Gardizi, Zayn al-Akhbār).

This year also marked the controversial execution of the Persian mystic Mansur al-Hallaj in Baghdad for his proclamation “Ana al-Ḥaqq” (“I am the Truth”). His execution is noted in historical chronicles, including those of al-Ṭabarī and Ibn al-Athīr.
363506.keywords: Samanid Nasr II gold dinar Samarqand AH309 rare al-Hallaj Ahmad ibn Sahl Nishapur

363507.description:
Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Muʿtazz. AH 251–255 / AD 866–869. AV Dinar (19.4 mm, 4.22 g, 8h). Marw mint. Dated AH 253 (AD 867–868). Album 235.1. Minor edge marks. Fine. A rare mint, with the Marw issue notably absent from Stephen Album’s Checklist of Islamic Coins.

This coin bears witness to significant events during AH 253. At that time, Marw was under Tahirid governance and served as a key stronghold of the dynasty. In the same year, Yaʿqub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar, founder of the Saffarid dynasty, launched his campaigns in Khurasan, capturing key cities such as Herat and Pushang. These conquests marked the decline of the Tahirid dynasty and the rise of the Saffarids.

This coin is potentially one of the last gold dinars struck in Marw, and broader Khurasan, bearing only the name of the caliph, before local rulers began asserting their names on coinage.

The date also coincides with the Anarchy at Samarra, a period of deep political instability within the Abbasid Caliphate, which ultimately led to al-Muʿtazz’s deposition and death in AH 255.
363507.keywords: Abbasid al-Muʿtazz Marw AV dinar AH253 Saffarid Tahirid rare Khurasan

364167.description:
I bring to your attention this 1/2 qirat from the Meknes mint. It could be an A#468, but it is not listed in the "Vives", nor in "La plata almoravide y postmoravide-El quirate" by F. Benito de los Mozos (2017), nor in the Tonegawa collection. 
On this 1/2 single-sided qirat of 10 mm and 0.45 g, we can read the first 2 lines of the reverse of the qirat Cc5 (or Vives 1707): علي (Ali) - قائد المسلمين (commander of the Muslims) and a last curved line (cf Cc5): مكناس (Meknes). 
Note: the 3rd line - and "Nasser al-din" - is missing and it is the characteristic of the classification in Cc; there is indeed an 1/2 qirat of Meknes (Cb13) but totally different from the legend of Cc5; so as the closest 1/2 qirat is the Cc6 which is double-sided, I named this one "Cc6a"...

365226.description:
From Classical Numismatic Group
Islamic Auction 4
LOT 54
Auction Date: 19.10.2023
'Abbasid Caliphate
'Abbasid Caliphate. temp. Al-Mu'tasim. AH 218-227 / AD 833-842. AV Dinar (20.4mm, 4.14 g, 11h). Surra man ra'a mint. Dated AH 226 (AD 840/1). Bernardi 151Jc = Miles, RIC 140 (same obverse die). Edge shaved. Near VF. Excessively rare, apparently the second published specimen.
This appears to be the earliest known date for gold dinars struck at Samarra, located on the banks of the Tigris about 75 miles north of Baghdad. Founded as the new caliphal capital by al-Mu'tasim in AH 221, Samarra remained the seat of the caliphate for about sixty years before al-Mu'tadid moved it back to Baghdad. Today, the historical city of Samarra is designated a World Heritage Site, famous for the spiral minaret of its Great Mosque.

365340.description:
Artuqids of Mardin

Husām al-Dīn Timurtash & Sher Bārik
AE fals, NM (Mardin), ND
c. 1120s

Historical framework

The Artuqid emirate of Mardin in the early 12th century functioned as a frontier polity in Upper Mesopotamia, where political authority, population structure, and monetary practice were markedly hybrid. Byzantine monetary conventions—particularly in bronze—continued well into the Artuqid period, especially in regions with substantial Christian populations such as Mayyāfāriqīn and its environs.

Within this context, Sher Bārik appears not as a dynastic ruler, but as a local authority operating under Artuqid sovereignty, most plausibly a military governor or frontier commander. Although absent from narrative sources, his repeated appearance on coinage demonstrates recognized and legitimate authority, exercised within a limited geographic and chronological frame.

Sher Bārik, the numismatic evidence:

Sher Bārik is securely attested on two closely related bronze coin groups, both naming Husām al-Dīn Timurtash and Sher Bārik together.

1. Pantokrator type (Byzantine-iconographic bronze)

Obverse:
Bearded bust of Christ Pantokrator, facing, in Byzantine style.

Reverse:
Arabic inscription in two lines naming both authorities.
Arabic:
حسام الدين
سير بارك
Transliteration:
Ḥusām al-Dīn / Shīr Bārik
Translation:
“Ḥusām al-Dīn / Sher Bārik”

Reference:
Sayles & Spengler 24 (SS24)
Album 1826.1

This group represents regular civic bronze, continuing Byzantine monetary language under Artuqid rule. As noted by sma (Zeno, 20 Dec 2020), the type names Timurtash as sovereign authority and Sher Bārik as local governor, plausibly operating at Mayyāfāriqīn. The occasional light weight or clipped appearance of some specimens is best understood as circulation-related, not diagnostic of a separate issue.

2. Epigraphic joint Timurtash–Sher Bārik type (present coin)

This type abandons figural imagery entirely and represents a more explicit Islamic epigraphic articulation of the same power relationship.

Description (present coin)

Obverse:
Arabic inscription naming Husām al-Dīn, arranged in compact lines, within a pelleted circular border.

Arabic:
حسام الدين
Transliteration: Ḥusām al-Dīn
Translation: “Ḥusām al-Dīn”

Reverse:
Arabic inscription naming Sher Bārik, within a pelleted circular border.

Arabic:
شير بارك
Transliteration: Shīr Bārik
Translation: “Sher Bārik”

Fabric and minting
Metal: Bronze (AE)
Weight: 5.00 g
Diameter: 23 mm
Flan: Irregular, non-canonical
Strike: Clear, intentional, complete legends

The irregular flan reflects non-standard bronze production, but the clarity of the strike and intact borders confirm that this is neither a post-strike clipping nor a trial. It is a deliberate, limited issue.

Interpretation

Both the Pantokrator type (SS24) and the epigraphic type document the same political relationship:

Husām al-Dīn Timurtash as Artuqid sovereign

Sher Bārik as a subordinate local authority

The Pantokrator type reflects continuity with Byzantine civic bronze traditions, appropriate for circulation among a mixed population. The epigraphic type, by contrast, represents a more explicit Islamic formulation of authority, emphasizing dynastic legitimacy through text alone.

Rather than indicating a change in hierarchy, the two types likely represent parallel or sequential monetary expressions of the same administrative reality during the early decades of Timurtash’s reign.

Rarity and state of knowledge
Epigraphic joint type (present coin):
5 specimens recorded
2 on Zeno (including the present example)
2 in the Kamil Eron collection
1 published by Artuk in TND#26
Type added to The Checklist of Islamic Coins as Album W1826 on 15th of Jan 2026.

The present specimen is among the very few known and is in exceptionally strong condition for the type.

Provenance
Burak Cebeci Collection
Ex - Levon Vrtanesyan Collection
Ex - SPQR Collections, Auction 10, Lot 1686

Published:
İ. & C. Artuk, Türk Nümismatik Derneği Bülteni, No. 26 (1975)

Online:
Zeno #365340
https://www.zeno.ru/showphoto.php?photo=365340&ppuser=268

Concluding note

Sher Bārik should be understood neither as a dynastic ruler nor as a purely “emergency” figure, but as a documented local governor whose authority is consistently expressed alongside that of Husām al-Dīn Timurtash. The coexistence of Byzantine-iconographic and purely epigraphic joint issues illustrates the adaptive monetary language of the Artuqid frontier in the early 12th century. The present coin stands as one of the clearest and rarest expressions of this political and cultural hybridity.

Rev. ‘li-llāh / Muḥammad / rasūl / Allāh / al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh’ (‘For Allah. He sent him with guidance and the religion of truth, so that He may make it overcome all religions, even though the unbelievers may dislike it’ in Arabic). Album 229.1. Rare. 366134.description:
From Leu Numismatik
Web Auction 30
LOT 3473
Auction Date: 13.07.2024
Early Medieval & Islamic
ISLAMIC, 'Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Muntasir, AH 247-248 / AD 861-862. Dirham (Silver, 18 mm, 2.40 g, 11 h), Surra man Raʾa, AH 248 = 862. ‘lā ilāha illā / Allāh waḥdahū / lā sharīka lahū’ (‘There is no deity but Allah, the One, there is no partner to Him’ in Arabic); inner margin, ‘bism Allāh ḍuriba hādhā al-dirham bi Madīnat al-Salām sana thamān wa arbaʿīn wa miʾatayn’ (‘In the name of Allah. This dirham was struck in Madinat al-Salam in the year 248’ in Arabic); outer margin, ‘li-llāh al-amr min qabl wa mi[n baʿd wa yaw]maʾidhin yafraḥu al-muʾminūn bi naṣr Allāh’ (‘To Allah belongs the command before and after, and on that day the believers will rejoice with the help of Allah’ in Arabic; Qurʾān 30: 4-5). Rev. ‘li-llāh / Muḥammad / rasūl / Allāh / al-Muntaṣir billāh’ (‘For Allah. Muhammad is the messenger of Allah. al-Muntasir billah’ in Arabic); in the margin, ‘Muḥammad rasūl Allāh arsalahū bi al-hudā wa dīn al-ḥaqq liyuẓhirahū [ʿalā al-dīn kullih wa law] kariha al-mushrikūn’ (‘Muhammad is the messenger of Allah. He sent him with guidance and the religion of truth, so that He may make it overcome all religions, even though the unbelievers may dislike it’ in Arabic). Album 232. Very rare. Crystallized and with some edge chipping and corrosion, otherwise, very fine.
Ex Classical Numismatic Group Islamic Auction 4, 19 October 2023, 1142.
Al-Muntasir was a son of al-Mutawakkil and a Greek slave concubine named Hubshiyya who organized the assassination of his father by members of the Turkish guard after al-Mutawakkil appointed a younger brother, al-Mu'tazz, as his successor. After the murder of their father, al-Mutawakkil had al-Mu'tazz renounce his rights to the throne. However, his victory proved to be short-lived, as he died under mysterious circumstances shortly thereafter.
366134.keywords: Abbasid AR dirham al-Muntasir Surra man Ra'a 248 AH

366359.description:
Webauktion: 35 Los 5033

https://leunumismatik.com/de/lot/63/5033

Umayyad Caliphate. temp. Mu'awiya I ibn Abi Sufyan, AH 41-60 / AD 661-680. Drachm (Silver, 34 mm, 4.14 g, 3 h), Arab-Sasanian type, citing governor Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan (AH 45-54 / AD 665-673), ST (Staxr/Istakhr), AH 54 = AD 673/4. Draped bust resembling Khosrau II to right, wearing an elaborate mural crown; behind head, ‘GDE / ʾp̄zwt’ (‘[may his] glory increase’ in Pahlavi); before head, ‘zyyʾt / Y ʾbwswp[y]ʾn’ (‘Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan’ in Pahlavi); in the outer margin, ‘bism Allāh – rabbī’ (‘In the name of Allah, my Lord’ in Arabic). Rev. Fire altar with ribbons, flanked by two attendants; above altar, star and crescent; to left, date in Pahlavi; to right, ‘ST’ (abbreviation for ‘Staxr’, the name of the mint in Pahlavi); traces of ink graffiti in the margin. Album 8. Toned. Minor deposits, hairlines and flan faults on the edge, otherwise, extremely fine.

From an important collection of Arab-Sasanian coins.
Startpreis:25 CHF
Zuschlag:45 CHF

366719.description:
Abbasid, dirham. 248h.
Found in Kouvola, Finland. The coin belongs to the archaeological collections of the Finnish Heritage Agency.

The reverse is very weakly struck, perhaps with a worn die, since two inner circles can be distinguished on the reverse, as well as two really faint lines in the centre. These lines are, however, illegible and, when examined under a loupe, appear merely as almost straight transverse lines. Look also #305193.

 Umayyad Caliphate. temp. Mu'awiya I ibn Abi Sufyan, AH 41-60 / AD 661-680. Drachm (Silver, 32 mm, 4.09 g, 3 h), Arab-Sasanian type, citing governor ʿUbayd Allah ibn Ziyad (AH 54-64 / AD 673-683), al-Basra, AH 57 = AD 676/7. Draped bust resembling Khosrau II to right, wearing an elaborate mural crown; behind head, ‘GDE / ʾp̄zwt'’ (‘[may his] glory increase’ in Pahlavi); before head, ‘ʾwbytʾlʾ / Y zyyʾtʾn’ = ‘Ubaydālā ī Ziyādān’ (‘ʿUbayd Allah son of Ziyad’ in Pahlavi); in the outer margin, ‘bism Allāh’ (‘In the name of Allah’ in Arabic). Rev. Fire altar with ribbons, flanked by two attendants; above altar, star and crescent; to left, date in Pahlavi; to right, ‘bclʾ’ = ‘Basra’ (‘al-Basra’ in Pahlavi). Album 12. Toned. Very minor doubling and flan faults on the edge, otherwise, extremely fine.

From an important collection of Arab-Sasanian coins.

367499.description:
Umayyad Dynasty

Anonymous (Temp. 'Abd al-Malik b. Marwan, AH 65-86 / 685-705 CE).

Solidus, without mint or date (but struck in Damascus circa AH 72-74). Three standing figures, as on Byzantine solidi showing Heraclius and his two sons; each crowned and holding in his right hand an orb surmounted by a globe (in place of the cross on the Byzantine prototype) / "bismillah la ilaha illa Allah wahdahu Muhammad rasul Allah". Staff surmounted by globe, on four steps. In field to left and right: B – I. 4,36g. Artuk 5; Bernardi 5; Lavoix 26; Miles, Earliest Arab Gold Coinage type B; Qatar 198; SICA 1, 607; Walker p.18, B.2.

Of the utmost rarity. Good very fine.

Provenance: Spink Zurich (18 February 1986), 87.

The first gold coin to bear the Kalima. Syria, Jordan and Egypt had been part of the Byzantine currency system, based on gold solidi and copper folles. Local cities in Syria, Jordan and Palestine began to issue their own copies of Byzantine folles. From AH 55 or so, the first copper coins with Arabic legends start to appear. By contrast with Arab-Byzantine copper coins, which were clearly produced in very large quantities, it seems that gold coins were never issued in significant numbers. While the caliph was apparently content for governors to strike Arab-Byzantine copper coins to meet local demand, issuing a gold coinage would have been another matter and one which would have required official approval. A small number of 'de-Christianized' Byzantine solidi have survived, all very close copies of seventh century Byzantine prototypes with the minimum of modification to remove overtly Christian symbols. The coin offered here is a very different proposition from these earlier patterns and is surely to be regarded as part of the first stage of 'Abd al-Malik's series of reforms which ultimately led to the adoption of a uniform silver and gold coinage throughout the Islamic world.
367499.keywords: `Abd al-Malik bin Marwán 65-86 h /685-705 AV dínár Dimašq

368047.description:
Found in Armenia.

Vardanyan, Aram. The Administration of the ‘Abbāsid North and the Evidence of Copper Coins (AH 142–218 / AD 759–833)
American Journal of Numismatics (1989-)
Vol. 28 (2016), pp. 201-230

p. 205:
Abdallāh ibn Muḥammad. According to the literary sources, Muḥammad 
ibn Zuhayr ibn Musayyib al-Ḍabbī, a former governor of Egypt in the 
790s ad,15 was the last governor appointed to Armīniyah by Hārūn 
al-Rashīd.16 His rule was short as a new governor was appointed to replace 
him in the same year. Silver dirhams prove that in ah 194–195 (ad 809–811) 
the province was controlled by Asad ibn Yazīd, who had been appointed 
governor of Armīniyah ten years before. he administrative authority of 
Asad was not limited to Armīniyah alone but also included the neighboring 
province of Arrān, where his deputy may have been a certain Mazyad cited 
on some rare dirhams.17 Similarly, a fals of Dabīl struck in the name of a 
previously unknown ‘Abdallāh ibn Muḥammad in ah 194 (ad 809–810) 
raises the question of whose authority, if not his own, this represented. Taking 
into account that ‘Abdallāh’s name appears on coins within the inscription 
--------, one can assume that he served as governor in Armīniyah. 
However, with the only help of available copper coins it is impossible to 
determine precisely the length of ‘Abdallāh’s governorship. New coins with 
his name may shed more light on the duration of his rule in the region. 

p. 224
37. Dabīl, ah 194, ‘Abdallāh ibn Muḥammad.

368285.description:
UMAYYADEN, KALIFEN IN DAMASKUS

Al-Walid I., 705-715. AV-Dinar, 94 AH (= 712/713), spanische Münzstätte; 3,33 g IN Nd NIN dZ NZ dS N dA (In nomine Domini non Deus nisi Deus solus non Deus alius) Achtstrahliger Stern//HI Z FRT IN SPN AN CXIIII (Hic solidus feritus in Spania anno XCIIII) Horizontale Legende: NdC XI (indictiones XI). Walker 181; Album, Checklist 122

Von großer Seltenheit. Avers min. dezentriert, leicht korrodiert, sonst gutes sehr schön

Die Prägung fällt in die Zeit der islamischen Expansion in Nordafrika und Spanien. Im Jahr 711 wurden die Westgoten in der entscheidenden Schlacht am Rio Guadalete besiegt und die Hauptstadt Toledo eingenommen. In den neu eroberten Gebieten wurden Goldmünzen im Stil der byzantinischen Solidi geprägt. Einige Golddinare wie unser Stück tragen in lateinischer Form das islamische Glaubensbekenntnis, daß es nur einen Gott gibt. Zudem beachten sie das Gebot der Hadithen, keine Lebewesen abzubilden. Lehmann, R., Islamische Münzen und ihre Inschriften: Der Aufstieg der Umayyaden, Teil 1, Münzen & Papiergeld 3, 2007, S. 17-24.

368289.description:
Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 11 23-24 Oct 2025; lot 3.
Estimate: 2000 USD
Pre-reform issues, Arab-Sasanian. Salm b. Ziyad. Circa AH 61-65 / AD 680-684. AR Drachm (33.7mm, 3.32 g, 9h). MRW (Marw) mint. Dated AH 65 (AD 684/5). Obverse margin: – / bism allah allah / akbar / –. Bactrian ambero (Anbir) in first quarter of reverse margin. Malek, Arab-Sasanian 852; Album 18 var. Near VF, mount removed from edge. Extremely rare.
Ex Morton & Eden 73 (23 April 2015), lot 7.

Album has ingeniously suggested that this extremely rare issue bears two different mint-names - Marw in Pahlawi on the obverse, and Anbir in Bactrian on the reverse - because the coin was issued at Marw, but struck under the auspices of the Hephthalites, whose capital was at Anbir (SICA 1, p.23).

This appears to be the earliest known Islamic coin to bear the famous slogan Allah Akbar. 
Sold $3,750
368289.keywords: Salm b Ziyad Merw Marw Anbir Amber

368290.description:
Ex CNG , Islamic Auction 11 23-24 Oct 2025; lot 4.
Estimate: 5000 USD
Pre-reform issues, Arab-Sasanian. al-Musayyib b. Shihr (?). fl. AH 79-80 / AD 698-700. AR Drachm (28.6mm, 1.85 g, 3h). MRW (Marw) mint. Dated AH 80 (AD 699/700). Obverse margin: – / bism allah / – / –. cf. Malek p.307, Fig. 9.42 (dated AH 79); Album A38. Broken and repaired, mount removed from edge. Near VF. Extremely rare, the date believed unrecorded.

The name of this governor is not certain because the Pahlavi name-legend itself is ambiguous. Album has proposed al-Musayyib b. Shihr, while Sears suggested al-Musayyab b. Shahr (or Shahl). No individual with this name is known, but he was presumably either a rebel or sub-governor based at Marw.

Like the rare drachms of 'Abd al-Rahman b. 'Abdallah struck at Kufa in AH 79, it appears that this coin was struck to the weight of the post-Reform Umayyad dirham rather than to that of the older Sasanian drachm. Since post-Reform dirhams of circa 2.9g had been introduced at Marw in AH 79, it would not be surprising that drachms struck there in the following year should also adopt this new standard. 
 Sold $17,000

368589.description:
ISLAMIC WORLD: UMAYYAD-CALIPHATE OF DAMASCUS
Al-Andalus Coins

Semissis o 1/2 Dinar. 95-98 H. (713-717 d.C.). al-Walid I ibn ´ Abd al-Malik o Suleiman ibn ´ Abd al-Malik. Ceca incierta en norte de África. Anv.: S [[h7]]S NISVNS CV (NN) alrededor de SIMI[[h0]]IS (todas las S excepto la primera en la leyenda central retrógradas) ``non est Deus nisi unus cui non est alius similis´´. Rev.: (NN) [[a8]]S [[h7]]S NISV [[h7]]SCVI N S A (todas las S retrógradas) ``non est Deus nisi unus Deus cui non Socius Alius´´. Cruz transformada sobre tres escalones. 2,07 grs. AU. 

La característica más distintiva de estas monedas es la cruz cristiana modificada, generalmente situada en el anverso. Esta cruz suele estar dispuesta sobre tres escalones, elemento que probablemente posee un significado religioso, y tal vez también jerárquico o imperial. La modificación del diseño original de la cruz parece reflejar una fusión entre la iconografía cristiana bizantina y ciertas influencias árabes. Los califatos, aunque mayoritariamente islámicos, gobernaban amplios territorios donde persistían tradiciones cristianas, lo que favoreció la conservación -aunque transformada- de motivos bizantinos en las emisiones locales. La cruz de tres escalones deriva directamente de la cruz bizantina tradicional, frecuente en las monedas de los emperadores orientales. Con la expansión árabe y la absorción de los antiguos dominios bizantinos, los nuevos gobernantes adoptaron y reinterpretaron estos símbolos, introduciendo ligeras variaciones en su forma y proporción. Los escalones podrían aludir a una elevación espiritual o jerarquía divina, nociones que podían armonizar tanto con las concepciones cristianas como con las islámicas del poder y la autoridad religiosa. En el aspecto ponderal, el número de escalones bajo la barra central también adquiere relevancia: indica la denominación de la pieza y corresponde, respectivamente, a fracciones de dinar -semisses y tremisses-, reflejando un sistema metrológico heredado de la tradición bizantina. MUY RARA. Bernardi-21; Walker, Arab-Byzantine, 168; A-120.1. MBC+.

370066.description:
Obolos Auction 39, Lot 886
https://nomosag.com/obolos-39/886

ISLAMIC, Umayyad Caliphate. temp. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, AH 65-86 / AD 685-705. Pashiz (Bronze, 19 mm, 3.21 g, 5 h), Anonymous (Ibn al-Ash'ath?), Susa / Shush / al-Sus (Iran, Khuzestan), 82 AH = 701/2 AD. Standing figure, both hands raised next to the head in the form of “Du’ā” (supplication); In Pahlavi to left: šwš (Susa); to right: lwb'k (ravāg = current). Rev. In three lines in Kufic: بسم الله / سنة اثنين / و ثمنين (In the name of Allah, in the year 82). Gyselen type 41. Zeno #281650. Third known example on the market. Extremely rare and of historical interest! Smoothed, otherwise, good fine.

This exceptional coin type was previously described as depicting a standing caliph; however, there is no evidence to attribute this piece to caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, especially considering another known coin type struck in Susa with the typical characteristics of the caliph, with his sword and whip hanging to his side (Gyselen 39). Instead, it seems that the figure is pointing to a different personality. Both hands are raised next to the head in the form of “Du’ā” (supplication), most probably with the back of the hands pointed to the head, as seen on other specimens. In Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh), this form of prayer is known when asking for supplication and salvation with complete submission to what God has decreed, the relief from hardship or when asking God for rain.
A possible attribution is that this coin was issued by Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn al-Ash'ath, a former Umayyad military commander who later led a failed revolt from Sistan against Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, the governor of Iraq, which ultimately even led to a rebellion against the entire Marwanid rule. Marching towards Iraq, he defeated a first army of al-Hajjaj at Tustar, not far away from Susa, and entered Basra victorious just at the end of 81 AH. But this did not last long, only a few months. In 82 AH, his army was defeated, and he withdrew to Kufa, where he took control of the city. Finally, in 83 AH, he was overwhelmed by the Syrian Umayyad army, and the revolt was broken down. Ibn al-Ash'ath fled eastward with some remaining men back to Susa. It seems that Susa was used from the beginning of the revolt as a sort of settlement and retreat camp for his army. One of the reports mentions that he was captured by Zunbil (the king of Zabulistan), who had agreed with Al-Hajjaj to his extradition. Fearing an encounter with Al-Hajjaj, he committed suicide.
It seems reasonable to assume that Ibn al-Ash'ath, in the context of his revolt, is depicted on this coin type, seeking God's help and victory in these difficult times. Probably, the coin was struck just after his entrance into Basra when news reached Susa, serving as a reminder for the people that God is on his side and that his prayer was accepted. The geographical and historical context at least allows to think in the direction of such an interpretation.

ISLAMIC, Umayyad Caliphate. temp. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, AH 65-86 / AD 685-705. Fals (Bronze, 12 mm, 2.76 g, 3 h), Uncertain mint in North Africa, circa AH 80-85 / AD 700-704. Two crowned facing imperial busts of the emperor Heraclius with his son and co-emperor Heraclius Constantine in the center; In the margin: Latin legend describing the oneness of God. Rev. T-bar on three steps in the center; In the margin: Latin legend glorifying one God. Album 118. Cf. Lavoix, Khalifes Orientaux 115-119. Very rare! Very fine.

From the Collection of Mr. Beat A. Klein, acquired from Bank Leu in the 1980s.

This very rare North African Fals has been the subject of discussion, with differing opinions. The question is: do we actually see a cross instead of a T-bar on the steps on the reverse? If so, this would be a unique find in the early North African Islamic coinage, never seen before. However, it could also be some sort of striking defect, playing with our imagination. What can be said with certainty is that this particular reverse die is not listed in the known catalogues or among an important collection which has been examined.

372559.description:
Ex Pars Coins E-Sale 46 11 Dec 2025 , lot 355.
Starting price: 2500 USD
ARAB-SASANIAN, Abdullah Ibn Zubayr (Rival Khalif of Umayyads). AR Dirhem (3.94 gm; 33 mm). Obverse, Sasanian Khosrau II style bust turning right, name and tile in Pahlavi " \"apdwla-i zubiran amīr-i -wurrishnikān", (Abdallah ibn Zubair-Commander of the faithful), Apzuty and GDH symbols behind the crown, phrase in Arabic " Bismillah -e Vali al-Amr" (in the name of Allah whose will shall be done) reverse, fire altar with attendants, mint: KRMAN-GRM (Garmsaar), year 56. Malek, Arab-Sasanian p. 151, note 305; SCC 123; Album 34C. Extremely rare type with Pahlavi name of Governor and phrase in Arabic: Bismillah-e Vali al – Amr, Type II of two types of this coin. The Type I replaces the name of the Governor with Shahadah for Prophet Mohammad written in Arabic. Similar coin sold in CNG Islamic Coins Auction 1 for $15,000 and in Islamic Auction 4 for $7,000. There is no example of this type on any web archives. Slight bent at 7 o'clock. Choice EF. Lightly toned.
Lot unsold

373052.description:
Abbasid Governors, Transoxiana: Ma'bad b. Khalil & al-Mahdi Muhammad (765 AD) AE Fals, Bukhara (Album-320; Nastich p. 20, fig. 16). Obv: Within a beaded circle, لا إله إلا الله وحده (There is no God but Allah alone); below ✶; in margin, separated by three annulets at intervals, ◉ بسم الله ضرب ◉ ببخارا فی سنة ◉ ثمان و اربعين و مئة (In the name of Allah, [this coin] was struck of Bukhara in the year eight and forty and [one] hundred)

Rev: Within beaded circle, محمد رسول الله (Muhammad is the apostle of Allah), below Bukhara tamgha; in margin, أمر به معبد في ولية ألمهدى ولي عهد المسلمين محمد بن أمير ألمؤمنين (Ordered by the amir Ma’bad in the service of al-Mahdi, crown prince of the Muslims, Muhammad son of the commander of the faithful)

Reference

Nastich, Vladimir N., A Survey of the Abbasid Copper Coinage of Transoxiana, Nastich, 2012
Nastich, Vladimir N., Early Islamic Copper Coinage of Transoxiana - A Generic Survey Focused on Newly Discovered Coin Types, 3rd Simone Assemani Symposium on Islamic Coins, 2012

373182.description:
Ex Stephen Album Rare Coins Auction 54 22-25 Jan, lot 138.
Starting price: 12 000 USD
ARAB-SASANIAN: 'Abd al-Malik b. Abi Shay(kh), fl. 692, AR drachm (2.68g), APRShT (Abarshahr, = Nishapur)), AH72, A-29, clipped down to slightly below the post-reform Umayyad standard, clear name, mint & date, stylistically identical to the first known example (sold in our Auction 17, lot 104, back in 2013, now Zeno-128271) but struck from a different pair of dies, VF, RRRR. This is the second known example of this governor, struck during the chaotic years in the early AH70s, when the collapse of the Zubayrid opposition and the petty rivalry in Khorasan and Sijistan after the brief Hephthalite invasions simultaneously troubled the eastern regions of the caliphate. The named governor is perhaps 'Abd al-Malik b. Abi Shaykh al-Qurayshi, who was active in the Kish battle in Central Asia in AH80.
Price realized: 36 000 USD

373185.description:
Ex Stephen Album Rare Coins Auction 54 22-25 Jan, lot 142.
Starting price: 260 USD
ARAB-SASANIAN: 'Amr b. Laqit, 702, AR drachm (3.85g), GLM-KLMAN ("warm kirman"), AH83, A-39, Malek-599, obverse margin bism Allah ShYLWY // 'amr lillah, standard reverse with full bold mint & date, extremely rare mint for this ruler (only KLMAN-LAM for Narmashir is relatively available for this ruler), lovely VF, RR. The Pahlavi word PYLWC, "victorious", appears before the governor's name, and the Arabic slogan 'umr lillah, "eternity belongs to God" in ObQ3. 373210.description:
Samanid multiple dirham, Nasr II b. Ahmad (AH 301-331/914-943 AD), Andaraba, mentioning the Caliph Al-Muqtadir (AH 295–320/908–932 AD).
So this would be a very early multiple, issued between 301 and 320. Some remarkable elements: 
- It is smallish for the type, 36 mm, and weighs only 4.6g, or about twice the weight of a dirham.
- Remarkable also: it has a pearl rim on the obverse; and there seem to be no words or signs outside the outer borders - which is very unusual.

374305.description:
Mamluk (Bahri). Muhammad I (al-Nasir Nasir al-Din Muhammad) (1st reign, 693-694 A.H. = 1293-1294 A.D.; 2nd reign 698-708 A.H. = 1299-1309 A.D.; 3rd reign, 709-741 A.H. = 1310-1341 A.D.)

Balog 261, Plate X 261a-b; Album 922

AE fals; Dimashq/Damascus mint, dated 30 A.H. (730 A.H.) = 1329-1330 A.D. (3rd reign); 2.99 g., 18.97 mm. max., 270°

Obv.: Circular line border; الملك الناصر (al-Malik al-Naasir = King al-Nassir) between two horizontal floral-scroll ornaments.

Rev.: Circular line in circle of dots border; Clockwise marginal legend: ضرب بدمشق سنة ثلثين (= darib bi dimashq sanat thuluthayn = struck in Damascus in the year thirty), center: round shield, in which concave, five-petaled rosette.

Muhammad I, the ninth Bahri Mamluk sultan, was the youngest son of Sultan Qala'un (of Turkic origin from the Kipchak tribe) and a mother of Mongol origin, and the brother of Sultan Khalil. After the assassination of Khalil in December 1293 by a faction lead by Lajin, Muhammad became sultan at age nine. In December 1294 Muhammad's regent, Kitbugha, deposed Muhammad with the support of Lajin and installed himself as sultan. In 1296 Kitbugha was deposed by Lajin, who then ruled as a sultan until he was murdered in 1299. Muhammad was recalled and reinstated as sultan at age 14, although power was held by Baybars. In 1309 Muhammad, who sought to free himself from the domination of Baybars, withdrew from Egypt and attempted to have Baybars arrested. This failed and Baybars installed himself as sultan, ending Muhammad's second reign. His second reign was dominated by Mongol threats in the Levant. After only ten months an Egyptian mob forced Baybars to flee and Muhammad was reinstated. at age 24. He reigned until his death 31 years later. His third reign was the apogee of Mamluk power and the high-water mark of culture in Egypt since Ptolemaic Alexandria. Eight of his sons and four of his grandsons would be enthroned as sultans.

374452.description:
Morton & Eden Ltd Auction 95-96, Lot 60 
24 Oct 2018

ABBASID, AL-RASHID (170-193h), Dirham, 'al-Muhammadiya' (i.e. Bajunays) 183h. Reverse:, citing Sallam and Mahbub. Weight: 2.77g. Good very fine and extremely rare, apparently unpublished. Somewhat confusingly, the epithet 'al-Muhammadiya' was used to denote two different mint-towns at this time: Rayy, and Bajunays (vide Bates, M.L., 'A Second Muhammadiyya, and the four mints of the Bajunays mine,' JONS 209, Autumn 2011, pp.14-17). Coins can be attributed to one or the other according to the governors named on the reverse. Sallam is one of the longest-serving governors known on this issue, but Mahbub seems to be previously unknown.

Estimate: 300 GBP
Price realized: 420 GBP

374782.description:
Baldwin's Islamic Coin Auction 20
Lot 210 

† ISLAMIC COINS. ABBASID CALIPHATE. temp. al-Rashid, Silver Dirham, Arran 189h, citing Huzayma b. Hazim, 2.74g (Low 189). Nearly extremely fine. Ubayd Allah bin al-Mahdi was a younger brother of the Caliph Harun al-Rashid. According to numismatic evidence he was made governor of Armenia in the year 172 and remained there until 175 H. This coin provides evidence that he was subsequently governor of Arran in 182, after which he seems to have disappeared from history. £300-350
374782.keywords: Abbasid AR dirham Arran 189 AH Khuzayma+Bashr

375102.description:
https://www.numisbids.com/sale/10406/lot/3068

'Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Muktafi, AH 289-295 / AD 902-908. Dinar (Gold, 25 mm, 4.41 g, 10 h), citing the Abbasid caliph al-Muktafī bi-llāh, Hims, AH 292 = AD 904/5. Central field, in three lines:
lā ilāha illā / Allāh waḥdahu / lā sharīka lahu
('There is no god but God alone, He has no associate' in Arabic).

Inner margin:
bism Allāh ḍuriba hādhā al-dīnār bi-Ḥimṣ sanat ithnatayn wa-tisʿīn wa-miʾatayn
('In the name of God, this dinar was struck in Ḥimṣ in the year two hundred and ninety-two' in Arabic).

Outer margin:
li-llāh al-amr min qablu wa-min baʿd wa-yawmaʾidhin yafraḥ al-muʾminūn bi-naṣr Allāh
('To God belongs the command before and after, and on that day the believers will rejoice in the help of God' in Arabic). Large pellet at bottom. Rev. Central field, in five lines:
li-llāh / Muḥammad / rasūl / Allāh / al-Muktafī bi-llāh
('For God / Muhammad is the Messenger of God / al-Muktafi bi-llah' in Arabic).

Margin:
Muḥammad rasūl Allāh arsalahu bi-l-hudā wa-dīn al-ḥaqq li-yuẓhirahu ʿalā al-dīn kullihi wa-law kariha al-mushrikūn
('Muhammad is the Messenger of God, whom He sent with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion, even though the polytheists may dislike it' in Arabic). Pellet in centre. Album 243.1. Bernardi -, cf. 226Gd (date not listed). Extremely rare for the mint, and apparently unpublished for this year. An exceptionally well centred and lustrous example. A tiny die break on the obverse, otherwise, virtually as struck.

By the final decade of the third century AH, Abbasid authority in Syria had been severely weakened. The Tulunids, ruling effectively from Egypt, had extended their power deep into the Syrian provinces, and mints such as Ḥimṣ operated outside direct caliphal control. Gold issues of Ḥimṣ dated 290 AH confirm that the city was still striking in the name of the Tulunid regime at that time.

The rapid collapse of Tulunid power shortly thereafter allowed the Abbasids to reassert control over Syria. The coinage provides unusually clear evidence for this transition. The present dinar, struck at Ḥimṣ in 292 AH, belongs to the earliest securely dated phase of restored Abbasid mint activity in the city. Its importance lies not merely in its rarity but in its chronological position: it demonstrates that within scarcely two years, the mint had resumed operation under full Abbasid authority and within the standard caliphal gold monetary formula.

Gold coins from Ḥimṣ under the Abbasids are extremely rare, and the present piece dated AH 292 appears to be unpublished. Unlike major administrative centers such as Madīnat al-Salām or Miṣr, Syrian provincial mints produced only limited gold output, likely tied to fiscal or military exigencies rather than sustained commercial minting. The survival of so few specimens suggests that production was brief and possibly transitional.

377622.description:
ARAB SASANIAN. Anonymous. AE. Pashiz. Struck circa AD 690-710. ( 0.85g, 22.5mm, 12h )
 
Meaningless garbled legend, two crowned facing imperial busts, crowns adorned with a cross.
Reverse meaningless garbled legend, Patriarchal cross on three steps, star and crescent either side.
Ref: Album 42.
Good very fine, about a third of the flan chipped off.
 
The design of the coin is after the Byzantine gold solidus and copies coins of Heraclius ( AD 610-641 ) in particular issues jointly with his son Heraclius Constantine for types see Sear 734-748a. It should be noted that Heraclius' coins never show a Patriarchal cross on the reverse, it is invariably a cross potent on steps.

From sold listing: https://www.vcoins.com/en/stores/simeon/131/product/arab_sas...

SARC auction 55, lot 92

Original description:
ABBASID: al-Mu'tamid, 870-892, AR dirham (2.91g), Ra's al-'Ayn, AH277, A-240.2, citing the heir of the west al-Mufawwad on the obverse, with the name muhammad below, and the unusual title dhu'l-sayfayn ("possessor of the two swords") below the reverse; about 12% flat strike and some double-striking on the obverse; unpublished and probably unique, VF, RRR. We found that the title "dhu'l-sayfayn" appears only on dirhams struck at al-Mawsil, unusual dated AH276, and this is the first from Ra's al-'Ayn, located about 150 miles west of al-Mawsil.

378371.description:
Blog format digital humanities website linking to resources on Islamic history 600-1000 AD.

Website isn't currently being updated, but the information and links are still useful.

About page:
"
While large digitalization projects are a good thing, it also makes it increasingly difficult to keep track of what is happening in the field. By listing important databases and other sources, this website intends to help scholars in the field of Early Islam and the Late Antique Near East with that. The focus is on material sources and we hope to encourage the use of such sources to get a fuller understanding of the history of Islam.

The website originates in the work of the project, Embedding Conquest: Naturalising Muslim Rule in the Early Islamic Empire (600-1000) (PI Petra Sijpesteijn) at Leiden University funded by the European Research Council (ERC), grant agreement No 683194. However, work done on the site is not limited to the scope of the project. Instead, it is conceived as a tool linking communities of scholars, and collaboration is welcomed.

The project offers a strong example of how to move away from ‘traditional sources’ like literary texts and integrate a variety of material sources ranging from coins to potsherds to papyri. By placing items that were initially mostly collected for their esthetic value, in a wider historical context, new connections start to appear. While the focus on documentary evidence is relatively new in this field, we found that the availability of handbooks and overview websites is still limited. Additionally scholars might feel some anxiety to move into a ‘new field’. Where do you start, when you want to incorporate a variety of material sources that you have not worked with before into your research? That is why we made this website, as a starting point to incorporate material sources to supplement ‘traditional’ historical research. An inherent part of working with collections is also to question collection-activity. Where did certain artifacts come from and how did they end up in the collection they are in. For a short introduction on provenance, read our blog.

The site is intended to outlive the five-year project and we welcome collaboration. The site is updated by a team of editors and contributors who check and update content. If you are interested in getting involved, then send an email to Edmund Hayes with “Material Sources Website” in the subject line.
"

Coin resources category:
https://materialsourcesforearlyislamandlateantiqueneareast.h...

Blog:
https://emco.hcommons.org/

378435.description:
Martin Escudero, F., Casal García, M. T., Canto García, A. "Feluses, dírhams y monedas en el arrabal de Šaqunda (Córdoba): análisis y clasificación tipológica". Lucentum (Vol. XLII), Alicante 2023: 289-316. 

Measurements on page 303:
6mm, 1.6g

Dated to 92-108 A.H., with the mint as Al-Andalus (although obviously the coin doesn't say that).

Seven Frochoso XIV-a types found during the excavations, out of eighty fulus total. In other words, nearly 10% of the Umayyad AE coins found in major excavations at the capital of Al-Andalus were of this type. These results imply that the coins originated from the Iberian Peninsula and were not scarce issues. 

Authors attribute this type to the earlier period of conquest (saying that-- figural types were earlier, epigraphical types were later).

On page 296:
https://lucentum.ua.es/article/view/22039

378439.description:
Datación: Periodo gobernadores omeyas. 92-138 AH (711-756 dC)
Sin ceca y sin fecha.
Valor: Felús.
Catálogo: Frochoso XIV-a.
Conservación: BC
Metal: AE.
Peso: 1,11 gr.
Diámetro: 10 mm.
Posición cuño: 5 h.
Anverso: Cabeza de guerrero con casco a derecha.
Leyenda marginal:
الله رسول محمد
Muhammad rassul Alláh.
Mahoma enviado de Dios.
Reverso: Dentro de la grafila en forma de corona de laurel leyenda:
لا اله الا
الله وحده
لا شرك له
la ilāh illā / Allāh wahdahu / lā sharika lahu
No Dios sino / Dios sólo Él / No compañero para Él
Felús del periodo de conquista, probablemente el primero que acuñaron los musulmanes en la Península. Es la única moneda andalusí con una representación humana.
El personaje representado tiene un casco semiesférico provisto de un ala ancha, cuya anterior hacía de visera y la posterior de cubrenuca y las ínfulas. Las ínfulas tienen paralelos en las acuñaciones tardorromanas y y el casco puede ser un tipo general de los primeros siglos de la Edad Media, consistente en un capacete semiesférico con un reborde vuelto por detrás a modo de cubrenuca.
El citado personaje seguramente no sea nadie en concreto, pues no está representada la efigie de ningún soberano en las monedas musulmanas de oro y plata de la época, no es lógico que en las acuñaciones de cobre, de carácter fiduciario y local, se intentara representar al soberano o a un jefe local, por lo que más bien se trata de una imitación de un tipo de moneda de cobre anterior, conocido y admitido en el comercio a ambos lados del Estrecho.
La probable ceca emisora es Córdoba y la fecha de emisiones entre los años 98 y 108 H, aproximadamente.
Pátina verde

Source:
https://wearenumismatics.com/numismatica/coleccion-museion/0...

378443.description:

On page 64:
https://wearenumismatics.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Manq...
"
Felús Frochoso III-a = Walker P. 116 reacuñado sobre el cospel de un felús de cabeza de guerrero con casco. Frochoso XIV-a = Walker Th. 12. 

Subasta Áureo y Calicó. Sin peso ni medidas.

Tipo reacuñado: Felús Frochoso III-a = Walker P.116.

Anverso: (Allah la i)lah / (illa estrella cinco puntas) Allah / espiga a derecha.

Reverso: Muha(mmad ra)/ línea serpenteante/ (sul Allah)

Tipo original: felús base más antiguo sobre el que se ha acuñado. Felús Frochoso XIV-a = Walker Th. 12.

Anverso: la ilah illa/Allah wahdahu/(la shari)ka lahu

Reverso: Centro: Cabeza de guerrero con casco.

Orla: Muhammad (rasul) Allah

Posición de la reacuñación sobre el cospel del felús original. IAs o anversos e IIAs o reversos.

IA., o anverso Frochoso III-a = Walker P.116 sobre IIA., o reverso Frochoso XIV-a = Walker Th. 12.

IIA., o reverso Frochoso III-a= Walker P.116 sobre IA., o anverso Frochoso XIV-a = Walker Th. 12.

Atribución de ceca y cronología de cada tipo de felús:

- Tipo reacuñado: felús Frochoso III-a = Walker P.116. Serie más primitiva, se atribuye a al-Andalus y periodo de
acuñación a partir de 92 hégira.15

- Tipo cospel base: felús de la cabeza del guerrero, Frochoso XIV-a = Walker Th.12. Serie más primitiva de alAndalus y periodo de acuñación 92 a 108 Hégira.16

- Tipo cospel base: felús de la cabeza del guerrero, Frochoso XIV-a = Walker Th.12. Serie más primitiva de alAndalus y periodo de acuñación

378663.description:
Classical Numismatic Group, Electronic Auction 328, Lot 690

ISLAMIC, Umayyad Caliphate. temp. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan or al-Walid I. AH 65-96 / AD 685-715. Æ Fals (12mm, 1.47 g, 5h). Uncertain North African mint. Struck circa AH 80-89 (AD 699-708). Beginning of Kalima in three lines / Continuation of Kalima around helmeted head right. Walker p. 222, Th. 12; Album C122. Near VF, green patina with earthen deposits.

Although this type is sometimes attributed to Spain, Album (p. 39) notes that some specimens bear the mint name Tanja (Tangiers) at the end of the Arabic legend.

379210.description:
CNG Islamic auction 9, lot 125

Original description:
'Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Radi. AH 322-329 / AD 934-940. AV Dinar (22.4mm, 4.04 g, 4h). Isbahan mint. Dated AH 326? (AD 937/8). Obverse margin reads: bism Allah duriba hadha al-dinar sitt wa 'ashrin wa thalath mi'a. Cf. Bernardi 288Mb (known only for a unique specimen dated AH 324); Album 254.1. Crudely struck, centres weak. Good Fine. Of the highest rarity, apparently unpublished and believed unique.

The only other 'Abbasid dinar of al-Radi from Isbahan known to Bernardi was dated AH 324, and is of similarly crude style. On this piece, the word sanat has been omitted from the mint/date legend, and the unit of the date is poorly engraved; it has been read here as '6', because the final tooth is notably higher than the others, but might be intended for '3'.

Isbahan came under the control of the Buwayhids in AH 323, and standard Buwayhid dirhams naming 'Ali b. Buwayh were issued there in AH 323 and 324. However, 'Abbasid dirhams were being struck in Isbahan once again by AH 326, and it appears that that control of the city was disputed during al-Radi's reign. The crude style of both this dinar and the Bernardi specimen suggests that they may have been produced at temporary or unofficial mints.

380566.description:
Ex Stephen Album Rare Coins Auction 55 14-17 May, lot 51.
Starting price: 19 000 USD
ARAB-SASANIAN: Aslam (Asram) b. 'Anfawa, fl. 686, AR drachm (2.66g), GD (Jayy), AH67, A-F27, standard obverse with the Pahlavi name read as aslm i awpawa, though the patronymic seems more like swphan, with small Pahlavi monogram in ObQ1 // standard reverse with clear mint & date, clipped down to a later standard, VF. The only other known example is in the Fitzwilliam Museum, #CM.IS.31-R. This is the second known example. The Fitzwilliam example is illustrated by Hodge Malek in Volume I, p. 272, with a brief discussion of what little might be known of this governor.
Price realized: 37 500 USD

380567.description:
Ex Stephen Album Rare Coins Auction 55 14-17 May, lot 53.
Starting price: 10 000 USD
ARAB-SASANIAN: Anonymous, AR drachm (3.48g), AKWLA (al-Kufa), A-34G, Malek-12 (different dies), with muhammad rasul Allah replacing the governor's name right of the portrait, with bism Allah la ilah / illa Alla wahdahu filling ObQ2 and ObQ3 // mint name in the usual location, but undeciphered symbol or monogram replacing the date; 4th outer circle added on the reverse; exceedintly rare, only the 2nd known example! XF, RRRR. This is a newly discovered Arab-Sasanian drachm with "Muhammad Rasul Allah" instead of the ruler or governor's name before the obverse portrait, and only one of two known from the mint of AKWLA (al-Kufa). The three previously known versions (A-34D, 34E, 34F) are likely all produced during the AH70s (690s) and all are of extreme rarity.
Price realized: 26 000 USD

380568.description:
Ex Stephen Album Rare Coins Auction 55 14-17 May, lot 55.
Starting price: 350 USD
ARAB-SASANIAN: Khalid b. 'Abd Allah, ca. 692-694, AR drachm (3.66g), BCLA (al-Basra), AH74, A-24A, Malek, with muhammad rasul Allah in ObQ3, pellet after bism Allah in ObQ2; extra outer circle added around the reverse, used at Basra AH73-75, of which only AH73 is occasionally available; evenly worn, Fine, RRR.
Price realized: 1000 USD

380569.description:
Ex Stephen Album Rare Coins Auction 55 14-17 May, lot 56.
Starting price: 8000 USD
ARAB-SASANIAN: Khusraw type, 691-693, AR dirham (2.87g), Dimashq, AH72, A-D6, Malek-524, standard obverse with the name of Khusro right of the portrait, and the Islamic statement bism Alah / muhammad rasul / Allah in the margin // normal reverse (fire altar & two attendants), mint name to left, date written out to right, both in Arabic; clipped down to the post-reform Umayyad standard, VF, RRR. This is the first Islamic coin to bear the Hijri date written out in Arabic, always in Pahlavi for earlier dates.
Price realized: 10 000 USD

380570.description:
Ex Stephen Album Rare Coins Auction 55 14-17 May, lot 57.
Starting price: 9500 USD
ARAB-SASANIAN: Khusraw type, 691-693, AR dirham (3.12g), Dimashq, AH73, A-D6, cf. Malek-525, standard obverse with the name of Khusro right of the portrait, and the full Islamic statement bism Alah la ilah illa Allah muhammad rasul Allah filling the entire margin // normal reverse (fire altar & two attendants), mint name to left, date written out to right, both in Arabic; some light porosity, nearly XF, RRR. Malek-525 has the mint name right and the date left on the reverse, but most examples, including this piece and all of the 6 examples filed on CoinArchives, have the mint left and the date right.
Price realized: 14 000 USD

380571.description:
Ex Stephen Album Rare Coins Auction 55 14-17 May, lot 58.
Starting price: 260 USD
ARAB-SASANIAN: al-Hajjaj b. Yusuf, 694-713, AR drachm (3.84g), BYSh (Bishapur), AH81, A-35.2, very rare subtype, with the name al-Hajjaj repeated in Pahlavi (hagag) in ObQ3; evenly worn, Fine, RR.
Price realized: 550 USD

380572.description:
Ex Stephen Album Rare Coins Auction 55 14-17 May, lot 60.
Starting price: 3250 USD
ARAB-ARMENIAN: Anonymous, early 700s, AR zuzun (2.76g), NM, stylized year "6", A-M97, in the name of the Sasanian king Hormizd IV, with the full Shahada filling the obverse margin after the phrase bism Allah, and with the denomination ZWZWN, Aramaic for "drachm", instead of a mint name on the standard position on the reverse, excellent strike for this type, XF, RRRR. There are three genuine examples of this type with the full Shahada posted on Zeno, #96964 with the additional phrase "rabbi Allah" added on the reverse margin (sold in M&E Auction 48, Lot 1), #153562 with "rabbi Allah" instead of ZWZWN at the mint location on the reverse, and #314067, without "rabbi Allah" (sold in our Auction 46, lot 173). The full Shahada was introduced on the Arab-Sasanian coinage during the governorship of al-Hajjaj b. Yusuf (694-713), whence it seems likely that this type could not have been introduced before 694, replaced shortly afterwards by the type that replaced the name Hormizd with Muhammad (A-E97) and the Arabic word "waf" in the obverse margin, introduced circa 700. The prototype was the relatively common Sasanian-Armenian type in the name of Hormizd, usually with year "6" and the phrase ZWZWN in lieu of a mint name (e.g., Zeno-17577).
Price realized: 3500 USD

380597.description:

Umayyad Caliphate, Silver coinage. AR Drachm (25mm, 2.66 g, 9h). Countermarked issue of al-Harith b. Surayj, rebel in Khorasan and Transoxiana. Manadhir mint. Dated AH 94 (AD 712/3). Senmurv head left countermark (cf. Göbl, Hunnen KM 11) at 6h on obverse. For coin: Klat 619; for c/m: S. Sears, "The Revolt of al-Ḥārith ibn Surayj and the Countermarking of Umayyad Dirhams in Early Eighth Century CE Khurāsān, " in Paul Cobb, ed. The Lineaments of Islam. Studies in Honor of Fred McGraw Donner, pp. 377-405. Iridescent toning. Coin Near VF; countermark Good VF. 
Price realized: 275 USD
